big-o.name: Big O Notation
big-o.desc: A language for describing how time and memory grow as input size n grows — ignoring constants and lower-order terms. The first thing an interviewer asks after you propose an algorithm.
big-o.q: Is O(2n) the same as O(n)?
big-o.qsub: Why do we ignore constants and lower-order terms? · How do you measure space complexity including recursion stack? · When is O(n log n) actually slower than O(n²) in practice?
big-o.what:
Both functions do exactly the same work. For 10 items, both respond instantly. For 1,000,000 items, one answers instantly while the other takes 4 minutes. The difference isn't how elegant the code is — it's how the work grows.

Big O is the way to describe that growth: as the input size n grows, how fast does the work grow? It doesn't give you seconds — it gives you the shape of the growth.

That's why a stopwatch is useless: your laptop may be fast, the interviewer's may be slow, and the server may be different again. But O(n²) remains O(n²) on every machine.
big-o.analogy: Picture a wedding with 100 guests. You shake each guest's hand once — 100 handshakes, O(n). Now every guest meets every other guest — 4,950 handshakes. If you double the guests (200), you need four times as many handshakes. That's the pain of O(n²).
big-o.why:
The interviewer asks "what's the complexity?" because that one question shows whether you just wrote the code or actually thought about it. If you can't state the cost of your own solution, you can't improve it either.

And in real work, that same O(n²) loop takes 200 ms on staging (100 rows) but 30 seconds on prod (50,000 rows). Same code, different data — and you only find out when the customer screams.

How to think:

1. Identify n — the part of the input that can get big: array length, string size, tree nodes.
2. Count the loops and recursive calls. A loop inside a loop = multiply (n × n). One loop after another = add (n + n).
3. In a sum, keep only the biggest term — n² + n + 50 becomes n². Because at n = 10,000, n² is 100 million and n is just 10 thousand — the small term vanishes.
4. Throw away constants — 3n → O(n).
5. Count space separately: extra arrays + recursion depth. Most people forget this step.
where: Array index, hash lookup · space: constant
Binary search on sorted input · space: constant
Single linear pass · space: usually constant
Merge/Quick sort, heap ops · space: O(n) for merge

qa.q: Is O(2n) the same as O(n)?
qa.a: Yes — we drop constant factors. Both describe linear growth; the constant doesn't change how the curve scales, and for large n the gap between 2n and n is negligible compared to the gap between n and n².

qa.q: What is the complexity of a while loop that halves n each iteration?
qa.a: O(log n) — each step removes half the input, so it takes log2(n) steps to reach 1. Binary search is the canonical example.

arrays.name: Arrays in JavaScript
arrays.desc: Contiguous-indexed storage with O(1) access by index. In JS, arrays are objects with length tracking — methods like push/pop/splice/slice cover most manipulation you'll need.
arrays.q: Why is unshift O(n) but push O(1)?
arrays.qsub: How do you detect if an array is sorted in O(n)? · How do you rotate an array right by k in O(1) space? · What does arr.slice() with no args return?
arrays.what:
Think of a shelf with numbered boxes — box 0, box 1, box 2. Need box 5? Just reach for it. No need to look at the whole shelf. That's arr[5] — O(1), whether the array has 10 elements or 1,000,000.

But one thing people miss: in JS an array is not a special native structure. It's just an object whose keys are numbers, and a length counter that updates automatically.

All the cost comes from this. Work at the end (push/pop) — nothing shifts, O(1). Work at the beginning or middle (shift/unshift/splice) — everything else has to shift one position, O(n).
arrays.analogy: In a train coach, you go directly to your seat by seat number — O(1). But if you insert a new passenger at seat 1, everyone else has to move one seat forward — O(n). That's what unshift does.
arrays.why:
The interviewer looks for two things. First: which methods modify the original array (push, splice, sort, reverse) and which return a new array (map, filter, slice). This confusion is the most common source of production bugs — mutating React state prevents a re-render.

Second: cost. If you use shift in a loop to "remove elements from the start of an array", it silently becomes O(n²).

How to think:

1. As soon as an array is created, the engine builds an object whose keys are the index numbers and sets a hidden length counter.
2. When you read arr[i], the engine resolves that key directly to a memory address — a constant-time step.
3. On push, the engine looks at length, places the value in the next slot, and increments the counter — nothing shifts.
4. When you splice in the middle, the engine shifts every remaining element one position — hence O(n).
5. map/filter/slice create a completely new array and do not touch the original.

qa.q: Why is unshift O(n) but push O(1)?
qa.a: push appends at the end, where the array has spare capacity, so it's amortized O(1). unshift inserts at index 0, forcing every element to shift right by one — O(n).

qa.q: In-place vs creating a new array — when does it matter?
qa.a: In-place avoids O(n) extra space and often lets you solve with two pointers in one pass. Problems like Rotate Array and Set Matrix Zeroes explicitly ask for in-place to test this.

objects-map-set.name: Objects, Map, and Set
objects-map-set.desc: Hash-based structures giving O(1) average lookups, inserts, and deletes. Map preserves insertion order and accepts any key type; Set enforces uniqueness. The single most-used tool in interviews.
objects-map-set.q: Map vs plain Object — which do you reach for and why?
objects-map-set.qsub: Why does checking Set.has beat indexOf on an array? · How do you build a frequency map of characters in a string? · What happens when you set a key that already exists in a Map?
objects-map-set.what:
Think of a phone's contact list: type a name and the number appears instantly. Whether you have 5 contacts or 5,000, the speed is the same. The phone doesn't scan the whole list; it converts the name directly to its location using a formula (hashing).

Object, Map, Set — all operate on the same principle. So insert, lookup, and delete are all O(1) on average.

The only difference: Object turns keys into strings. Map accepts any key and remembers insertion order. Set stores only values and automatically removes duplicates.
objects-map-set.analogy: Like the index at the back of a book — if you want to find “Recursion” you don’t flip through the whole book, you go straight to page 142 from the index. The hash function is that index.
objects-map-set.why:
This is the most useful tool in interviews. Whenever your solution turns into an O(n²) “for each element, search all the others” problem, the answer is almost always a hash.

Second test: choose the right one among Map, Object, and Set, and explain why you chose it.

How to think:

1. As soon as a key is inserted, a hash function converts it into a number.
2. That number decides which bucket in the internal array will be used.
3. On lookup the same hash function runs again — it goes directly to the correct bucket, no full data scan.
4. If two keys produce the same hash (collision) the engine creates a small list inside that bucket — so the worst case is O(n), average O(1).
5. Map keeps an extra linked structure so that insertion order is also remembered.

qa.q: Map vs plain Object — which do you reach for and why?
qa.a: Map. It accepts any key type, preserves insertion order, has a size property, and avoids prototype-key collisions (like a key named 'constructor'). For simple string-keyed counting either works, but Map is the safer habit.

qa.q: Two Sum — why does a Map make it O(n)?
qa.a: Store each number with its index as you scan. For each x, check if target - x is already in the map — that lookup is O(1), so one pass suffices instead of a nested loop.

recursion.name: Recursion
recursion.desc: A function that calls itself with a smaller version of the same problem. Two mandatory parts: a base case that stops, and a recursive case that makes progress toward it. Backbone of trees, backtracking, and DP.
recursion.q: What is the space complexity of recursion?
recursion.qsub: What happens if a recursive function has no base case? · How deep can recursion go in JS before RangeError? · Why is naive Fibonacci exponential but memoized version O(n)?
recursion.what:
Imagine cleaning a wardrobe full of boxes, where those boxes contain more boxes. You don't think of the whole wardrobe at once — you say "clean this box, and do the same work again for the box inside".

Recursion is exactly that: a function calls itself with a smaller input. Two parts are always needed — base case (where to stop) and recursive case (how to make it smaller).

And here is something most people forget in interviews: every call leaves a frame on the call stack. So recursion's space is not O(1) but O(depth) — even if you never create an array.
recursion.analogy: Matryoshka doll — each doll contains a smaller doll. Keep opening until you reach the smallest solid doll (base case). Then close them one by one while coming back up — this is the unwind, and this forms your answer.
recursion.why:
Trees, graphs, backtracking, DP — all these topics sit on top of recursion. If you don't know recursion, nothing from Phase 4 onward will make sense.

And the bug that catches candidates fastest in interviews is this: missing or wrong base case → RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.

How to think:

1. As soon as a function is called, a new frame is pushed onto the call stack with its local variables.
2. First, the base case is checked — if the input is already in its simplest form, return the value directly.
3. If no base case is found, the function calls itself again with a smaller input.
4. This chain continues until a base case appears — the stack keeps growing upward. The maximum height of the stack is your space.
5. Once the base case is hit, values return downwards, and each pending call finishes its work and pops from the stack.
where: O(depth) space · space: d is recursion depth
O(n) · space: O(h) where h = height

qa.q: What is the space complexity of recursion?
qa.a: O(depth) for the call stack, not O(1). A function recursing n deep uses O(n) stack space even if it takes no other memory. That's why deep recursion can stack overflow while an iterative loop won't.

qa.q: How do you convert recursion to iteration?
qa.a: Replace the call stack with an explicit stack (LIFO for DFS-style) or queue (for BFS-style). The iterative version uses O(1) stack memory instead of O(depth) — the reason iterative tree traversals exist.

5-step.name: The 5-Step Problem Framework
5-step.desc: A repeatable interview loop: understand → examples → brute force → optimize → code → test. Interviewers grade process as much as the final answer; this framework keeps you from freezing.
5-step.q: What should you do in the first 60 seconds of a problem?
5-step.qsub: What clarifying questions do you always ask? · How do you decide brute force is too slow? · Why should you state the brute force even when you know the optimal?
5-step.what:
Imagine getting a ticket with incomplete requirements and starting to code straight away — halfway through you realize you're building the wrong thing. The same happens in interviews.

That's why there is a fixed loop: understand → examples → brute force → optimize → code + test. Each step has its own purpose, and each step leads you to the next.

Most important: the interviewer isn’t only giving points for the final code. They are watching how you break down a tangled problem — because that’s what you do every day in real work.
5-step.analogy: When you go to a doctor, they don’t write a prescription right away — they first ask questions (understand), then match symptoms (examples), then think of a common cause (brute force), then confirm with tests (optimize), and only then write the prescription (code). Who would trust a doctor who writes the prescription immediately?
5-step.why:
The interviewer has 45 minutes and is looking for an answer to one question: “What would it be like to work with this person?” Typing in silence is their biggest red flag.

And the practical benefit: the framework protects you from panic. When an unfamiliar problem shows up and no solution comes to mind, step 1 can still always be done — and in those 3 minutes your mind usually opens up.

How to think:

1. Understand — state the problem out loud in your own words. Ask about constraints: how large can n be? Can there be negative numbers, duplicates, or empty input?
2. Examples — create a small input yourself and manually compute the output. Also try an edge case (empty, single element, all same).
3. Brute force — propose the simplest solution you can think of, even if it’s slow, and also state its complexity. This is your safety net — you’ll have something in hand.
4. Optimize — ask "which operation is repeated?" That’s where a hash map, two pointers, or sorting can cut it down. Name the pattern.
5. Code + test — now write. Then trace line-by-line on your own example, and cover edge cases.
where: State it, then optimize · space: 5 min
Name the pattern + complexity · space: 5-10 min
Write + trace edge cases · space: remaining

qa.q: What should you do in the first 60 seconds of a problem?
qa.a: Restate the problem in your own words, confirm constraints (input size, negatives, empty input, duplicates), and ask a clarifying question. This anchors the problem and signals structured thinking.

qa.q: What if you're stuck after 10 minutes?
qa.a: Go back to examples — brute-force one more small case by hand. If still stuck, say what you know and what's blocking you out loud; interviewers prefer a clear 'I'm stuck because...' to silent panic.

space-complexity.name: Space Complexity
space-complexity.desc: How much extra memory your algorithm needs beyond the input, as a function of n. Counts new arrays, hash maps, and the recursion call stack. Interviewers ask it as often as time complexity.
space-complexity.q: What's the space complexity of a recursive tree traversal?
space-complexity.qsub: What does 'in-place' strictly mean? · Does slice() count as extra space? · What's the stack space of an iterative vs recursive binary search?
space-complexity.what:
Think of your function as getting a room to work in. Space complexity asks: how much new stuff did you place in that room?

The input itself isn’t counted — it was already there. Only the space that your solution itself creates is counted: new arrays, hash maps, and — the most commonly missed one — the recursion call stack.

So a function that creates no arrays but recurses n levels deep uses O(n) space, not O(1). Each pending call on the stack occupies its own space.
space-complexity.analogy: Say you come to the office carrying a tiffin — that’s your input, it was always going to be there. But to heat the food you used an extra container from the office — that is your extra space. And if 10 people are standing in line waiting for their turn, that space is also occupied — that’s the call stack.
space-complexity.why:
In the rush to improve time, people secretly increase space — they create a hash map, make a copy — and keep saying "the solution is O(1) space". The interviewer catches that.

And many problems explicitly state "solve in O(1) extra space" — that line is telling you that a two-pointer or in-place swap solution is required, not a hash map.

How to think:

1. Look at which new arrays, objects or maps are created inside the function that weren’t in the input.
2. See how the size of those structures grows with n — that’s their order.
3. Is the function recursive? Then consider the maximum number of calls that can be pending on the stack at any one time — that’s the depth. (Not total calls — only simultaneous calls.)
4. Combine both and keep the largest term.
5. Only variables that don’t grow with n are O(1), even if there are 10 of them.
where: O(n) extra · space: avoid unless asked

qa.q: What's the space complexity of a recursive tree traversal?
qa.a: O(h) where h is the tree height — the call stack holds one frame per level. For a balanced tree that's O(log n); for a degenerate (linked-list shaped) tree it's O(n).

qa.q: When would you trade time for space, or vice versa?
qa.a: Caching (memoization) trades O(n) space for O(1) time per subproblem. If the constraint forbids extra space, you accept a slower algorithm — the problem statement usually dictates the trade.

fibonacci.name: Fibonacci & Recursion Trees
fibonacci.desc: The canonical recursion lesson: fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) with no memoization explodes into an exponential tree that recomputes the same subproblems. Memoizing collapses it to O(n). The same tree shape underlies Climbing Stairs and House Robber.
fibonacci.q: Why is naive fib O(2^n) when it only recurses n levels deep?
fibonacci.qsub: How many nodes are in fib(5) naive vs memoized? · Why does the iterative version use only two variables? · Which problems share the exact same recurrence tree as fib?
fibonacci.what:
Break down fib(5): fib(4) + fib(3). Then break down fib(4): fib(3) + fib(2). Wait — fib(3) is computed twice. And each time it does the whole work again.

This pattern doubles at every level. In fib(5) there are 15 calls, in fib(30) there are more than 1.3 million — all repeatedly recomputing the same answers. That is O(2ⁿ).

The cure is one line: once you compute a result, write it down. That is memoization, the gateway to full Dynamic Programming.
fibonacci.analogy: Imagine asking the class, "What was yesterday’s homework?" Each student asks two friends, who each ask two more… and the whole class gets noisy. If one student writes the answer on the board, everyone else can just read it. The board is the memo.
fibonacci.why:
This topic isn’t just about Fibonacci. It’s about recognizing overlapping subproblems — the skill that unlocks the entire Phase 7 (DP).

In an interview, stopping after presenting an exponential solution earns only half credit. “The same subproblem repeats here; applying memoization brings it down to O(n)” — that’s the real test.

How to think:

1. fib(n) calls itself twice — fib(n-1) and fib(n-2).
2. Those each make two more calls — the tree roughly doubles at every level.
3. Small values (fib(2), fib(3)) appear repeatedly in different branches of the tree.
4. Every repeated call does the whole work again because the answer isn’t stored anywhere.
5. As soon as you add memoization, each repeated branch becomes an O(1) lookup — the tree collapses into a chain of n distinct subproblems.
6. Note: depth was always n. Time comes from branching, space from depth.

qa.q: Why is naive fib O(2^n) when it only recurses n levels deep?
qa.a: Depth is O(n), but each node spawns TWO children, so the tree has ~2^n nodes and the same work is recomputed at every branch. Depth sets SPACE; branching factor sets TIME.

qa.q: What does memoization actually do here?
qa.a: It caches the answer for each n the first time it is computed. Every duplicate branch becomes an O(1) lookup, reducing ~2^n calls to exactly n distinct subproblems — O(n) time, O(n) space.

arrays-2.name: Arrays & Strings
arrays-2.desc: Contiguous-indexed storage with O(1) index access. The default container for most problems; mastery means knowing which JS methods mutate vs copy and their costs.
arrays-2.q: What's the time cost of arr.shift()?
arrays-2.qsub: How do you find the second largest element in one pass? · When is arr.sort() O(n log n) but still fine to use? · How do you merge two sorted arrays in place from the end?
arrays-2.what:
In Phase 0 we saw how arrays work. Now the real question: which method changes the original, and which returns a new array?

This is not just trivia. If you write state.push(item) the array will change, but its address (reference) stays the same. React looks at the reference, doesn't peek inside — it will think nothing changed, and the re-render will be skipped.

There is no error and no warning — the UI just stays stale. That's why it's asked in interviews and also bites in production.
arrays-2.analogy: Think of a paper register. If you overwrite an entry on the same page (mutate), an outside observer who only checks the page won't notice anything. If you write a new page and put it on top (copy), the change is immediately visible. React only checks the page, not the writing on it.
arrays-2.why:
The interviewer can tell in one sentence whether you only used React or actually understand it. push/splice/sort/reverse mutate; map/filter/slice/spread return a new array.

On the DSA side this has another form: in-place solutions. "O(1) extra space" means you are not allowed to create a new array — you must solve it with two pointers.

How to think:

1. Check if the method directly changes the array's length or order — if yes, it is mutating.
2. If the method returns a completely new array and leaves the original unchanged — it is non-mutating.
3. For React state, first make a copy: [...arr] or arr.slice().
4. Make changes on the copy, then pass that same copy to setState — a new reference goes in, a re-render happens.
5. In DSA you want the opposite — where O(1) space is required, modify the original with two pointers.

qa.q: What's the time cost of arr.shift()?
qa.a: O(n) — every remaining element must move down one index. For a queue-like structure prefer a head-pointer index or a proper Deque implementation.

qa.q: In-place algorithms — why do interviews love them?
qa.a: They prove you can manage O(1) extra space. Problems like Rotate Array and Set Matrix Zeroes explicitly require it, and in-place techniques (two pointers, cycle sort) show up in hard problems.

strings.name: Strings & Characters
strings.desc: Immutable sequences of characters. In JS, string methods return NEW strings — building strings in a loop is O(n²) if done naively. Character codes and palindrome checks are the core patterns.
strings.q: Why is string concatenation in a loop slow?
strings.qsub: How do you check if a string is a valid palindrome ignoring non-alphanumerics? · What does charCodeAt return for emoji vs ASCII? · How do you reverse words in a sentence in place?
strings.what:
A string is like a printed book. If you want to change a word, you have to print an entirely new page — you can't edit the old page. In JS, strings are immutable.

So s += c looks like a small operation, but internally it copies the entire old string, appends one character, and creates a new string.

If you do it n times in a loop, the amount copied grows each time — 1 + 2 + 3 + … + n = O(n²). The fix is one line: push into an array, then join('') once at the end.
strings.analogy: Think of a photocopier: to add one line, you have to photocopy the entire old sheet again with the new line on it. To create a ten-line document you end up photocopying 55 lines. Array + join means: write all lines separately, then staple them together once at the end.
strings.why:
This is the classic “small change, big impact” signal. The interviewer wants to see whether you recognize the hidden cost of +=.

And the rest of string questions — anagram, palindrome, sliding window — all rest on the same principle: a string cannot be modified, only read. So the work is done with a frequency map or the two-pointer technique.

How to think:

1. s += c creates a new string object — the old string is never touched.
2. To create the new one, all characters of the old string are copied. This work is proportional to the string’s current length.
3. The length grows each iteration, so each copy is more expensive than the previous.
4. Summing all: 1+2+3+…+n = n(n+1)/2 → O(n²).
5. Push into an array instead — arrays are mutable, so nothing is copied and each push is O(1).
6. At the end, a single join('') walks the whole thing once — O(n) in total. That's it.

qa.q: Why is string concatenation in a loop slow?
qa.a: Strings are immutable. Each += allocates a brand new string copying the whole previous content — n concatenations cost O(1+2+...+n) = O(n²). Collect pieces in an array and join() once for O(n).

qa.q: Anagram detection — what's the optimal approach?
qa.a: Sort both strings and compare (O(n log n)), or build two frequency maps (O(n)). For a single string pair, the frequency-map comparison is cleanest; sort-and-compare is shorter to write.

hashmaps.name: Hash Map
hashmaps.desc: Key-value storage with O(1) average insert/lookup/delete by hashing the key. The #1 interview tool: it converts 'scan the array for something' from O(n) per check to O(1).
hashmaps.q: HashMap vs Array — when does each win?
hashmaps.qsub: How do you count frequencies of every character? · Why is 'value -> index' a Map in Two Sum but a plain array in others? · How do you build a map of anagram groups?
hashmaps.what:
Two Sum: find two numbers in an array whose sum is the target. Straightforward method — for each number, search the rest of the array for another. Nested loop, O(n²).

Now flip it: for each number, ask "I need target - x — has it appeared before?" If you record the numbers you've already seen in a map, that question is answered in O(1).

That's it. The whole solution in one pass, O(n). The job of a hash map is exactly this: “searching” becomes “remembering”.
hashmaps.analogy: Imagine a wedding with 500 guests where you need to find your friend. Going to each table to look = O(n). But at the entrance there's a register listing every guest's name and table number — give the name, get the table. The register is the hash map.
hashmaps.why:
This is the interview tool with the highest return. A single pattern — "have you seen it before?" — unlocks dozens of problems.

Interviewers specifically look for this: after you mention the brute-force O(n²) approach, you either reach the hash-map solution on your own or need a hint. It tests pattern-recognition, not memory.

How to think:

1. Traverse the array once from left to right.
2. For each element first ask: is the needed value (complement or previous count) already in the map?
3. If found → that is the answer, return immediately.
4. If not found → insert the current element into the map (value → index, or value → count).
5. Move to the next element. The entire array is traversed only once — O(n) time, O(n) space.
6. Order matters: check first, then insert. Doing it the other way makes an element match itself.

qa.q: HashMap vs Array — when does each win?
qa.a: Array wins when keys are dense integers 0..n-1 (frequency by index, cycle sort). HashMap wins for arbitrary keys — strings, objects, sparse integers — giving O(1) average access.

qa.q: What's the worst case for a hash map and why don't we worry?
qa.a: With a bad hash function or pathological inputs, everything lands in one bucket → O(n) operations. In interviews we assume a good hash → O(1) average, but knowing the caveat shows depth.

linked-lists.name: Singly Linked List
linked-lists.desc: Nodes holding a value and a next pointer, chained linearly. No O(1) index access — traversal is O(n). The superpowers are O(1) insertion/deletion at a known node and pointer tricks (fast & slow, dummy nodes).
linked-lists.q: Why use a dummy head node?
linked-lists.qsub: What's the cost of finding the k-th node? · Why can't you do arr[i] access on a linked list? · When reversing, why must you save next before rewiring cur.next?
linked-lists.what:
Think of a treasure hunt: each clue contains the location of the next one. You have to start from the first clue, because you can't jump straight to the 50th.

A linked list is exactly that. Every node holds a value and a next — the address of the next node. There is no index, so a jump like arr[50] is not possible. Need the 50th node? Follow next 50 times — O(n).

The trade-off gives you a superpower: if you already have a reference to a node, inserting after it or removing it is just changing two pointers — O(1). The same operation in an array requires O(n) shifting.
linked-lists.analogy: Treasure-hunt clues — you can’t open a middle clue directly; you have to move forward one by one. But if you have a clue in hand, inserting a new clue after it is very easy: you only need to change two addresses, the rest of the hunt stays the same.
linked-lists.why:
The interviewer tests the array vs linked list trade-off: arrays win at random access, linked lists win at insert/delete when the node is known.

It is also a test of pointer manipulation. Reverse, cycle detection, merge — in any of these, changing a pointer in the wrong order breaks the entire list. The interviewer checks whether you remember to save next.

How to think:

1. head points to the first node. There is no other entry point to the list.
2. To reach any node, start at head and follow next one hop at a time.
3. Insert: set the new node’s next first, then set the previous node’s next to the new one. Doing it the other way loses the rest of the list.
4. Delete: point the previous node’s next directly to the next node — the middle node removes itself from the list.
5. Reverse: three pointers — prev, cur, next. At each step, save next first, then set cur.next = prev.

qa.q: Why use a dummy head node?
qa.a: It eliminates special-casing the head: you never write 'if this is the first node'. Operations like insertion before head, or building a result list, all start from a dummy and return dummy.next — less branching, fewer bugs.

qa.q: How does the fast & slow pointer detect a cycle?
qa.a: Two pointers move at speed 1 and 2. If there's a cycle the fast pointer laps the slow one and they meet — O(n) time, O(1) space. Same idea finds the middle node (fast reaches end, slow is at middle).

stacks.name: Stack
stacks.desc: LIFO (last-in, first-out). Push/pop/peek all O(1). Used wherever the most recent thing matters: matching brackets, undo, function calls, monotonic-pattern groundwork, parsing.
stacks.q: What's the difference between a Stack and a Queue?
stacks.qsub: What does a stack's depth represent in bracket matching? · How do you evaluate Reverse Polish Notation with a stack? · When should you use a stack vs recursion for DFS?
stacks.what:
Think of a pile of plates. The plate placed on top last is the first one lifted, and no plate in the middle comes out directly. This is called LIFO — Last In, First Out.

Push and pop both happen on the same end, so nothing slides — both O(1).

And this isn't just an analogy — it's exactly how JavaScript's call stack works. The function that was called last returns first. If you understand recursion, you understand the stack, and vice versa.
stacks.analogy: A pile of washed plates at a dhaba — the top one is lifted first. Or the browser's back button: the page opened last returns first when you press back. Wherever you need “the most recent thing”, that's a stack.
stacks.why:
A stack is a signal. When a problem shows nesting — brackets, tags, expressions — or you need the "previous one", the answer is almost always a stack.

And this is the Phase 1 topic that takes you the furthest: monotonic stack, iterative DFS, expression parsing, undo — all built on this single structure.

How to think:

1. A new element always goes to the top — push.
2. Removal also always happens from the top — pop. It never reaches the lower elements.
3. peek only looks at the top, does not remove — in JS arr[arr.length-1].
4. Both operations are on the same end, so no shifting — O(1).
5. Bracket matching: when an opening arrives, push. When a closing arrives, pop and check that it was the correct pair. At the end the stack should be empty — if anything remains, some bracket was never closed.

qa.q: What's the difference between a Stack and a Queue?
qa.a: Stack is LIFO — the newest element is removed first (think stack of plates). Queue is FIFO — the oldest is removed first (think ticket line). That single property decides which fits the problem.

qa.q: How would you implement a queue using two stacks?
qa.a: Use one stack for push (inbox). On pop, if the outbox is empty, dump all of inbox into outbox (reversing order), then pop from outbox. Amortized O(1) per operation.

queue.name: Queue
queue.desc: FIFO (first-in, first-out). Enqueue/dequeue O(1). The engine behind BFS — level-order tree traversal and shortest-path-on-unweighted-graph exploration. In JS, a plain array works but shift() is O(n); use a head index or a real queue.
queue.q: Why does BFS give the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
queue.qsub: How does BFS prevent infinite loops on graphs? · In level-order traversal, why snapshot the queue size? · What changes if edges are weighted? (→ Dijkstra)
queue.what:
Think of a ration-shop line. Whoever came first leaves first, and no one can cut in the middle. This is called FIFO — First In, First Out.

It’s the opposite of a stack: in a stack both operations happen at the same end, while a queue has two separate ends — back for insertion (enqueue), front for removal (dequeue). Hence both are O(1).

And this is not just a data structure — it’s the entire engine of BFS. All nodes of one level are processed before the next level starts. That guarantee comes from the queue, and that guarantee creates the shortest path on an unweighted graph.
queue.analogy: The ration shop line — first come, first go. And think of BFS like throwing a stone into a pond: waves expand in circles, one ring at a time. First all points at distance 1, then distance 2. So the first one you encounter is the closest.
queue.why:
You can't understand BFS without understanding a queue, and BFS is only half as useful without Phase 4 (trees) and Phase 5 (graphs). Level-order traversal, shortest path, rotting oranges, word ladder — all come from here.

And there’s a JavaScript-specific trap that interviewers watch for: arr.shift() is O(n). Using it inside the BFS loop silently turns the whole algorithm into O(n²) — the answer stays correct, but it will hit a time limit (TLE) on large inputs.

How to think:

1. A new element always joins at the rear (back) — enqueue.
2. Removal always happens from the front — dequeue.
3. Two separate ends mean nothing gets in the way — both O(1).
4. In BFS: dequeue a node, then enqueue all its unvisited neighbors at the back.
5. Need level order? Before starting the loop, capture size = queue.length and process exactly that many nodes. Otherwise the next level mixes with the current one.
6. A visited set on the graph is essential — otherwise the queue never empties in a cycle.

qa.q: Why does BFS give the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
qa.a: Because it explores level by level — all nodes at distance d are processed before any at distance d+1. The first time a node is reached, it's reached by a shortest route. DFS has no such guarantee.

qa.q: Why is arr.shift() bad for a queue?
qa.a: shift() reindexes every remaining element — O(n) per dequeue, O(n²) total for n operations. A head-pointer index (or linked list) makes dequeue O(1).

hashset.name: Hash Set
hashset.desc: An unordered collection of unique values with O(1) add/remove/check. Whenever a problem says 'distinct', 'unique', or 'have I seen this', a Set is the tool — cleaner than a Map of booleans.
hashset.q: Set vs Map — when do you use each?
hashset.qsub: How do you find the intersection of two arrays with O(n)? · When does a Set become worse than sorting? · How do Sets dedupe objects (identity vs equality)?
hashset.what:
Set is basically a Map that only stores a value, not a key-value pair. It answers a single question: "Is this item inside or not?" — in O(1) time.

In an array you ask the same question with includes(), which checks every element — O(n). Placing that inside a loop silently becomes O(n²).

As a bonus, duplicates disappear automatically. [...new Set(arr)] — one line, O(n), and the order is preserved.
hashset.analogy: Outside the club, the bouncer has a guest list. You say a name, and he goes straight to that page — he doesn’t read the whole list. And a name cannot appear twice on the list — trying to write it again does nothing.
hashset.why:
Interviewers look for one thing: when a problem mentions "distinct", "unique", "have I seen this before" or "visited", a Set should immediately come to mind.

This is a pattern-recognition test, not a syntax test. Use a Map when you need to remember something extra along with the value (index, count). When you only need “is it there or not” — Set is the clear choice.

How to think:

1. When a value is added, a hash function converts it to a number.
2. That number determines a slot in an internal array.
3. The value is placed in that slot. If two values get the same hash (collision) a small list is created in that slot.
4. On has(x) the same hash is computed again — directly to the slot. The whole set isn’t scanned.
5. When adding, the same check happens first — so duplicates are automatically rejected.
6. Hence add, has, delete — all average O(1), worst case O(n).

qa.q: Set vs Map — when do you use each?
qa.a: Set when you only need membership (do I have this? is it distinct?). Map when each value carries associated data (count, index). A Set is a Map without values — no lookup key for the count.

qa.q: Contains Duplicate — Set or sort?
qa.a: Set: one pass, if set.has(x) return true, else add — O(n) time O(n) space. Sorting is O(n log n) with O(1) space; for small arrays both fine, but the Set answer is the one expected.

doubly-linked-lists.name: Doubly Linked List
doubly-linked-lists.desc: Like a singly list, plus a prev pointer on every node. The prev pointer enables O(1) deletion of a node you already have — no need to find its predecessor. This is what makes LRU Cache possible.
doubly-linked-lists.q: Why can a doubly linked list delete a known node in O(1) but a singly one can't?
doubly-linked-lists.qsub: Why do LRU implementations use sentinel head/tail nodes? · When is a doubly list worse than a singly list? · What breaks if you forget to fix both prev and next links?
doubly-linked-lists.what:
A singly linked list has a limitation. You have a reference to the node you want to delete — but to delete it you need to change the previous node's next, and there is no way to go backwards. You have to start from the head again — O(n).

A doubly linked list fixes this in one line: each node also has a prev. Now the previous node is in hand, so deletion only requires changing two pointers — O(1).

This is what makes an LRU Cache possible: the hash map gives you the node instantly, and because of prev moving it forward in the list is also O(1).
doubly-linked-lists.analogy: On a local train, passengers hold each other's hands — on both sides, the one in front and the one behind. If the middle passenger wants to get off, the two neighbors simply hold each other's hands directly. No one has to count their way from the door.
doubly-linked-lists.why:
This topic is for a single design question, but that question is asked very often: the LRU Cache. Its whole trick is exactly this — find the node with a Map in O(1), and move it to the head with the DLL in O(1).

The interviewer also looks to see if you understand the cost: an extra pointer per node uses memory, and each operation requires the discipline of fixing links on both sides.

How to think:

1. Each node stores three things — value, next, and prev.
2. During insertion, four pointers are set: both pointers of the new node, and one pointer of each neighboring node.
3. During deletion, two: node.prev.next = node.next and node.next.prev = node.prev. No traversal needed.
4. Keep a sentinel (dummy) head and tail — then no real node’s prev/next will ever be null, and all if (node === head) checks disappear.
5. Moving a node "forward" is not a single step, it is two: first unlink, then insert. If the order is wrong the list breaks.

qa.q: Why can a doubly linked list delete a known node in O(1) but a singly one can't?
qa.a: Deletion needs the predecessor to rewire its next pointer. A doubly list reaches it directly via node.prev. A singly list must traverse from the head to find it — O(n).

qa.q: How does LRU Cache combine a Map and a DLL?
qa.a: The Map gives O(1) lookup by key; the DLL tracks recency order so the least-recently-used node is at the tail. On get/put you move the node to the head; eviction removes the tail — every operation O(1).

circular-linked-lists.name: Circular Linked List
circular-linked-lists.desc: A linked list whose tail points back to the head, forming a loop. Common in round-robin scheduling, Josephus-style problems, and as the mental model for cycle detection.
circular-linked-lists.q: How does Floyd's algorithm find the entry point of a cycle?
circular-linked-lists.qsub: Why must fast advance two steps but never more? · What happens if the cycle is the whole list? · How do you safely iterate a circular list without an infinite loop?
circular-linked-lists.what:
In a normal list the last node ends with null. In a circular list that last node points back to the head. That's the only difference — and the whole behavior changes.

Now the list has no end. Traversal keeps looping automatically, and the "first after the last" operation becomes free — you don't need to apply % length.

The other side matters more: if a list accidentally forms such a loop, a plain while (cur) never terminates. To catch this, we use Floyd's slow-fast pointer trick.
circular-linked-lists.analogy: Think of Antakshari: the last singer finishes and the turn passes back to the first. There is no “last person”. And the trick to catch a cycle: two runners on a circular track. One runs slowly, the other twice as fast. On a circular track the fast one will eventually lap the slow one and catch it. On a straight track they would never meet.
circular-linked-lists.why:
The interviewer looks for two things. First: you know a stopping condition is needed, otherwise you get an infinite loop — a very common mistake.

Second, and more important: why Floyd's algorithm works. Simply reciting the code isn’t enough. The answer is: inside the ring, the distance between the two pointers decreases by exactly 1 on each step, so they are guaranteed to meet. If the fast pointer moved three steps, this guarantee could break.

How to think:

1. Set the last node’s next to head instead of null — that creates the ring.
2. To traverse, use do { ... } while (cur !== head) — one full loop, then stop. while (cur) would never stop here.
3. To detect a cycle, move slow 1 step and fast 2 steps.
4. If there is no ring, fast will reach null first — no cycle.
5. If there is a ring, both enter it, and the gap between them decreases by 1 each step — they will meet.
6. Need the start of the cycle? After they meet, reset slow to head, then move both one step at a time — the node where they meet is the entry point.

qa.q: How does Floyd's algorithm find the entry point of a cycle?
qa.a: After slow and fast meet inside the cycle, reset slow to head. Then advance both one step at a time — the math shows they meet exactly at the cycle's start. Total O(n) time, O(1) space.

qa.q: What's the difference between a circular list and a list with a cycle?
qa.a: A true circular list deliberately points the tail at the head — traversal is well-defined. A 'cycle' bug is usually unintended. The detection algorithm is identical, but a circular list is a design, not a defect.

monotonic-stack.name: Monotonic Stack
monotonic-stack.desc: A stack that always stays sorted (increasing or decreasing) by values — you pop elements that violate the order before pushing. Every element is pushed and popped at most once, so it's O(n) and solves 'next greater / next smaller' problems elegantly.
monotonic-stack.q: Why is a monotonic stack O(n) even though there's a nested while?
monotonic-stack.qsub: How do you get the previous greater element instead of next? · What changes for next smaller? · How does Largest Rectangle in Histogram use a monotonic stack?
monotonic-stack.what:
Say that for each element you need the first larger element to its right. The straightforward way: scan forward from each element — O(n²).

Now reverse it. When a new larger element arrives, it becomes the answer for many previous elements at once — all those that were still waiting for a larger element.

So keep those "waiting" elements in a stack, always in decreasing order. When a new element arrives — any that are smaller than it get their answer, pop them. Each element is pushed once and popped once — total work O(n).
monotonic-stack.analogy: People in a line are ordered by height, tallest at the front. When a taller person appears from behind — all the shorter ones behind him hide behind him. Their answer to "who is my first taller person" is settled all at once, and they are removed from the line.
monotonic-stack.why:
This is the most "algorithm-like" topic in Phase 1. The interviewer looks for one thing: can you think in amortized terms.

The code has a while inside a for — at first glance it looks like O(n²). But each element is pushed at most once and popped at most once during the whole run, so the total work is 2n — O(n). Explaining that is the real answer.

How to think:

1. Keep indices in the stack, not values — you need the index to compute distance.
2. For each new element: while the top of the stack violates the invariant, pop it.
3. The element that gets popped — its answer is the current element. Write the answer at pop time, not at push time.
4. Then push the current index.
5. At the end, any indices left in the stack have no answer (default 0 / -1).
6. To remember the direction: for next greater keep the stack decreasing. For next smaller keep it increasing.

qa.q: Why is a monotonic stack O(n) even though there's a nested while?
qa.a: Each element is pushed exactly once and popped at most once across the whole run. The inner while only runs across total pops = n, so the algorithm is O(n) amortized — no element is processed twice.

qa.q: Should the stack store values or indices?
qa.a: Indices. Values alone lose the distance information (Daily Temperatures needs days = i - idx) and can't handle duplicate values cleanly. Store indices and read the value via the array.

deque.name: Deque (Double-Ended Queue)
deque.desc: A queue that supports O(1) push/pop at BOTH ends. The workhorse for sliding-window maximum/minimum problems, where candidates must be added at the back and expired at the front.
deque.q: Why is Sliding Window Maximum O(n) and not O(nk)?
deque.qsub: What invariant does the deque maintain for window maximum? · How would you get the minimum instead? · Why compare nums[dq[last]] <= nums[i] with <= (not <)?
deque.what:
Deque = a queue where both ends are open. You can insert and remove from the front as well as from the back. All operations are O(1).

Why is it needed? Think of Sliding Window Maximum. As the window slides forward, you need to discard the old index from the front (it left the window), and discard smaller values from the back (they can never become the maximum in front of the new larger element).

Two different ends, two different reasons. Hence a simple queue isn’t enough — you need a deque. The elements inside are always kept in decreasing order, so the front is always the maximum of the window.
deque.analogy: Imagine a queue of people: those at the front leave as the window moves forward, and when a taller person arrives at the back, the shorter ones in front of them become pointless (they can never be the maximum). The tallest person always stays at the front of the line.
deque.why:
The interviewer asks about Sliding Window Maximum because the naive solution is O(n·k) while the deque solution is O(n). Understanding the difference is the test.

And a JavaScript-specific trap: dq.shift() is O(n). Even with the correct algorithm you can fall back to O(n·k) — pointing out that "you need a real deque or a head index" earns extra points.

How to think:

1. Keep indices in the deque, not values — the index tells you when an element leaves the window.
2. When a new element i arrives: pop from the back all elements whose value is less than or equal to nums[i] — they can never become max again.
3. Then push i at the back.
4. Look at the front: if its index has left the window (<= i - k), remove it.
5. Once the window is full (i >= k-1) the nums[front] is the maximum for this window.
6. Each index enters once and leaves once — total work O(n), just like a monotonic stack.

qa.q: Why is Sliding Window Maximum O(n) and not O(nk)?
qa.a: Each index enters the deque once and leaves once. The inner while only pops total n times across the run. The window maximum is always at the front — O(1) to read. No element is ever rescanned.

qa.q: Why use a deque instead of a max-heap here?
qa.a: A heap answers max in O(log k) but can't cheaply evict the element leaving the window. The deque keeps candidates in decreasing order, evicts expired indices from the front in O(1), and reads max from the front in O(1).

matrix-2d.name: 2D Matrix Traversal
matrix-2d.desc: Arrays of arrays as grids. Patterns: row/column iteration, diagonal walks, spiral order, and in-place transforms (rotate, transpose, zero-out) — heavy favorites at Google/Meta.
matrix-2d.q: How do you rotate a matrix 90° in place with O(1) space?
matrix-2d.qsub: How do you zero out rows/columns with O(1) extra space? · What are the edge cases for spiral on a single row or column? · How do you check neighbors without index errors?
matrix-2d.what:
A 2D matrix is essentially an array of arrays. Any cell can be accessed with matrix[r][c] in O(1). Up to that point everything is easy.

The difficulty lies in the traversal pattern. Row-by-row is straightforward. But spiral? Diagonal? 90° rotate without an extra array? Here the whole work is done by index arithmetic.

Two tricks solve about 80% of matrix problems: rotate = transpose + reverse each row, and spiral = four boundaries that shrink after each loop.
matrix-2d.analogy: Think of a chessboard. Identifying a single square is easy (row, column). But “spiral from the outer ring inward” means remembering the four edges and sliding all four inward by one step after each loop.
matrix-2d.why:
Rotate Image, Spiral Matrix, Set Matrix Zeroes — are favorites at Google and Meta. They test index discipline rather than algorithmic cleverness. Forget a bounds check in one place and the code crashes.

And this is the foundation for Phase 5 (graphs): on a grid, BFS/DFS means each cell is a node and it has four neighbors. The same dirs array you learn here will be useful a hundred times later.

How to think:

1. m = matrix.length (rows), n = matrix[0].length (cols). Assume it is rectangular, not necessarily square — assuming square is the classic first mistake.
2. Rotate 90°: first transpose (swap [i][j] with [j][i] only when j > i — otherwise you swap twice and end up where you started). Then reverse each row. Done.
3. Spiral: keep four variables — top, bottom, left, right. One cycle goes right → down → left → up. After finishing each side, move that boundary one step inward.
4. In a spiral, a final single row or column can be counted twice — so before the left and up steps, re-check top <= bottom and left <= right.
5. Neighbors: use a dirs array like [[1,0],[-1,0],[0,1],[0,-1]]. For each neighbor do a bounds check first, then read the cell.

qa.q: How do you rotate a matrix 90° in place with O(1) space?
qa.a: Two mechanical steps: transpose (swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i]) then reverse each row. 90° counter-clockwise is reverse each row first, then transpose. No new matrix needed.

qa.q: Spiral traversal — what's the cleanest loop structure?
qa.a: Track four boundaries (top/bottom/left/right). Walk right, down, left, up, shrinking a boundary after each full pass, and stop when boundaries cross. It's four simple loops inside one while.

static-dynamic-arrays.name: Static vs Dynamic Arrays
static-dynamic-arrays.desc: How arrays actually live in memory. A static array has a fixed capacity allocated once; a dynamic array (ArrayList in Java, vector in C++, every JS array) grows by allocating a bigger block and copying. Understanding the doubling strategy explains why append is O(1) amortized.
static-dynamic-arrays.q: Why is push on a dynamic array O(1) even though resizes copy everything?
static-dynamic-arrays.qsub: How do you insert at index 0 of an array? What is the cost? · Why would you ever prefer a static array over a dynamic one? · How many times does an element get copied over n appends?
static-dynamic-arrays.what:
In C, an array is static — you give the size when you create it, and that's it. If it fills up, that's it.

In JavaScript, an array is dynamic. When space runs out the engine silently allocates a block twice as large, copies all the old elements over, and then inserts the new one. You don't even notice.

So why do we call push O(1) when occasionally it does an O(n) copy? Because a resize happens only at exponentially increasing sizes. The total copy work for n pushes is roughly 2n — about two steps per push. This is called amortized O(1).
static-dynamic-arrays.analogy: Your wardrobe is full. You buy one that is twice as big and move all the clothes over — that day takes the whole afternoon. After that, putting clothes away is a one-second job for a long time. The next move will take even longer, but it comes much later. Averaged over all the days, the moving hardly shows up.
static-dynamic-arrays.why:
This is a vocabulary question. Saying ‘push is O(1)’ is only half the answer. ‘O(1) amortized, worst-case O(n) when a resize occurs’ — that’s the full answer.

And this is another form of the amortized thinking introduced in Phase 0. Hash-map resizing, stack growth — all rely on the same idea. Once you get it, it works everywhere.

How to think:

1. An array stores two things — size (how many elements are present) and capacity (how many can fit). They are separate.
2. On push, first check if size < capacity. If yes → place the element directly, O(1).
3. If not → allocate a new block of capacity × 2, copy all old elements — this is O(n).
4. Resizes happen when the size reaches 1, 2, 4, 8, 16… — the gap between resizes doubles each time.
5. Total copies for n pushes: 1+2+4+…+n ≈ 2n. Distribute over pushes → ~2 steps → O(1) amortized.
6. We double instead of adding 1 because adding 1 would cause a resize on every push and total work would become O(n²).

qa.q: Why is push on a dynamic array O(1) even though resizes copy everything?
qa.a: Amortization: the sum of all copy costs over n pushes is less than 2n (each element is copied only when the array doubles, at most log n times). Total work O(n), average O(1).

qa.q: What is the space overhead of a dynamic array?
qa.a: Capacity is always at least size, and often up to 2x. That is O(n) extra slack worst case — the price for amortized O(1) append.

hash-impl.name: Hash Table Implementation
hash-impl.desc: A hash table maps keys to values using an array of buckets and a hash function. Collisions are handled by chaining (linked list per bucket) or open addressing (probe for the next free slot). Hash quality decides whether lookups are O(1) or degrade to O(n).
hash-impl.q: How do you handle two keys hashing to the same bucket?
hash-impl.qsub: What makes a good hash function for a HashMap? · Compare chaining vs open addressing. · Why is a JS object lookup not always O(1)? · When does a hash table degrade to O(n)?
hash-impl.what:
So far you've used Map and Set. Now let's look inside — because the interviewer may also ask you to "build a HashMap" yourself.

Inside there is just an array of buckets. When a key arrives → the hash function turns it into a number → % buckets.length gives the bucket index → store the value there.

The whole game is about two things. Collision — when two keys end up in the same bucket, what do you do? And load factor — when the buckets get too full, double their number. If the hash is bad, all keys go into one bucket, and O(1) drops to O(n).
hash-impl.analogy: Think of post-office compartments organized by pin code. The pin code directly tells you which compartment to put a letter in — you don’t have to read all letters. Two letters with the same pin code? Put both in that compartment (chaining) — now you’ll have to read the small stack in that compartment. And when the compartments fill up, get double the compartments.
hash-impl.why:
Two reasons. First: "Design a HashMap" is a straight interview question (LeetCode 706).

Second, and bigger: so far you have been saying O(1) average. The interviewer asks "why average, why not always?" — the answer is collision and load factor. Explaining this distinguishes junior from senior.

How to think:

1. Create an array — say 16 buckets.
2. Hash: Convert the key into a number. For a string, add/mix the character codes, then % buckets.length — you get the bucket index.
3. Collision (chaining): Keep a small list in the bucket. Push new entries into it, and on lookup search that small list.
4. Collision (open addressing): If the bucket is full, find the next empty slot. Uses less memory, but deletion becomes tricky.
5. Load factor: entries ÷ buckets. When it crosses ~0.75, double the buckets and re-hash all keys (rehash) — because the % result changes.
6. A good hash spreads keys evenly across buckets. A bad hash puts everything in one bucket = O(n).
where: O(1) avg / O(n) worst · space: O(1)
O(1) avg / O(n) worst · space: O(1)
O(1) avg / O(n) worst · space: O(1)

qa.q: How do you handle two keys hashing to the same bucket?
qa.a: Separate chaining: each bucket is a linked list (or tree). Open addressing: probe linearly (or quadratically) to the next empty slot. Chaining is simpler and what most textbook maps use.

qa.q: Why does the load factor matter?
qa.a: It is the ratio of keys to buckets. Above ~0.75 the average chain length grows and lookups slow down, so the table resizes (rehash) — costing O(n) but only rarely, so amortized O(1).

linear-search.name: Linear Search
linear-search.desc: Scan every element until the target is found — O(n). Simple and correct, it's the baseline you improve from. Its real interview value is recognizing when a linear scan is all you need (arrays are usually small or unsorted).
linear-search.q: When is linear search the right answer?
linear-search.qsub: What structure does an array need for binary search to work? · Why is a single pass the lower bound for unsorted search? · How would you find the second-largest in one pass?
linear-search.what:
Look at each element one by one until you find it. That's it. It is the simplest algorithm in Phase 2 — which is exactly why people miss its real point.

The real point is: if the array is unsorted, nothing can be faster than O(n). The answer might be in the last box, and you don't know that beforehand. So you have to open every box.

This is not a weakness of the algorithm — it's a lower bound. And this is the baseline against which every later algorithm is compared.
linear-search.analogy: Your clothes are scattered in a wardrobe with no order, so to find one shirt you pull them out one by one. If you organized the wardrobe properly first, you could find any shirt instantly — but organizing everything for just one shirt is wasted effort. If you grab clothes every day, organizing pays off.
linear-search.why:
The interviewer isn’t just checking whether you can write a for loop. They want to see whether you can make judgment calls.

There’s another hidden trap that many fall into: applying binary search on an unsorted array. It doesn’t crash — it just gives a silently wrong answer. Asking "Is the array sorted?" earns points in an interview.

How to think:

1. Start at index 0 and go to the end.
2. Compare each element with the target. If found → immediately return i.
3. Loop finishes and nothing is found → return -1. Forgetting this "not found" case is the most common mistake.
4. In a single pass you can also compute min, max, count, or the second-largest. Don’t write separate loops; track everything in one.
5. Decision: If you need to search only once → linear. If you need to search repeatedly → sort or build a hash once, then each search is cheap.

qa.q: When is linear search the right answer?
qa.a: When the input is unsorted and you need a single pass anyway (min/max, counting) — O(n) is optimal because you must inspect every element. The interview skill is knowing binary search doesn't apply without structure.

qa.q: Can you do better than O(n) to find a max in an unsorted array?
qa.a: No — the max could be anywhere, so every element must be inspected. That's an information-theoretic lower bound, not a weakness of the algorithm.

binary-search.name: Binary Search
binary-search.desc: Repeatedly halve a sorted search space: check the middle, eliminate the half that can't contain the answer. O(log n) time, O(1) space. Variants: basic search, lower/upper bound, and search on an answer space ('minimize the maximum').
binary-search.q: What does 'binary search on the answer' mean?
binary-search.qsub: How do you find the first and last position of a target? · How do you search a rotated sorted array? · Why must the feasibility function be monotonic for answer-space search?
binary-search.what:
The biggest advantage of sorted data: by looking at the middle element you can discard half the data in one go. Is the middle smaller than the target? Then the entire left side is useless. Gone.

At each step you halve it — n → n/2 → n/4 → … → 1. 1,000,000 elements in just 20 steps. That’s O(log n).

But the real point is: binary search isn’t only for arrays. Anywhere there is a monotonic property — once true it stays true — binary search can be applied. This is called "binary search on the answer", and that’s what shows up in interviews.
binary-search.analogy: Dictionary search — open the middle page, see whether your word comes before or after, and discard half the dictionary. No one reads a dictionary from the start. And remember: it only works because the dictionary is sorted. If the words were scattered, the middle page would tell you nothing.
binary-search.why:
Everyone can write the basic version of binary search. In interviews, variants appear, and that’s where people get stuck — first occurrence, last occurrence, insertion position, rotated array.

And the biggest level: binary search on the answer. The problem doesn’t even have a sorted array — “what is the minimum speed required so that the work finishes in h hours?” Here you binary-search over the range of answers [lo, hi]. Figuring that out is the real test.

How to think:

1. lo = 0, hi = n - 1. Compute middle: mid = lo + ((hi - lo) >> 1).
2. arr[mid] is the target? Found.
3. Smaller? Then target must be to the right → lo = mid + 1.
4. Larger? Target to the left → hi = mid - 1.
5. lo > hi → not present, -1.
6. Answer search: instead of an array, take the answer range [lo, hi]. Create a feasible(x) function that in O(n) tells “can it be done with x?” That function must be monotonic — once true, always true thereafter. That’s the binary search.
where: O(log R) × O(n) check · space: O(1)

qa.q: What does 'binary search on the answer' mean?
qa.a: Instead of searching an array, search the space of possible ANSWER values. For 'minimum speed to eat all bananas in h hours', speeds range 1..max; binary search that range, and each check simulates eating in O(n). Feasibility must be monotonic (if speed works, any higher speed works).

qa.q: When does while (l <= r) fail?
qa.a: l <= r with l=mid+1/r=mid-1 works for exact search but can infinite-loop or miss boundaries for lower-bound problems. For first/last occurrence, the cleaner pattern is while (l < r) with r = mid, converging to a single index.

merge-sort.name: Merge Sort
merge-sort.desc: Divide & conquer sort: split in half, sort each half recursively, then merge two sorted halves in O(n). Guaranteed O(n log n), stable, but needs O(n) extra space. The merge step is a reusable interview pattern.
merge-sort.q: Why is merge sort always O(n log n) while quick sort isn't?
merge-sort.qsub: What makes merge sort stable? · How does the merge step count inversions? · Why does merge sort need O(n) space?
merge-sort.what:
Merging two already sorted lists is easy — compare the front elements of both, take the smaller one. One pass, O(n).

Merge sort does the opposite: split the array in half repeatedly until only one element remains (a single element is already sorted). Then, as you go back up, merge each pair.

Splitting always occurs at the exact middle, so the depth is always log n — it never degrades like quick sort. Guarantees O(n log n). Cost: O(n) extra space.
merge-sort.analogy: Two teachers each have a stack of answer sheets sorted by marks, and you need one combined stack. Compare the top sheet of each stack, take the smaller one, and repeat. Nobody has to look through a whole stack again, because both are already sorted.
merge-sort.why:
When asked to “show a sort”, merge sort is the safest answer — even the worst case is O(n log n), and it is stable.

But the real reason is the merge step. That single step is useful on its own: merging two sorted lists, counting inversions, sorting a linked list, external sorting (when data doesn’t fit in RAM). Remembering merge sort is less important than remembering the merge itself.

How to think:

1. Is the array length 1 (or 0)? It’s already sorted — return it. Base case.
2. Split into two halves at the middle.
3. Recursively sort both halves. (Trust this step — don’t trace by hand.)
4. Merge: two pointers at the start of each list. Take the smaller element, advance its pointer.
5. One list exhausted? Append the remaining part of the other list directly — it’s already sorted.
6. For stability use <= instead of < — when equal, the left one comes first. That’s the distinction between stable and unstable.
where: O(n log n) · space: O(n) extra
O(n log n) · space: O(log n) stack

qa.q: Why is merge sort always O(n log n) while quick sort isn't?
qa.a: Merge sort always splits exactly in half, so depth is always log n and each level costs O(n). Quick sort's pivot can land badly — on already-sorted input it degenerates to O(n²). Merge trades guaranteed time for O(n) space.

qa.q: Why is merge sort good for linked lists?
qa.a: Linked lists have no O(1) random access, so array-sort strategies like indexing and quicksort's partitioning are awkward. Merge sort only needs to walk and rewire pointers — O(n log n) with O(log n) stack space.

partition-algos.name: Quick Sort
partition-algos.desc: Pick a pivot, partition the array so smaller elements sit left and larger right, then recurse on both sides. O(n log n) average, in-place, no extra space — but worst case O(n²) on sorted input with a bad pivot choice.
partition-algos.q: Quick sort vs merge sort — which do you choose and when?
partition-algos.qsub: Why is quick sort not stable? · What does the partition step leave behind that Quick Select reuses? · How much stack space does recursion cost in the worst case?
partition-algos.what:
Pick an element as the pivot. Now rearrange the array so that all elements smaller than the pivot are on the left, larger ones on the right.

Notice one thing — the pivot has reached its final sorted position. You don’t touch it again. Then repeat the same process separately on the left and right subarrays.

It’s the opposite of merge sort: merge sort’s job is joining, quick sort’s job is splitting. So quick sort doesn’t need merge sort's extra array — everything happens in place. But a bad pivot choice leads to O(n²).
partition-algos.analogy: Line up a class by height. Pick one child as the reference: shorter children go to the left, taller ones to the right. Now that child is in the correct position, and you can ignore it from then on. Then do the same separately for the two groups. But if you always pick the smallest child as the reference, each round places only one element correctly, and the work takes n rounds.
partition-algos.why:
Two things are tested. First: pivot selection. If you make the first element the pivot on an already-sorted array, every partition is completely unbalanced — O(n²). Choose a middle or random pivot. This is the answer interviewers want to hear.

Second, and more useful: the partition step itself is an algorithm. Quick Select and Dutch National Flag — the next two topics — are built on exactly this step. Forget quick sort, but don’t forget partition.

How to think:

1. Choose a pivot — middle or random. Don’t fix the first/last.
2. Two pointers: i from the left, j from the right.
3. Move i forward until you find an element that is greater than (or equal to) the pivot. Move j backward until you find a smaller element.
4. When both stop and i <= j → swap, then move both one step.
5. As soon as i > j the array is split into two parts. Recurse on both.
6. Balanced partition → depth log n → O(n log n). If one side is empty each time → depth n → O(n²).
where: O(n log n) · space: O(log n) stack

qa.q: Quick sort vs merge sort — which do you choose and when?
qa.a: Quick sort for in-place O(1) space with average O(n log n) — great for arrays. Merge sort when you need guaranteed O(n log n), stability, or linked lists. If worst-case guarantees matter, merge sort; if memory is tight, quick sort.

qa.q: How do you avoid quick sort's O(n²) worst case?
qa.a: Choose a good pivot — middle element, or median-of-three. A fixed first/last pivot on already-sorted input causes the worst case. Randomizing or taking the middle keeps partitions balanced in practice.

kadanes.name: Kadane's Algorithm
kadanes.desc: Find the maximum-sum contiguous subarray in one pass: at each element, decide whether to EXTEND the current subarray or START a new one. O(n) time, O(1) space. Behind Maximum Subarray and its circular variant.
kadanes.q: What is the ONE decision Kadane's makes per element?
kadanes.qsub: How do you extend Kadane's to return the subarray itself? · How does the circular variant handle all-negative arrays? · Why does best start at -Infinity?
kadanes.what:
Say you have a month of daily profit/loss figures, and you want the continuous stretch with the maximum total.

Brute force: try all stretches — O(n²). Kadane solves the problem with a single question. On each day you make only one decision: extend the previous stretch or start a new one here?

The answer is always one line: if the previous total is negative, staying with it will only reduce your future profit. Drop it and start fresh. That’s it — one pass, O(n), one variable.
kadanes.analogy: Think of an expense ledger. Last week’s balance is −5,000. Today you earn 2,000. Adding to the old balance gives −3,000. Starting a new ledger gives +2,000. Stop carrying the weight that drags you down.
kadanes.why:
This is the smallest version of DP — instead of a full table you keep only one number. That mindset will be needed repeatedly in Phase 7.

And there’s a hidden trap in interviews that many fall into: initializing best = 0. If all numbers are negative ([-3, -1, -7]) the answer becomes 0 — but an empty subarray isn’t allowed. The correct answer is -1.

How to think:

1. Two variables: cur (the total of the current stretch) and best (the best so far).
2. For each element x make one decision: cur = max(x, cur + x).
3. If x wins → start a new stretch here (the previous weight was bad). If cur + x wins → extend the previous stretch.
4. Then best = max(best, cur). Keeping this separate is essential — cur may drop later, but best remembers.
5. Initialize best to -Infinity, not 0.
6. Need indices? When x wins note start = i, and when best updates store [start, i].

qa.q: What is the ONE decision Kadane's makes per element?
qa.a: Whether to extend the current subarray (cur + x) or start a new one at x (cur = x). We extend only when it improves the sum; otherwise the new element starts fresh. The best answer seen is tracked along the way.

qa.q: Why does Kadane's work but brute force is O(n²)?
qa.a: The key insight is optimal substructure — the best subarray ending at i is either just nums[i] or nums[i] plus the best subarray ending at i-1. That single recurrence collapses all O(n²) candidate subarrays into O(n) states.

boyer-moore.name: Boyer-Moore Voting
boyer-moore.desc: Find the majority element (appears more than n/2 times) in O(n) time and O(1) space. Maintain a candidate and a counter: matching votes increment, non-matching decrement, and when the counter hits zero, adopt the current element. A favorite at Meta.
boyer-moore.qsub: Why can't a non-majority element win the voting? · How do you extend it to n/3? · Why is this better than a frequency map here?
boyer-moore.what:
In an array, some element appears more than half the time. We need to find it — O(n) time and O(1) space. A hash map is not allowed (it uses O(n) space).

The trick is hidden in the constraint. "More than half" means: even if you cancel each majority vote with a different vote, some majority votes will remain. All others will be completely eliminated.

So: maintain a candidate and a count. Match → +1. Mismatch → −1. When count becomes 0 → new candidate. At the end, whatever remains is the majority.
boyer-moore.analogy: Think of tug-of-war (rassa-kashi). Each vote pulls to one side, and two opposite votes cut each other out. If a team has more than half the people, after all cancellations some member of that team will still stand. The rope points to them.
boyer-moore.why:
With a frequency map this problem can be solved in 30 seconds — O(n) time, but O(n) space. The interviewer asks the real question: "Can you do it in O(1) space?"

This tests whether you can turn the constraint into a weapon. "> n/2" is not just a condition — it is the core of the algorithm. Recognizing that is the real answer.

How to think:

1. candidate = null, count = 0.
2. For each element x: is count === 0? Then set candidate = x. (The previous candidate has been completely cancelled.)
3. x === candidate → count++. Otherwise count--.
4. That's it. At the end candidate is the majority.
5. Why it works: Each count-- actually cancels one majority vote with one non-majority vote. Non-majority elements have fewer than half the votes, so they can never completely cancel the majority.
6. No guarantee of a majority? Then run a second pass to count the candidate and confirm it.

qa.q: Why does Boyer-Moore work?
qa.a: Pair up each occurrence of the majority element with a non-majority element; there are more majority elements than all others combined, so after all cancellations something survives — and it must be the majority. The counter is just bookkeeping for the pairing.

qa.q: Does it need a verification pass?
qa.a: If the problem guarantees a majority exists, no. If not, the candidate could be wrong — count it and confirm it exceeds n/2. Safe interview practice is to verify even when the guarantee exists.

quick-select.name: Quick Select
quick-select.desc: Find the k-th smallest/largest element without fully sorting: run the partition step, and only recurse into the side that contains the target index. O(n) average, O(1) extra space, O(n²) worst case.
quick-select.q: Why is Quick Select O(n) average instead of O(n log n)?
quick-select.qsub: What's the target index for k-th smallest vs k-th largest? · How does partition order guarantee the left side is all smaller? · Why doesn't the worst case show up on random data?
quick-select.what:
We need the k-th largest element. The simplest way is to sort the whole array and pick the index — O(n log n). But that ranks the entire list even though we only need one rank.

Quick Select uses the same partition step as Quick Sort. After partition the pivot is in its final position — say p. Now one of three things is true:

p === k → found. p < k → the answer is on the right. p > k → on the left. Each time you go to only one side and discard the other completely. So the work is n + n/2 + n/4 + … = 2n — O(n) average.
quick-select.analogy: A race is over and you only need to know who came 5th. Ranking the whole list is wasteful. Pick one runner as a reference and split everyone into those ahead of him and those behind — now his rank is fixed. If he finished 8th, the 5th-place runner must be in the group ahead of him, so look only there and forget the rest.
quick-select.why:
The interviewer asks about “kth largest” because there are three possible answers, each correct in different situations:

Sort + index — O(n log n), the simplest. Min-heap of size k — O(n log k), best for streaming. Quick Select — O(n) average, but it mutates the input and has a worst-case of O(n²). Mention all three and say when to use which — that’s the complete answer.

How to think:

1. Want the k-th largest? Convert to an index: target = n - k. (k-th smallest → target = k - 1.) This conversion is the most common mistake.
2. Run partition from lo to hi — the same Lomuto scheme used in quick sort.
3. Partition returns the pivot’s final position p.
4. If p === target → nums[target] is the answer. Stop.
5. If p < target → lo = p + 1. Otherwise hi = p - 1. Only one side.
6. To avoid the worst case, choose the pivot randomly — otherwise a sorted input gives O(n²).

qa.q: Why is Quick Select O(n) average instead of O(n log n)?
qa.a: Because we recurse into only ONE side, not both. The work is n + n/2 + n/4 + ... which converges to 2n. It's O(n²) worst case when every pivot is extreme — same risk as quick sort.

qa.q: Quick Select vs a heap for k-th largest — which when?
qa.a: Heap is O(n log k) and reads the top k in order. Quick Select is O(n) average for just the one answer, but mutates the array and doesn't preserve order. If you need the sorted top-k, heap; if only the k-th value, quick select.

dutch-national-flag.name: Dutch National Flag
dutch-national-flag.desc: Sort an array of three distinct values (like 0s, 1s, 2s) in one pass with O(1) space using three pointers. It's the three-way partition technique powering Sort Colors.
dutch-national-flag.q: Why don't you advance mid after swapping with hi?
dutch-national-flag.qsub: What's the exact invariant at the start and end of each iteration? · How would this generalize to k colors? · Why is it called the 'Dutch national flag'?
dutch-national-flag.what:
The array contains only three distinct values — 0, 1, 2. It must be sorted in a single pass and without extra space.

Three pointers create three zones. Everything to the left of lo is already 0. Everything to the right of hi is already 2. mid moves in the middle — and everything between lo and mid is 1.

The one mistake everyone makes: after swapping with hi, mid should not be advanced. The element that came from the right has not been examined yet.
dutch-national-flag.analogy: Imagine sorting laundry into three zones — white on the left, colored in the middle, black on the right — while picking items from the middle. If it's white → toss it to the left and move forward. If it's colored → leave it where it is and move forward. If it's black → toss it to the right — but the item that came from the right hasn't been seen yet. Don't move forward; examine it first.
dutch-national-flag.why:
This is the three-way version of Quick Sort's partition — useful when the array contains a lot of duplicates. A normal two-way partition performs poorly with duplicates; three-way groups all equal elements together.

Interviews often add a twist: counting sort (two passes — count, then write) is also O(n). The interviewer will say "do it in a single pass". That's when DNF is needed.

How to think:

1. lo = 0, mid = 0, hi = n - 1.
