2. Remember the invariant: [0, lo) all 0 · [lo, mid) all 1 · (hi, n) all 2 · [mid, hi] not yet examined.
3. nums[mid] === 0 → swap with lo, then both lo++ and mid++. (The element that came from lo was a 1 — already examined.)
4. nums[mid] === 1 → already in the right place. Only mid++.
5. nums[mid] === 2 → swap with hi, hi--, and leave mid unchanged. The new element has not been examined yet.
6. Stop when mid > hi. One pass, O(n), O(1) space.

qa.q: Why don't you advance mid after swapping with hi?
qa.a: The value swapped in from hi is unexamined — it could be a 0 that belongs at lo. So the loop re-checks it at the same mid index. Swaps with lo DO advance mid because the value swapped in was just checked (it was a 1, or was already < mid).

qa.q: When is three-way partitioning better than counting and rewriting?
qa.a: Counting 0s/1s/2s and rewriting is also O(n) but needs a second pass. Dutch National Flag is one pass in place — required when the problem forbids extra arrays or counts, and it generalizes the two-pointer pattern.

insertion-sort.name: Insertion Sort
insertion-sort.desc: Build the sorted array one element at a time: take each element and insert it into the already-sorted prefix, shifting larger elements right. O(n^2) worst but O(n) on nearly-sorted input — and stable, in-place, and the fastest sort for tiny arrays.
insertion-sort.q: When is insertion sort actually the right choice?
insertion-sort.qsub: What happens on an already-sorted array? How many shifts? · Why does the best case run in O(n)? · How does shifting differ from swapping?
insertion-sort.what:
Think of playing cards. You pick up a new card, and the cards already in your hand are sorted. You insert the new card into its correct position, shifting larger cards slightly to the right. You don’t rebuild the whole hand.

This is insertion sort. Treat the array’s prefix as always sorted, and insert each new element into that prefix at its proper spot.

Its key property: it is adaptive. When the data is already nearly sorted, no shifts are needed — O(n). Merge sort and quick sort still run the full O(n log n) in that case.
insertion-sort.analogy: Think of a hand of cards. A new card arrives — you look at it and place it directly in the right spot, shifting larger cards a bit. If the cards are already in order, each new card simply goes at the end — no work at all.
insertion-sort.why:
The interviewer will not ask you to implement an O(n²) sort just for the sake of it. They want to see that you understand that the choice of algorithm depends on the shape of the input.

And a real fact: actual sorting libraries rely on this. Timsort (Python, Java, V8) runs insertion sort on small runs, then merges. Introsort (C++) also switches to insertion sort on small partitions. That's because for small n, the constant factors of O(n log n) cost more than a simple O(n²) pass.

How to think:

1. Start with i = 1. Assume [0, i) is already sorted (a one-element prefix is always sorted).
2. Save cur = arr[i] in a variable — its spot will be overwritten.
3. Move backward with j = i - 1. While arr[j] > cur, shift that element one position right: arr[j+1] = arr[j].
4. When the loop stops, the remaining gap is where cur belongs — arr[j+1] = cur.
5. Note: this is shifting, not swapping. A shift does one write, a swap does three, so it’s faster.
6. Use >, not >= — stopping on equality gives stability.

qa.q: When is insertion sort actually the right choice?
qa.a: Nearly-sorted data: each element shifts only a little, so the inner loop is O(1) on average and the whole thing is O(n). Also tiny arrays (n < ~15) where O(n^2) beats the recursion and allocation overhead of merge/quick.

qa.q: Why is it stable?
qa.a: The inner loop only shifts elements that are STRICTLY greater than cur (arr[j] > cur). Equal elements are never moved past each other, so original relative order is preserved.

string-matching.name: String Matching (KMP / Rabin-Karp)
string-matching.desc: Finding a pattern in a text. Naive scanning is O(n*m); KMP precomputes a prefix function so the text pointer never backtracks (O(n+m)); Rabin-Karp uses a rolling hash to compare in O(1) per window. Know both: KMP for worst-case guarantees, Rabin-Karp for multiple patterns.
string-matching.q: Why is KMP O(n+m) when naive is O(n*m)?
string-matching.qsub: What does the lps array store, conceptually? · Why does Rabin-Karp use modulo arithmetic? · What is the worst case for Rabin-Karp and when does it hit it? · How would you find all occurrences of a pattern in a text?
string-matching.what:
We need to find a pattern in a long text. The straightforward way is to try matching at every position. Mismatch? Move one step forward in the text and start over — O(n×m).

This is wasted work: before the mismatch you are re-comparing characters that have already matched.

KMP avoids this work. It first preprocesses the pattern itself into an lps table, which tells it how far to shift the pattern on a mismatch. The text pointer never moves backward. Hence O(n + m).

Rabin-Karp takes a completely different route: keep a rolling hash for each window. If the hash doesn’t match → skip, O(1). If the hash matches → then compare the characters.
string-matching.analogy:
KMP: If you slip up on a line in the middle of a song, you don’t restart the whole song. You know how much of the lyrics already matched, so you continue from there.
Rabin-Karp: Give each page a short summary code. If the code isn’t found, don’t open the page. If the code is found, then read the whole page.
string-matching.why:
This topic shows two fundamentally different ways to speed up the same problem: pre-processing the pattern (KMP) and hashing (Rabin-Karp).

Practically: in an interview, if strStr comes up, just saying indexOf isn’t enough. Explaining the KMP idea — “the text pointer never backtracks” — can earn points even without writing full code. Rabin-Karp is better when you need to search many patterns at once, or find duplicate substrings.

How to think:

1. lps table: For each position i — the length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix of it. For "ABAB", lps[3] = 2 because "AB" appears on both sides.
2. How to build the table: match the pattern against itself — same loop, advance i, and on a mismatch set j to lps[j-1].
3. Scan: run i over the text, j over the pattern.
4. If characters match → advance both. If mismatch → j = lps[j-1] — don’t move i.
5. When j === m → pattern found, index i - m + 1.
6. Rabin-Karp: compute the hash of the first window. When moving forward, subtract the old character and add the new one — O(1). If the hash matches, still compare the characters — two different strings can have the same hash.

qa.q: Why is KMP O(n+m) when naive is O(n*m)?
qa.a: The lps table tells KMP exactly how far back to shift on a mismatch, so the text pointer never resets. Naive restarts from the next text position on every mismatch, revisiting characters O(n*m) times.

qa.q: When is Rabin-Karp the better choice?
qa.a: When searching for many patterns at once (like detecting duplicate code or searching a corpus), because you can keep one rolling hash and test every pattern hash in O(1). Its weakness is hash collisions, fixed with re-checking.

two-pointers.name: Two Pointers
two-pointers.desc: Two indices scan the array from the ends (or different speeds) to replace an O(n²) nested loop with one O(n) pass. The two ends of the array 'meet in the middle', exploiting the sorted structure.
two-pointers.q: When can two pointers replace a nested loop?
two-pointers.qsub: How do you avoid duplicate triples in 3Sum? · When do you use fast/slow pointers instead of left/right? · Does two pointers require the array to be sorted?
two-pointers.what:
The array is sorted. We need to find two numbers whose sum equals the target. First idea: pair every number with every other number — a nested loop, O(n²).

But wait — the array is sorted. It contains information you’re ignoring.

Place two pointers — one at the start, one at the end. If the sum is too large, move the right pointer inward (remove the larger number). If the sum is too small, move the left pointer forward. At each step the search space shrinks by one, so the whole array is processed in a single pass — O(n), with no extra space.
two-pointers.analogy: Imagine two ticket inspectors on a local train: one starts at the front coach and walks toward the back, the other starts at the rear and walks toward the front. They meet in the middle, and the whole train has been checked without either of them walking its full length.
two-pointers.why:
The interviewer asks this because the pattern reveals whether you think beyond brute force — can you spot extra information (sorted order, monotonic property) and use it to eliminate an entire loop. Without that, your solution remains at O(n^2), while the interviewer expects O(n).

How to think:

1. Place one pointer at the start of the array and the other at the end.
2. Compute the sum of the values at both pointers and compare it to the target.
3. If the sum is greater than the target, move the right pointer one step left — because you need to remove the larger number.
4. If the sum is less than the target, move the left pointer one step right — because you need a bigger value in place of the smaller one.
5. If the sum equals the target, you have found the answer.
6. Continue this process until the two pointers meet — each step reduces the search space by one, so the total work is only proportional to the array’s length.

qa.q: When can two pointers replace a nested loop?
qa.a: When the array has structure (sorted, or a monotonic property) that lets you commit to moving one pointer without checking all remaining pairs. Two Sum: if the sum is too small, every pair with the left pointer is too small — so move left, no rescan needed.

qa.q: Why shrink the shorter side in Container With Most Water?
qa.a: The area is bounded by the shorter line. Moving the taller line inward can never increase area (height stays bounded by the shorter, width shrinks). Moving the shorter one is the only move that could improve — so that's the only one worth trying.

bucket-sort.name: Bucket Sort
bucket-sort.desc: Distribute elements into k ordered buckets by value range, sort each bucket (often with insertion sort), then concatenate in order. O(n + k) average when values spread uniformly; degenerates to O(n^2) when they all land in one bucket.
bucket-sort.q: Why is average case O(n + k)?
bucket-sort.qsub: How do you pick the bucket index formula? · What is the space overhead if k = n? · Why does uniform distribution matter so much?
bucket-sort.what:
Here is a well-known fact: sorting by comparison cannot be faster than O(n log n). This is a theorem.

Bucket sort breaks that limit — because it doesn’t compare at all. It leverages the values' range: by looking at each value it can directly tell which bucket it belongs to.

Three steps: scatter (distribute according to range) → sort (each bucket is small, insertion sort suffices) → gather (concatenate the buckets in order). The only condition is that the data must be evenly spread. If everything ends up in one bucket then O(n²).
bucket-sort.analogy: Think of a post office. Letters are first placed into separate bags based on pincode range — no comparison, just read the pincode and put them in the bag. Then the letters inside each bag are sorted individually. The order of the bags is the actual sorting — finally just concatenate.
bucket-sort.why:
This topic answers a conceptual question: "Is a sort faster than O(n log n) possible?" Answer: not with comparison-based sorts. But if you know something about the values' range/distribution, then yes.

The same idea underlies counting sort and radix sort. The most common interview form is "top K by frequency" — there the frequency (0 to n) becomes the bucket index, and the whole work becomes O(n).

How to think:

1. Extract min and max, and decide how many buckets (k) are needed. Often we take k = n.
2. Scatter: compute each value’s bucket index — ((x - min) / (max - min)) × k, then floor.
3. The largest value may give an index equal to k — out of range. Clamp it with Math.min(k - 1, idx).
4. Sort: sort each bucket separately. Buckets are small, so insertion sort is best.
5. Gather: concatenate the buckets from 0 to k-1 in order — total work O(n + k). That's it — the whole array is sorted.
6. Uniform distribution → about 1 element per bucket → O(n) overall. If everything ends up in one bucket → one big O(n²) insertion sort → the speed-up is lost.

qa.q: Why is average case O(n + k)?
qa.a: Scattering and gathering each touch every element once (O(n)). If the distribution is uniform, each bucket holds ~n/k elements, and insertion-sorting them costs O((n/k)^2) per bucket — k buckets total O(k·(n/k)^2) = O(n²/k), which for k ≈ n is O(n).

qa.q: When does it degenerate to O(n^2)?
qa.a: When the distribution is NOT uniform — e.g. all values pile into one bucket. That bucket now contains n elements and insertion sort on it is O(n²). Bucket sort is only fast for known well-spread distributions.

search-range.name: Binary Search on a Range
search-range.desc: The lower-bound/upper-bound form of binary search: find the FIRST index where the predicate becomes true (or the first element >= target). Unlocks first/last occurrence, insertion position, and counting occurrences — problems where plain 'find target' binary search is not enough.
search-range.q: Why hi = mid instead of hi = mid - 1 here?
search-range.qsub: Why does hi start at arr.length (not length-1)? · What does lowerBound return when the target is absent? · How do you adapt this for a peak or rotated array?
search-range.what:
Normal binary search looks for a value. This version looks for a boundary — the first position where a condition changes from false to true.

The whole idea in one line: view the array as F F F F T T T T instead of actual values. You need the first T. That's it.

It is more powerful because it works with duplicates (first or last occurrence), and because the "condition" can be anything — e.g., "Will task x finish in h hours at a given speed?" This is binary search on the answer.
search-range.analogy: Think of mobile network in a tall building: absent on the lower floors, present on the higher ones — and once it appears it stays present above. You need to find the first floor where the network starts. You don’t have to stop at every floor — jump to a middle floor, check, and discard half the building.
search-range.why:
This is the base of the "binary search on the answer" family — and that family shows up most often in FAANG interviews.

The problem may not give you a sorted array at all. It might ask: "What is the minimum speed required so that the work finishes in h hours?" You have to recognize that the answer range has a monotonic yes/no condition — and that recognition is the actual answer. After that the code is only 8 lines.

How to think:

1. lo = 0, hi = n — not n - 1, because the answer could be “insert at the end”.
2. Loop with while (lo < hi), not <=. This template converges on the answer instead of exiting on a match.
3. Compute mid = lo + ((hi - lo) >> 1) and check the condition at mid.
4. If the condition is false (for example arr[mid] < target) → the answer is later → lo = mid + 1.
5. If the condition is true → mid itself could be the answer → hi = mid. Not hi = mid - 1 — that could discard the answer.
6. The loop ends when lo === hi — that is the boundary. Return lo.

qa.q: Why hi = mid instead of hi = mid - 1 here?
qa.a: We are converging to a BOUNDARY, not pinning a match. When arr[mid] >= target, mid could itself be the first such index, so discarding it with mid-1 can skip the answer. Keeping mid lets the range shrink to exactly the boundary.

qa.q: How does this find first AND last occurrence?
qa.a: lowerBound finds the first index with value >= target. To find the last occurrence, compute the first index > target and step back one. The gap between the two bounds is exactly the count of target.

sliding-window.name: Sliding Window
sliding-window.desc: Maintain a contiguous window with two pointers that 'slide' across the array. For each element, either extend the window or shrink it to restore the invariant. Converts O(n²) substring scans into O(n).
sliding-window.q: What is the ONE question to ask before sliding window?
sliding-window.qsub: Why is each element visited at most twice? · How do you prove the O(n) bound? · What changes for a fixed-size window?
sliding-window.what:
In a string or array, find the longest (or shortest) contiguous segment that satisfies a condition. Naive method: try every start and end — O(n²).

But when moving from one start to the next, there is no need to redo the entire work. Just consider: what is new, and what has left.

This is the sliding window — a moving range that you expand (right moves forward) and shrink (left moves forward) so that the condition is satisfied again. Right moves through the whole array once, left also once — total O(n).
sliding-window.analogy: Imagine in a WhatsApp group chat you need to show the context of the last 5 messages as a new message arrives — you don't reread the entire chat history, you just remove the oldest message from the list and add the new one, so the window always stays at 5 messages.
sliding-window.why:
This pattern tests whether you can avoid redundant recomputation. Both fixed-size windows (e.g., 'subarray of size k') and variable-size windows (e.g., 'smallest subarray with sum ≥ target') show the interviewer that you know how to go from O(n^2) to O(n) without breaking correctness.

How to think:

1. Place both a left and a right pointer at the start of the array — the window is initially empty.
2. Move the right pointer forward, add the new element to the window, and update the window state (sum, count, or set).
3. Check whether the window is still valid or the condition has been violated.
4. If the condition is violated (in a fixed-size case the size grew, or in a variable-size case the invariant failed), move the left pointer forward and remove that element from the window until the condition is restored.
5. For every valid window, keep updating the answer (length, sum, or count).
6. The right pointer traverses the entire array only once and the left pointer also only moves forward, never backward — therefore the total movement is O(n).

qa.q: What is the ONE question to ask before sliding window?
qa.a: What invariant must the window satisfy? For 'longest without repeating' it's 'no duplicate chars in window'; for 'minimum window with all chars' it's 'contains all needed chars'. Everything else — shrink logic and answer updates — follows mechanically from the invariant.

qa.q: When does sliding window NOT apply?
qa.a: When the answer can't be represented as a contiguous window — subsequences (order-preserving, skippable) need DP, and problems with negative weights may break the monotonic shrink property. If adding an element doesn't monotonically violate the condition, the window can't slide.

binary-search-2.name: Binary Search (minimize/maximize)
binary-search-2.desc: The same halving idea applied to the space of answers, not just arrays: when feasibility is monotonic, binary search the answer value. Behind Koko, Split Array, and Capacity-to-Ship problems.
binary-search-2.q: How do you recognize this pattern?
binary-search-2.qsub: What if the answer range is huge (10^9)? · How do you pick lo for a 'maximize minimum' variant? · Why does the check have to be monotonic?
binary-search-2.what:
“What minimum eating speed finishes all the bananas before the guard returns?” There is no sorted array here — but the answer lies in a range, say from 1 to 1,000,000.

Trying every value is slow. But notice one thing: speeds below a certain point fail, and from that point on every speed works. This is monotonic — F F F F T T T T.

So run binary search on the value of the answer, not on array indices. For each guess perform a feasible(x) check (usually O(n)) and discard half of the range based on the result. Total O(log R × n).
binary-search-2.analogy: Imagine you're haggling for a TV: you ask the seller “will you give it for 5000?”, and if not, “7500?”. You keep halving the price range until you find the minimum acceptable price. There's no array here — just a search along a number line.
binary-search-2.why:
This is a big mental shift that interviewers specifically test — whether you can recognize that binary search is applicable not only to sorted arrays but to any monotonic feasibility function. Without this, candidates keep trying linear search or brute force and exceed the time limit, while this pattern gives O(log(range) * check_cost).

How to think:

1. Decide the possible minimum and maximum values of the answer — this becomes your search range, not an array.
2. Take the middle value of the range (mid) and run a 'feasibility check' function — can the problem be solved with this mid value?
3. If mid is feasible and you need the minimum, record the answer and move the range to the lower half (try smaller values).
4. If mid is not feasible, move the range to the upper half (try larger values).
5. In the maximize case the logic is reversed — if feasible, try larger values; if not, try smaller.
6. When the range converges to a single point, that is your optimal answer.

qa.q: How do you recognize this pattern?
qa.a: The answer is a single number with a natural range (1..max), and checking 'does answer x work?' is easy but you'd otherwise have to test every value. The deciding feature: feasibility is MONOTONIC — once a value works, everything beyond it works too.

qa.q: Why while (lo < hi) instead of while (lo <= hi)?
qa.a: In answer-space search we converge to a single boundary index rather than find an exact hit, and there's always a valid answer in range. The lo < hi with hi = mid form converges cleanly without checking mid twice or risking an off-by-one on exact matches.

prefix-sum.name: Prefix Sum
prefix-sum.desc: Precompute prefix[i] = sum of the first i elements. Then any subarray sum [l, r) is prefix[r] - prefix[l] in O(1). The extension — prefix-sum counts in a hash map — solves 'subarray sum equals k'.
prefix-sum.qsub: How does 2D prefix sum answer rectangle queries? · What does the Map[[0,1]] seed do? · How would you find the longest subarray with sum k?
prefix-sum.what:
"What is the sum from index 3 to 7?" — and this question keeps coming up for different ranges. Running a loop each time costs O(n) per query. 1,000 queries would be very slow.

Compute prefix[i] once — the running total from the start up to i. Now the sum of any range becomes a difference: prefix[r] − prefix[l]. One O(n) preprocessing, then each query is O(1).

And the real power comes next: store prefix sums in a hash map. Now you can also count how many subarrays have sum exactly k in a single pass — because you can check in O(1) whether sum − k has been seen before.
prefix-sum.analogy: Imagine a ledger (register) where each day’s “total expense up to today” is recorded, not just that day’s expense. If you want the total expense from date 5 to date 10, you subtract the running total of date 4 from the running total of date 10 — you don’t have to add anything anew each time.
prefix-sum.why:
This pattern tests whether you can make repeated range queries fast by precomputing. Without it, problems like range-sum or subarray-sum-equals-k stay at O(n^2). Adding a hash map to prefix sums (prefix-sum-to-count) tests another level — can you convert cumulative state into a lookup-friendly structure.

How to think:

1. Create a new array where the first element equals the first element of the original array.
2. At each subsequent index, add the previous prefix value to the current original value — this builds the running total up to that position.
3. To get the sum of any range (i to j), subtract prefix[i-1] from prefix[j].
4. If you need to count subarrays whose sum equals k, create a hash map that stores the frequency of each prefix sum.
5. While traversing the array once, compute the current prefix sum and check how many times current_prefix - k has already appeared in the hash map — add that count to the answer.
6. After each step, also update the hash map with the current prefix sum.

qa.q: Why does prefix[0] = 0 help?
qa.a: It makes range queries uniform — sum [l, r) is prefix[r] - prefix[l] without special-casing l = 0. Many off-by-one bugs disappear once you keep the zero-sentinel prefix.

qa.q: How does the hash-map trick count subarrays equal to k?
qa.a: A subarray [i, j] sums to k iff prefix[j] - prefix[i-1] = k, i.e. prefix[i-1] = prefix[j] - k. As you scan, every earlier running sum equal to current - k yields one valid subarray — a single O(1) map lookup per step.

intervals.name: Intervals
intervals.desc: Problems about ranges [start, end] — merging, inserting, counting overlaps. The near-universal trick is to SORT by start time, then compare each interval's start against the running end. Overlap test: next.start <= current.end.
intervals.q: What's the first move for almost every interval problem?
intervals.qsub: What's the difference between 'merge' and 'insert' strategies? · How does the greedy proof work for arrows/balloons? · When do you compare by start vs by end?
intervals.what:
There is a list of meetings, each with a start and end. You need to find overlaps, or merge them all into a clean schedule.

Comparing every interval with every other costs O(n²). But if you first sort everything by start time, the whole game changes.

In sorted order, if an interval doesn't overlap the one right after it, it can't overlap any later one either. So checking only the neighbor is enough — one pass, and the total cost is just the sorting: O(n log n). Merging, inserting, counting — all rely on this single trick.
intervals.analogy: Imagine a conference room booking sheet — if you sort all bookings by their start time, you only need to check that each next booking does not start before the previous booking ends — you don’t have to cross-check the entire list repeatedly.
intervals.why:
The interviewer wants to see that you know overlap detection can be done in O(n log n) (thanks to sorting) instead of O(n^2) — and how sorting simplifies the problem’s structure. Without sorting, handling edge cases (partial overlap, containment, touching intervals) in merge and insert operations becomes very messy.

How to think:

1. Sort all intervals by their start value.
2. Start a ‘result’ list and insert the first interval into it.
3. Process the remaining intervals one by one — compare the current interval with the last interval in the result.
4. If the current interval’s start is less than or equal to the last interval’s end, they overlap — merge them (keep the larger end).
5. If there is no overlap, add the current interval to the result list as a new entry.
6. Continue until all intervals are processed — the result list is now the final merged, non-overlapping intervals list.
where: O(n log n) · space: O(n) output

qa.q: What's the first move for almost every interval problem?
qa.a: Sort — by start for merging, by end for 'max non-overlapping'. Intervals have no inherent order, so sorting imposes the structure that makes a linear sweep meaningful.

qa.q: Why does sorting by end maximize the number of non-overlapping intervals?
qa.a: A greedy choice: taking the interval that ends earliest leaves the most room for the rest. This is the classic interval-scheduling proof — if any optimal solution differs, swapping in the earliest-ending interval never hurts.

weekly-mock.name: Weekly Timed Mock
weekly-mock.desc: From this phase onward: one 45-minute timed mock every week — 2 problems, no hints, talking out loud. Solving in your room and solving under a clock are different skills; start training the second one now, not in week 23.
weekly-mock.q: Which problems go into a weekly mock?
weekly-mock.qsub: Did I say the brute force and its complexity within the first 5 minutes? · Did I go silent for more than 30 seconds? · Did I test with an example before saying "done"?
weekly-mock.what: Once every week, set a 45-minute timer, pick two problems, and solve them out loud — as if the interviewer is sitting in front of you. Record the screen and audio on your phone.
weekly-mock.why:
Google’s round tests performance more than knowledge: in about 20–25 minutes you solve a Medium problem while thinking out loud and catching edge cases yourself. This habit doesn’t develop in four weeks — so start from Phase 3 (week 7) so that by Phase 9 you have completed around 15 mocks.

How to think:

0-5 min: restate the problem, clarify constraints and examples.
5-10 min: state the brute-force solution and its complexity, then propose a better approach.
10-30 min: write code while continuing to talk.
30-40 min: dry-run, consider edge cases, discuss complexity.
Afterwards watch the recording: note where you went silent or got stuck — fix that habit for next week.
where: 10-15 min after · space: log in P9 → Timed Mock template

qa.q: Which problems go into a weekly mock?
qa.a: One from the current phase and one from an older phase you have not touched in 2+ weeks. Pick problems you have NOT solved before when possible (use the LeetCode list for the same pattern). The old-phase problem doubles as spaced repetition.

qa.q: What if I fail the mock?
qa.a: That is the point — a failed mock in week 8 is cheap, a failed onsite is not. Write down WHERE you got stuck (understanding, approach, code, or bugs) and re-solve that exact problem 3 days later without looking.

binary-tree.name: Binary Tree Structure
binary-tree.desc: A hierarchical structure where each node has at most two children (left, right). Recursive by nature — every subtree is itself a binary tree, which is why recursion is the natural tool.
binary-tree.q: Why is recursion natural for trees?
binary-tree.qsub: What's a leaf node? A full vs complete vs perfect tree? · Why does height() return 0 for null? · How would you build a tree from an array representation?
binary-tree.what:
Each node has at most two children — left and right. That's all.

But the key point is: every subtree is itself a complete tree. Pick any node — its left subtree is a valid binary tree on its own. The structure repeats itself.

That’s why tree problems are solved with recursion. You don’t have to think about the whole tree — just three things: what to do with this node, what answer comes from the left, what answer comes from the right. The rest is handled by recursion.
binary-tree.analogy: Company org chart. You ask your two direct reports, "what's the status of the people below you?" — they themselves handle the accounting for the 200 people under them. You don’t need to see the whole company, just the two people.
binary-tree.why:
This is the foundation of the entire Phase 4. Anyone who can break a problem down into “what to do with this node + the answers from its two children” finds DFS, BFS, height, diameter — all easy.

And there’s a hidden trap: binary tree and BST are different things. In a binary tree the values have no order. Assuming a “tree” is sorted is the most common mistake — ask first.

How to think:

1. Each node has three parts: its value, a reference to left, and a reference to right.
2. No child? The reference is null — that’s your base case.
3. root is the topmost node with no parent. Lose it and you lose the whole tree.
4. Every recursive function follows the same pattern: if (!node) return <empty answer> → get answer from left → get answer from right → combine both with this node.
5. The “empty answer” depends on the problem — 0 for count, 0 for sum, false for exists, [] for list.
6. Space is O(h) — the stack holds one frame per level of the tree. Balanced: O(log n), skewed: O(n).

qa.q: Why is recursion natural for trees?
qa.a: A binary tree is defined recursively: a node plus two (possibly empty) binary trees. The recursive function mirrors the definition exactly — handle the empty case, trust the call for each child, combine results. Iteration needs a manual stack/queue instead.

qa.q: What's the space complexity of tree recursion?
qa.a: O(h), the height — the call stack holds one frame per level of the tree. Balanced: O(log n). Degenerate (every node has one child): O(n). An iterative traversal with an explicit stack has the same worst case but no native stack-overflow risk.

dfs.name: DFS (Preorder / Inorder / Postorder)
dfs.desc: Depth-first search visits a node and recurses down one whole subtree before the other. The three orders differ only in WHEN you process the node: before children (pre), between (in), after (post).
dfs.qsub: How do you write DFS iteratively? · What's the difference between a 'path' and a 'subtree' in DFS? · Why does preorder + inorder uniquely reconstruct a binary tree?
dfs.what:
DFS means: go all the way down in one subtree before moving to the other. It's a single path — the three "orders" are not different traversals.

The only difference is: when do you touch the node? Before visiting children (preorder), after left but before right (inorder), or after both (postorder).

And this timing is not a useless detail — the problem determines it. Does the answer depend on the children (height, diameter)? Postorder. Need sorted output from a BST? Inorder. Want to copy or serialize a tree? Preorder.
dfs.analogy:
Imagine boxes inside a cupboard, with more boxes inside those. You open one box, go in completely through its first sub-box, and only then come back to open the next.
The three orders depend on when you jot a note: as soon as you open the box, in the middle, or while closing it. The route stays exactly the same.
dfs.why:
The interviewer isn’t looking for whether you can write three functions. They want to see if you can choose the correct order or not.

The most useful insight: you need postorder when a node’s answer is built from its children’s answers. Height, diameter, "is it balanced", "sum of this subtree" — all are postorder. And inorder is the BST’s "secret weapon" — sorted output for free.

How to think:

1. if (!node) return — always the first line.
2. Preorder: process the node → go fully into left → go fully into right.
3. Inorder: go fully into left → process node → go into right.
4. Postorder: left → right → then process node. At this point the node already has both children’s answers.
5. Need to remember the path (path problems)? Carry an array down, and on the way back pop() — that’s backtracking.
6. Time is always O(n) — each node once. Space O(h) — stack.

qa.q: When do you use postorder?
qa.a: When the answer at a node depends on its children's answers — height, diameter, max path sum, balance checks. You must compute children first, which is exactly postorder. Preorder is for when you can decide at the node before descending.

qa.q: What is inorder traversal of a BST useful for?
qa.a: It visits nodes in sorted order. That powers Kth Smallest in a BST and validating a BST (check the sequence is strictly increasing).

bfs.name: BFS (Level Order)
bfs.desc: Breadth-first search visits level by level using a queue: process all nodes at depth d before any at depth d+1. The queue-size snapshot trick cleanly separates levels.
bfs.q: Why do you snapshot the queue size?
bfs.qsub: How do you find the tree's minimum depth with BFS early-exit? · What's the queue's worst-case width? · How would you detect if a tree is a perfect binary tree with BFS?
bfs.what:
Think of a building floor by floor. First all rooms on the ground floor, then the first floor, then the second. You don’t jump straight to the top from a single room.

Recursion can’t do this — recursion’s nature is to go down in one direction. That’s why you need a queue here: first in, first out.

The only trick for the whole BFS is: measure the queue size before starting a level. That many nodes belong to the current level — nodes added afterwards belong to the next level. This single line cleanly separates levels.
bfs.analogy: Throw a stone into a pond. The ripples spread in concentric rings — first all at distance 1 step, then those at distance 2 steps. So the thing you encounter first is the closest. The entire answer to the shortest-path problem lies in this one fact.
bfs.why:
Two reasons. First: you need a level-wise answer — "average per level", "right side view", "zigzag". It can be done with DFS but gets heavy.

Second, and bigger: shortest path. Need the minimum depth? DFS may wander deep into a subtree while the answer was in a shallow branch. BFS reaches a node the first time at the smallest distance — guaranteed.

How to think:

1. Create a queue and enqueue root. (Check !root first.)
2. While the queue is not empty, run the loop.
3. At the start of the loop, set size = queue.length — this is the count for the current level.
4. Exactly size times: dequeue a node from the front, process it, and enqueue its left and right children if they exist.
5. After removing that many nodes, one level is done. The next iteration handles the next level.
6. In JS, don’t use shift() — it’s O(n). Keep a head index and increment it.

qa.q: Why do you snapshot the queue size?
qa.a: Without it, the inner loop would keep draining newly-enqueued children, merging levels together. The snapshot fixes how many nodes belong to the current level before you add any of the next level.

qa.q: BFS vs DFS on a tree — when do you choose BFS?
qa.a: BFS when the answer is level-based or you want shortest path (fewest edges). DFS when you need recursion's simplicity for path/sum computations. BFS typically uses more memory (queue width) than DFS (stack depth) on wide trees.

bst.name: Binary Search Tree
bst.desc: A binary tree with the ordering invariant: left subtree < node < right subtree. Searches halve the space each step — O(log n) on balanced trees. Inorder traversal yields sorted order.
bst.q: How do you validate a BST without comparing to global min/max?
bst.qsub: What makes a BST unbalanced, and what's the worst-case height? · How do you insert without breaking the invariant? · How would you find the lowest common ancestor in a BST (using values)?
bst.what:
In a binary tree, values have no order. In a BST, a rule applies: all values in the left subtree are smaller than the node, all values in the right subtree are larger.

With just this rule, each comparison eliminates half the tree. Binary search, but on a tree instead of an array — O(h).

And a free bonus: inorder traversal yields sorted values. Because inorder means "first all smaller, then the node, then all larger". Hence many BST questions (kth smallest, validate, range sum) are solved with inorder.

But remember: O(log n) only when the tree is balanced. If you insert sorted data, the tree becomes a linked list — O(n).
bst.analogy: Imagine a register where each page follows a rule: smaller names go on the left, larger names on the right. Need to find a name? You don't read the whole register — each page makes a single decision: left or right. But if the names are entered in alphabetical order, they all end up on one side — and the register becomes a long list again.
bst.why:
Validating a BST is a classic interview trap. People compare only with the parent — which is wrong. A node must respect the limits of all its ancestors. So you have to pass (lo, hi) bounds down.

Another test: claim O(log n) without mentioning balance. On a skewed BST everything is O(n). Stating this caveat earns extra points.

How to think:

1. Search: start at root. Target smaller → left. Larger → right. Equal → found.
2. Insert: follow the same path until null is reached — insert the new node there.
3. Validate: give each node a (lo, hi) range. When going left set hi = node.val, when going right set lo = node.val. Comparing only with the parent is wrong.
4. Kth smallest: perform inorder traversal and count — the k-th element is the answer.
5. Delete has three cases: no child → remove. One child → replace with that child. Two children → bring the inorder successor (smallest in the right subtree), then delete it.
6. Everything is O(h). Balanced → log n. Skewed → n.

qa.q: How do you validate a BST without comparing to global min/max?
qa.a: Pass the allowed range (lo, hi) down: the left child must be < node.val, the right > node.val. This catches the classic trap — a node can be within bounds of its parent yet violate an ancestor (e.g. a 15 in the right subtree of a 10).

qa.q: Why does inorder traversal give sorted order?
qa.a: By the BST invariant, everything in the left subtree is smaller than the node and everything on the right is larger. Visiting left → node → right therefore emits values in ascending order — that's the definition of sorted.

construct-tree.name: Construct Tree from Traversals
construct-tree.desc: Two traversals can uniquely rebuild a binary tree. Preorder + inorder: the first preorder value is the root; find it in inorder to split left/right subtrees. Recursion + an index map does the rest.
construct-tree.q: Why does preorder + inorder uniquely determine a tree?
construct-tree.qsub: How does the version with postorder differ? · What does the index map save you? · When does the recursion need the current root's position?
construct-tree.what:
Only two lists are given — preorder and inorder — and you need to rebuild the entire tree. At first glance it seems impossible: traversals don’t show the structure.

But one fact is certain: the first value in preorder is always the root. Now find that value in inorder. Everything to its left is the entire left subtree, everything to its right is the entire right subtree.

Then — repeat this on both sides. Each time the next preorder value is a new root, and inorder splits around that root into two parts.

Another point: searching for the root in inorder each time is O(n) — overall work becomes O(n²). Create a hash map (value → index), lookup becomes O(1) and total becomes O(n).
construct-tree.analogy: Imagine a story told in two ways. The first version tells you where it starts (the first preorder element = the root). The second version lists everything in left-to-right order. Find the starting element in the second list — everything before it is the “left branch”, everything after it is the “right branch”.
construct-tree.why:
This tests three things together: recursion, hash map, and index tracking. In a naive solution people keep slicing arrays with slice — that makes it O(n²). Passing indices is the correct answer.

And a conceptual question that often comes up: why preorder + postorder isn’t enough? Answer: they don’t reveal whether a single child is a left or right. Inorder is the list that separates left and right.

How to think:

1. Build a hash map for inorder: value → index. This gives O(1) lookup.
2. Keep a pointer on preorder that only moves forward — pre = 0.
3. Give recursion the range of inorder: build(lo, hi). lo > hi → null.
4. Create a new node from preorder[pre++]. Get its index from the inorder map — call it i.
5. Build left first: build(lo, i-1). Then right: build(i+1, hi). Order matters — the entire left portion appears before the right in preorder.
6. If you have inorder + postorder? The root is the last value, the pointer moves backward, and you must build the right first.

qa.q: Why does preorder + inorder uniquely determine a tree?
qa.a: Preorder's first element is the root. Inorder tells you exactly which nodes are in the left and right subtrees (everything before/after the root). Recursing with those split ranges reconstructs the whole tree — one root per preorder element, one split per inorder lookup.

qa.q: Why can't you reconstruct from preorder + postorder alone?
qa.a: Those two orders both describe the tree from the 'outside' — you can't always tell left from right children when a node has one child. Preorder + postorder determines a tree only up to mirror images.

tree-measurements.name: Height, Depth, Diameter
tree-measurements.desc: The measurement family: height (node → deepest leaf), depth (root → node), diameter (longest path between two nodes). Height uses postorder; diameter is 'left height + right height' computed along the way.
tree-measurements.q: What's the difference between depth and height?
tree-measurements.qsub: Is the diameter always through the root? · How do you count nodes instead of edges? · How would you return the actual diameter path, not just its length?
tree-measurements.what:
Three questions that look similar but are different:

Height — how far the farthest leaf is below this node. Depth — how far this node is below the root. Height is the opposite direction. Diameter — the longest path between any two nodes in the whole tree.

Height requires postorder — because you need the heights of both children before knowing your own height. Depth requires preorder — it comes from top to bottom.

The real trick for diameter is different: the path does not necessarily pass through the root. It can be entirely within a subtree. So the function returns height but diameter is tracked separately — both in a single pass.
tree-measurements.analogy: Family tree. Height = how many generations the farthest descendant is below you. Depth = how many generations you are below the earliest ancestor. Diameter = the longest relationship between any two relatives in the whole family — and it can be between two cousins without going through a common ancestor.
tree-measurements.why:
Diameter is a classic interview trap. Naive solution: recompute height at every node — O(n²). The interviewer looks for you to compute height and track diameter in a single traversal.

This pattern is useful later: the function returns one thing while tracking another separately. Max Path Sum, Longest Univalue Path, Balanced check — all follow this shape.

How to think:

1. Height: null → 0. Otherwise 1 + max(left, right). Postorder.
2. Depth: carry a counter down from the root — depth + 1. Preorder.
3. Diameter: at each node the longest path that goes through it = leftHeight + rightHeight.
4. Update an external best with that value.
5. But return 1 + max(left, right) — because for the parent only one side’s path matters (the path cannot turn at the node).
6. Master the "return something, track something else" pattern — it appears repeatedly throughout Phase 4.

qa.q: What's the difference between depth and height?
qa.a: Depth of a node: number of edges from the root down to it (root depth 0). Height of a node: number of edges from it down to its deepest leaf (leaf height 0, or 1 depending on convention — agree before coding). Depth is computed top-down, height bottom-up.

qa.q: Why does the diameter function return height but track diameter separately?
qa.a: The diameter at a node is left height + right height, but to let its PARENT compute a path, only the node's own height (1 + max child height) matters. So the function returns height and writes the diameter to a shared best as a side effect.

dfs-iterative.name: Iterative DFS
dfs-iterative.desc: The explicit-stack version of depth-first traversal. Useful when recursion depth might overflow, or when the interview asks you to avoid recursion. A stack (LIFO) mimics the call stack exactly.
dfs-iterative.q: How does iterative inorder keep the 'left first' order?
dfs-iterative.qsub: How do you do iterative postorder? · What's the space advantage of iterative traversal? · When is recursion still the better answer?
dfs-iterative.what:
Recursive DFS also uses a stack — it’s just implicit. The JS engine keeps each function call’s frame on the call stack. That’s what remembers the traversal path.

Problem: that stack is small. In JS, after about 10,000 frames you get RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded. A skewed or very deep tree hits this limit.

Iterative DFS does the same work with its own stack — a normal array. It lives on the heap, which is much larger. Traversal is identical, control is in your hands.

But note: space in both is O(h). Iterative doesn’t use less memory — it just uses a different location. It’s important to mention this in an interview.
dfs-iterative.analogy:
A waiter who memorizes every order and runs to the kitchen himself — that’s recursion. It works, but his memory is limited.
Now keep a notebook where pending orders are written, and anyone can pick the top order and work on it. Same job, but the notebook can be as thick as needed.
dfs-iterative.why:
"Can you do it iteratively?" — this is the most common follow-up. It’s not just a syntax question. The interviewer wants to see that you understand recursion is essentially a stack.

In preorder there’s a small detail that shows full understanding: push the right child first, then the left. Because the stack is LIFO — the last pushed comes out first. A single line written wrong flips the order.

How to think:

1. Preorder: push the root onto the stack. Loop: pop, process, then push right, then left. Left is pushed last → it pops first. Done.
2. Inorder: two phases. While cur exists, push it while moving down to the left. Then pop, process, and set cur = cur.right.
3. Don’t forget to write cur = cur.right in inorder — otherwise the same node repeats.
4. Postorder (easy way): run preorder in reverse — node → right → left — and finally reverse the whole result.
5. Postorder (real way): keep a flag with each node — on first visit push it again (with the flag), on second visit process it.
6. Loop condition: while (stack.length). Inorder needs while (cur || stack.length) — both are required.

qa.q: How does iterative inorder keep the 'left first' order?
qa.a: Push every node along the left spine first — the stack holds them root-to-leaf. Pop the deepest leftmost, visit it, then step to its right child and descend that node's left spine again. This exactly reproduces recursion's left→root→right rhythm.

qa.q: Why is iterative preorder just a stack?
qa.a: Preorder visits the node BEFORE children, so you can push children onto a stack and immediately pop the next one to visit. Pushing right before left makes the stack pop left first — no extra bookkeeping needed.

balanced-bst.name: Balanced BSTs (AVL / Red-Black)
balanced-bst.desc: A plain BST can degenerate into a linked list, making every op O(n). Balanced trees rebalance on insert/delete to keep height O(log n): AVL enforces a 1-height-difference invariant using rotations; Red-Black uses color rules to bound imbalance to a factor of 2.
balanced-bst.q: Why not just use a plain BST and get O(log n)?
balanced-bst.qsub: What invariant does an AVL tree maintain? · How many rotations does an AVL insert need at most? · Why does a balanced BST beat a sorted array for inserts? · Name two real data structures built on balanced trees.
balanced-bst.what:
In a plain BST, insert 1, 2, 3, 4 in that order. Each new number becomes a right child and attaches. Your "tree" essentially becomes a straight linked list.

Now search, insert, and delete — all become O(n) instead of O(log n). The whole advantage of a BST disappears. And this is not a rare case — inserting sorted data is very common.

Balanced BST fixes this problem after every insert/delete: it checks whether the tree has become tilted to one side, and if so, rotates some nodes to bring the height back to O(log n).

AVL is strict — the height difference at each node must be ≤ 1. Red-Black is looser — its color rules keep the height from exceeding twice the minimum.
balanced-bst.analogy: In a wardrobe, clothes keep piling up on one side while the other side stays empty. The wardrobe could tip over. A smart system, after each new piece of clothing, checks how much tilt has occurred and, if needed, shifts some clothes to the other side. A little extra work — but the wardrobe never falls.
balanced-bst.why:
This topic is not for implementation — it’s for talking. It’s rare to be asked to write out all AVL rotations in an interview.

The test is this: do you know that saying "BST O(log n)" is an incomplete answer? The correct answer is: "balanced BST gives O(log n), plain BST worst-case is O(n)".

And it ties into system design: Java’s TreeMap, C++’s std::map, database indexes (B-tree, which belongs to the same family) — all rely on this guarantee.

How to think:

1. Balance factor = left height − right height. In an AVL this must always be -1, 0, or 1.
2. Insert as in a normal BST. Then, while moving back up, check the balance factor at each node.
3. If the factor becomes 2 or -2, rotate.
4. Four cases: LL (one right rotation), RR (one left rotation), LR and RL (two rotations — these are often forgotten).
5. A rotation does not break the BST property — it only changes the shape, not the order. The inorder traversal remains the same after rotation.
6. Red-Black takes a different path — colors on nodes and color rules. Fewer rotations, so insert/delete are faster; height is a bit larger, so search is slightly slower.

qa.q: Why not just use a plain BST and get O(log n)?
qa.a: Inserting sorted data into an unbalanced BST makes a linear chain — every op becomes O(n). Balancing guarantees the height bound structurally, regardless of insertion order.

qa.q: AVL vs Red-Black: which do you pick and why?
qa.a: AVL for search-heavy workloads (tighter height, faster lookups). Red-Black for write-heavy workloads (fewer rotations on insert/delete). They trade search speed against rebalance frequency.

graph-repr.name: Graph Representation
graph-repr.desc: How you store edges decides how fast every operation is. Adjacency list: node → list of neighbors, O(V+E) space, the default. Adjacency matrix: V×V booleans, O(V²) space, O(1) edge lookup. Edgelist: array of [u, v, weight], compact for sorting.
graph-repr.q: Adjacency list vs matrix — how do you choose?
graph-repr.qsub: How do you store a directed acyclic graph? · When would an edge list beat an adjacency list? · What's the space of each representation for n=1000, e=10000?
graph-repr.what:
The first step in a graph problem is to turn the edge list into a structure that instantly answers “who are this node’s neighbors?”.

Adjacency list — a list of actual neighbors in front of each node. Space O(V + E). This is the default answer for about 95 % of problems.

Adjacency matrix — a V × V grid where each cell indicates "edge present or not". Space O(V²) even if the graph is empty. Benefit: edge lookup O(1).

Edge list — simply an array of [u, v, weight]. Good for Kruskal because edges need to be sorted there.
graph-repr.analogy: List = phone contacts — only the people who actually exist are saved. Matrix = a wedding chart with a slot reserved for every possible pair of guests, even if the two don’t know each other. In a sparse graph, 99 % of the matrix remains empty.
graph-repr.why:
The interviewer spots this within the first two minutes. Choosing the wrong representation silently turns your O(V + E) solution into O(V²).

And the most common bug is: forgetting to add the reverse edge in an undirected graph. The code runs, doesn’t crash — half the graph is missing and the answer is wrong.

How to think:

1. Input is often an edge list: [[0,1],[1,2],[0,3]].
2. Create an array of arrays: Array.from({length: n}, () => []). Don’t write Array(n).fill([]) — all rows would reference the same array.
3. For each edge [u, v]: g[u].push(v). Is the graph undirected? Then also g[v].push(u) — both.
4. Weighted? Store the neighbor as a pair: g[u].push([v, w]).
5. Nodes start at 1? Create an array of size n + 1, or subtract 1 everywhere. This off-by-one is a frequent pitfall.
6. Use a matrix only when the graph is dense (E ≈ V²) or when you need frequent edge checks.

qa.q: Adjacency list vs matrix — how do you choose?
qa.a: List wins when the graph is sparse (most real graphs) — O(V+E) space and neighbor iteration is cheap. Matrix wins for DENSE graphs or when you need O(1) 'is there an edge between u and v' checks, at the cost of O(V²) space.

qa.q: What's the most common bug in the first 2 minutes of a graph problem?
qa.a: Missing the second push for undirected graphs (only adding u→v, never v→u). Also confusing 1-indexed input with 0-indexed arrays. Checking these two up front saves entire wrong solutions.

bfs-graphs.name: BFS on Graphs
bfs-graphs.desc: Queue-based level-by-level exploration. On unweighted graphs it finds the SHORTEST path in edges. The visited set (or distance array) is mandatory — unlike trees, graphs have cycles.
bfs-graphs.q: Why must you mark visited when ENQUEUEING, not when popping?
bfs-graphs.qsub: When is BFS the right choice over DFS? · What's the queue's worst-case memory? · How do you reconstruct the actual path, not just the length?
bfs-graphs.what:
BFS on a graph is the same as on a tree — queue, level by level. But there is a new danger: graphs have cycles. In a tree there was no way to go back.

Therefore the visited set is no longer optional, it is required. Without it the queue will never become empty.

The real gift of BFS: shortest path on an unweighted graph. Because it expands one ring at a time, the node that is encountered for the first time is reached with the fewest edges — guaranteed. DFS cannot provide this.

One point many people get wrong: mark a node as visited when you add it to the queue, not when you remove it. Otherwise a node can enter the queue many times.
bfs-graphs.analogy:
Think of rocks thrown into a pond. The ripples spread one ring at a time — first all those one step away, then two steps away. So whatever touches first is the closest.
If you don’t mark where the ripple has already reached, it will keep circling endlessly.
bfs-graphs.why:
A single question can test the whole topic: "Do you mark visited on enqueue or on dequeue?"

If you mark on dequeue, a node can enter the queue many times — the work can grow from O(V + E) to exponential. The answer may be correct, but you’ll get TLE.

Another test: Used DFS for shortest path? That’s wrong — DFS gives no guarantee that the first path found is the shortest.

How to think:

1. Create a queue, insert the source, and at the same time add it to visited.
2. Need level-wise? Measure size at the start of the loop — the same tree trick.
3. Dequeue a node from the front, examine its neighbors.
4. For each unvisited neighbor: mark visited first, then enqueue it. This order is essential.
5. Need distances? Either keep a level counter, or write dist[v] = dist[u] + 1.
6. Multi-source: initially enqueue all sources. Then they all expand together — Rotting Oranges, 01 Matrix rely on this.

qa.q: Why must you mark visited when ENQUEUEING, not when popping?
qa.a: If you mark on pop, the same node can be enqueued by multiple parents before it's popped — duplicates flood the queue and you can even corrupt distance values. Marking at enqueue guarantees each node enters once.

qa.q: What is multi-source BFS and when do you use it?
qa.a: Seed the queue with ALL starting nodes at distance 0 (rotting oranges start as all rotten cells; 01-matrix starts as all zeroes). The wavefront expands uniformly from every source — the first time a cell is reached is its true minimum distance.

dfs-graphs.name: DFS on Graphs
dfs-graphs.desc: Recursive (or stack-based) exploration that dives deep before backtracking. Great for connectivity (components, islands), cycle detection, and path existence. The visited set prevents infinite loops on cycles.
dfs-graphs.q: How does DFS detect cycles in a directed graph?
dfs-graphs.qsub: Why does DFS use less memory than BFS on wide graphs? · How do you count the size of each connected component? · What's the difference between visited and on-stack in cycle detection?
dfs-graphs.what:
In a maze, pick a path and go all the way inside. Hit a dead end? Turn back and take another route. That’s DFS.

On a graph, DFS differs from the tree version: the visited set is required, otherwise recursion never stops in a cycle.

But the real point comes next. In a directed graph, just "visited" is not enough to find cycles. Encountering a node again can mean two things: either its processing is already finished (which is fine), or it is currently on your call stack (a cycle!).

So you need three colors: 0 = not visited yet, 1 = currently on the stack, 2 = finished. Reaching a node with color 1 indicates a cycle.
dfs-graphs.analogy:
While walking through a maze, place two kinds of marks. Chalk — "I am currently on this path". Sticker — "I have fully explored this path, found nothing new".
If you return to a chalk mark, it means you looped back onto your own path — a cycle. If you reach a sticker, just skip it.
dfs-graphs.why:
This is the most frequently tested concept in Phase 5: directed cycle detection requires three states, not two.

People try to find cycles with a binary visited and end up labeling a DAG as having a "cycle" — because a node can be reached by two different paths without forming a cycle.

And in undirected graphs the story is different: two colors are enough, you just have to skip the parent — otherwise every edge would appear as a "cycle".

How to think:

1. Create a state array for each node — initially all 0.
2. When you enter a node in DFS set state[u] = 1 (on the stack).
3. For each neighbor v: if state[v] === 1 → cycle found, return. If state[v] === 2 → skip. If 0 → recurse into it.
4. After all neighbors are processed → state[u] = 2 (finished). Then return.
5. Undirected: binary visited works, but pass parent in recursion and skip when v === parent.
6. A graph can have multiple components — so start DFS from every node that is not yet visited.

qa.q: How does DFS detect cycles in a directed graph?
qa.a: Use three colors: unvisited, on-stack, done. If during DFS you hit a node that's still 'on-stack', you've found a back edge — that's a cycle. The on-stack marker matters because a finished node is NOT a cycle (that's just a shared subtree).

qa.q: BFS vs DFS on a graph — how do you decide?
qa.a: BFS for shortest path and anything level-based; DFS for connectivity, components, cycles, and when recursion gives cleaner code. Memory: BFS uses queue width O(V), DFS uses stack depth O(V) worst case — comparable on dense graphs.

union-find.name: Union-Find (Disjoint Set)
union-find.desc: A data structure for dynamic connectivity: 'are u and v in the same set?' and 'join u and v's sets'. With path compression and union by rank, both operations are nearly O(1) — inverse Ackermann. Perfect for components and cycle checks in undirected graphs.
union-find.q: How does path compression make find nearly O(1)?
union-find.qsub: Why union by rank, not just path compression? · How does union-find detect a cycle in an undirected graph? · What's the memory footprint vs an adjacency list?
union-find.what:
The same question keeps being asked: "are u and v in the same group?" And occasionally two groups also merge.

Running BFS/DFS each time is O(V + E) — and this question can appear thousands of times.

The Union-Find idea is simple: each group has a leader (root). find(x) tells you who the leader of x is. If two nodes have the same leader → they are in the same group. union(u, v) joins the two leaders.

A naive version can be as slow as O(n) — a chain forms. Two small optimizations (path compression + union by rank) make it practically O(1).
union-find.analogy:
Each WhatsApp group has an admin. "Are these two people in the same group?" — ask each admin; if they are the same, answer yes.
To merge two groups, attach one admin below the other’s.
Path compression = each time you ask the admin, give all intermediate people the admin’s number directly — next time no chain traversal is needed.
union-find.why:
The interviewer asks two things. First: why need both optimizations? Path compression alone works, but without union by rank a long chain can still form at first.

Second, and more useful: cycle detection in an undirected graph. Before adding an edge, ask — are these two already in the same group? If yes, this edge will create a cycle. Kruskal’s entire MST hinges on this single line.

How to think:

1. parent[i] = i — initially each node is its own leader.
2. find(x): while parent[x] !== x, move up.
3. Path compression: while moving up, link every node on the path directly to the root. One line: parent[x] = find(parent[x]).
4. union(u, v): find both roots. If they are the same, do nothing (and this signals a cycle).
5. Union by rank: attach the smaller tree under the larger one — otherwise the tree keeps growing tall.
6. Want to count components? Start a counter at n and decrement it on each successful union.

qa.q: How does path compression make find nearly O(1)?
qa.a: After find(x), we rewire x and every node on its path to point directly at the root. The tree flattens over time, so subsequent finds are single pointer hops. Combined with union by rank (attach shorter tree under taller), total is inverse-Ackermann — effectively constant.

qa.q: Union-Find vs BFS/DFS for connected components?
qa.a: Union-Find shines when connections are discovered incrementally or you need many 'are they connected' queries without re-traversing. BFS/DFS is simpler when you just need a one-time component count on a static graph. Both are O(V+E) class; UF adds near-O(1) point queries.

grid-problems.name: Grid Problems
grid-problems.desc: A 2D grid IS a graph — each cell is a node, adjacent cells are edges. Add a visited set and BFS/DFS to solve islands, rotting oranges, flood fill, and surrounded regions without building an explicit graph.
grid-problems.q: Why is sinking the cell in-place a valid visited set?
grid-problems.qsub: How do you find the largest island's area? · How does Surrounded Regions flip only boundary-connected cells? · How would you BFS multi-source from all boundary cells?
grid-problems.what:
A grid looks like a matrix, but in reality it is a graph. Each cell is a node, and the cells above, below, left, and right are its neighbors.

Once you realize this, problems like "Number of Islands", "Rotting Oranges", "Flood Fill" all become ordinary BFS/DFS.

An advantage: you don’t need to build an adjacency list at all. Neighbors are generated on the fly with a small dirs array: [[1,0],[-1,0],[0,1],[0,-1]].

And a clever trick: you don’t need a separate visited set. Just modify the cell itself (turn land into water) — O(1) extra space, and the code stays short.
grid-problems.analogy:
Think of a building's floor plan. Each room is a node. Doors exist only between adjacent rooms — there’s no direct path to diagonal rooms (unless the problem says so).
And once a room has been seen? Mark it — no need to keep a separate register.
grid-problems.why:
The interviewer wants to see whether you can recognize a grid as a graph. Someone who starts building a separate adjacency list hasn’t yet grasped that "grid is an implicit graph".

And a bug that occurs every time: missing bounds check. Reading grid[nr][nc] without first verifying that nr, nc are inside the grid leads to a crash on undefined. Check bounds first, then the cell.

How to think:

1. m = grid.length, n = grid[0].length. Assume rectangular.
2. dirs = [[1,0],[-1,0],[0,1],[0,-1]] — four directions. Use eight if diagonals are needed — confirm from the problem.
3. Loop over every cell. When you find land that hasn’t been seen → start DFS/BFS there and increment a counter +1.
4. Inside that DFS/BFS: immediately mark the cell (or turn it into '0'), then try the four neighbors.
5. For each neighbor, first check bounds, then visited, then value — in that order.
6. Choose DFS if you need area/shape. Choose BFS if you need distance/steps, or the grid is very large (to avoid recursion overflow).
where: O(m × n) · space: O(m × n) worst

qa.q: Why is sinking the cell in-place a valid visited set?
qa.a: Mutating grid[r][c] = '0' marks it visited without O(m×n) extra memory. As long as '0' was already not-a-cell-of-interest, the mutation can't confuse later logic — a classic memory win the interviewer will appreciate.

qa.q: BFS or DFS for islands?
qa.a: Both give O(m×n). DFS is shorter to write (recursion). BFS avoids recursion-depth limits on huge grids and is the natural fit when the problem asks for distance spreading (Rotting Oranges). Know both and justify by grid size.

dijkstra.name: Dijkstra's Algorithm
dijkstra.desc: Shortest path in a graph with NON-NEGATIVE weights. BFS with a priority queue: repeatedly extract the closest unvisited node and relax its edges. O((V + E) log V) with a min-heap.
dijkstra.q: Why does Dijkstra fail on negative edge weights?
dijkstra.qsub: How is Dijkstra like BFS? · When do you use a visited set in Dijkstra (and when not)? · What changes if you want the path itself?
dijkstra.what:
BFS gives the shortest path — but only when every edge has the same weight. That’s not the case on Google Maps: some roads are long but fast, others short but congested.

Dijkstra is the same idea as BFS, just using a min-heap instead of a queue. Each time pick the node whose currently cheapest path has been found.

For every edge leaving that node ask: “Does going through it make any other node cheaper?” If yes → update its distance and push it into the heap. This is called relaxation.

One condition: no weight may be negative. Dijkstra assumes that once a node is identified as the cheapest, it can never become cheaper later — a negative edge breaks this assumption.
dijkstra.analogy:
A metro map where each line has its own fare. You always choose the station that you can reach with the currently cheapest cost, then examine all connections from there, and if a new cheaper route appears you update the chart.
Now imagine a line that gives you money (negative) — the “this station is final” reasoning collapses.
dijkstra.why:
This is the default answer for weighted shortest-path questions, and interviewers immediately ask “why does it fail on negative weights?” Explaining this shows you understand the core concept.

Another point: stale entries. The same node can appear in the heap multiple times with older distances. When popping, check — if the heap’s distance is larger than dist[], it’s an outdated entry, skip it. Missing this check makes the code slower and sometimes incorrect.

How to think:

1. Create a dist array, initialize all to Infinity. Set dist[src] = 0.
2. Insert [0, src] into the min-heap — distance first, so the heap sorts by it.
3. Extract the node u with the smallest distance from the heap.
4. Stale check: Is d > dist[u]? Then it’s an old entry — continue.
5. Relax: For each neighbor v — if dist[u] + w < dist[v] then update dist[v] and push [dist[v], v] into the heap.
6. When the heap is empty → finish. dist now holds the cheapest path to every node. Time O((V + E) log V).
where: O((V + E) log V) · space: O(V + E)

qa.q: Why does Dijkstra fail on negative edge weights?
qa.a: It greedily finalizes the closest node assuming no later path can improve it. A negative edge can reopen that assumption — a finalized distance might shrink after being locked. Bellman-Ford handles negatives by relaxing all edges V-1 times.

qa.q: Why skip stale heap entries?
qa.a: A node can be pushed to the heap multiple times as better distances are found. When the stale copy (larger distance) is popped, relaxing from it would be wrong and wasteful. Skipping when d > dist[u] keeps the result correct with lazy deletion instead of tracking membership.

topological-sort.name: Topological Sort
topological-sort.desc: Order the nodes of a DIRECTED ACYCLIC GRAPH so every edge u→v has u before v. Kahn's algorithm (BFS on in-degrees) is the go-to: peel off zero-in-degree nodes repeatedly. Detects cycles when not all nodes get processed.
topological-sort.q: Why does a zero-in-degree node always start a valid order?
topological-sort.qsub: What's the DFS-based alternative to Kahn's algorithm? · How do you produce a lexicographically smallest valid order? · Why is topo sort only defined on DAGs?
topological-sort.what:
There are courses, some of which have prerequisites. We need an order where no course appears before its prerequisite.

Kahn's algorithm is straightforward: first take any course that has no remaining dependencies — i.e., in-degree = 0.

After processing it, the in-degree of every course that depends on it decreases by 1. Any course whose in-degree becomes 0 is now “unblocked” — add it to the queue. This chain continues.

Bonus: if at the end not all nodes appear in the order, the graph contains a cycle — because inside a cycle each node is waiting on another, so no node ever gets an in-degree of 0.
topological-sort.analogy:
Tasks in an office. First pick any task that has no pending dependency. Once it’s completed, some of the tasks that were waiting on it become unblocked.
If you can’t find any task that can start, it means two (or more) tasks are waiting for each other — a deadlock. That’s exactly a cycle.
topological-sort.why:
Topological sort solves two questions at once: ordering and cycle detection. Course Schedule I only asks “is it possible?”, while II requires the full order — the code is almost identical.

Another common mistake: reversing the edge direction. “[a, b]” means “do b before a” — read it carefully. If the direction is flipped, the order will be reversed, but the code won’t crash.

How to think:

1. Build the graph and an indeg array. For each edge u → v: g[u].push(v) and indeg[v]++.
2. Add every node with indeg === 0 to the queue — not just one, all of them.
3. Dequeue a node u and append it to order.
4. For each neighbor v, decrement indeg[v]--. If it becomes 0, enqueue it.
5. When the queue is empty, check: order.length === n? Yes → valid order. No → there is a cycle.
6. Want the lexicographically smallest order? Use a min-heap instead of a queue.

qa.q: Why does a zero-in-degree node always start a valid order?
qa.a: A node with no incoming edges has no prerequisites — it can be scheduled immediately without violating any dependency. Removing it only DECREASES other nodes' in-degrees, which is exactly 'satisfy one prerequisite'. Repeat until everything's scheduled.

qa.q: How does topological sort detect cycles?
qa.a: In a DAG, every step finds at least one zero-in-degree node. If the algorithm gets stuck with nodes remaining, all leftover nodes are in a cycle — none can ever drop to zero in-degree. So order.length < V means a cycle.

mst.name: Minimum Spanning Tree (Prim / Kruskal)
mst.desc: The MST connects every vertex with the minimum total edge weight. Kruskal sorts all edges and greedily adds them via union-find (O(E log E)). Prim grows one tree from a start vertex, always taking the cheapest frontier edge (O(E log V) with a heap).
mst.q: When should you use Kruskal over Prim?
mst.qsub: State the cut property in one sentence. · Why does Kruskal need the graph to be undirected? · How would you build the MST of a complete graph from (x,y) points? · What if the graph is not connected — what does Kruskal return?
mst.what:
In a new housing society, an electricity cable must reach every house. Cable is expensive — all houses should be connected with the minimum total length, and no house should be left out.

The answer is always a tree: to connect n nodes you need exactly n - 1 edges. Any extra edge creates a cycle, and a cycle means an edge is useless.

Kruskal: sort all edges by weight. Start from the cheapest and keep taking them — but skip any edge that would create a cycle. Cycle detection is done by Union-Find.

Prim: start from a node. Each time pick the cheapest edge that goes from your set to a vertex outside. The tree grows. It uses a min-heap.
mst.analogy:
Kruskal = a property dealer who lists all available roads by price and takes the cheapest first — but never reconnects an area that is already linked.
Prim = a growing tree: it takes root at one place and always expands toward its nearest (cheapest) branch.
mst.why:
MST and Dijkstra are the two algorithms that cause the most confusion — both are greedy, both use a heap, both "minimum".

But their tasks are completely different. MST: minimize the total cost to connect everyone. Dijkstra: find the shortest path from one node to every other node. In an MST the path between two nodes is not necessarily the shortest.

And a practical point: if the graph is not connected, an MST does not exist. So at the end check whether n - 1 edges were used.

How to think:

1. Kruskal: sort all edges [u, v, w] by w.
2. Create a DSU. For each edge try union(u, v). If it returns true → take the edge. If false → it would create a cycle, skip it.
3. When you have n - 1 edges → MST is complete, stop.
4. Prim: start from any node. Insert all its edges into the heap.
5. Extract the cheapest edge from the heap. Is its other endpoint already in the set? Skip. If not, take it and insert all edges of the new node into the heap.
6. Which to choose: if you have an edge list or the graph is sparse → Kruskal. If you have an adjacency list or the graph is dense → Prim.

qa.q: When should you use Kruskal over Prim?
qa.a: Kruskal when the edge list is already available (easy to sort) or the graph is sparse. Prim when you have adjacency and dense graphs — no global sort needed, just a heap of frontier edges.

qa.q: How do you detect a cycle in Kruskal?
qa.a: Union-find: if the two endpoints of an edge are already in the same component, adding it creates a cycle, so skip it. Path-compressed union-find makes this nearly O(1) per check.

bellman-ford.name: Bellman-Ford (negative weights)
bellman-ford.desc: Single-source shortest paths that also handle negative edge weights, unlike Dijkstra. Relax every edge V-1 times: each pass extends valid distances by one more edge. A V-th pass that still improves anything proves a negative cycle exists.
bellman-ford.q: Why does Bellman-Ford need exactly V-1 passes?
bellman-ford.qsub: When is Dijkstra wrong but Bellman-Ford right? · What does "relax an edge" mean? · Why is Bellman-Ford slower than Dijkstra? · How would you enforce a max of K edges (hops)?
bellman-ford.what:
Dijkstra assumes that once a node is extracted as the cheapest, its distance is final. A negative edge breaks this assumption — a later path can make it cheaper.

Bellman-Ford makes no such assumption. It repeatedly relaxes all edges — exactly V - 1 times.

Why V - 1? Because any shortest path can have at most V - 1 edges (more would mean a node repeats, i.e., a cycle, which cannot be part of a shortest simple path). Each round extends the known distances by one more edge.

As a bonus, run a V-th round. If something still improves, the graph contains a negative cycle — where looping keeps decreasing the distance forever, and a shortest path is undefined.
bellman-ford.analogy:
News spreading in a city. In the first round it reaches only the source's direct neighbors. In the second round it reaches their neighbors. After V-1 rounds even the farthest node gets the fresh news.
Now if you run one more round and the news still changes — it means there is a rumor cycle that keeps updating itself.
bellman-ford.why:
The interviewer's first question: "Why not Dijkstra?" Answer: negative weights. And this is not just theory — negative weights appear in currency arbitrage and some routing protocols.

But the most common interview variant is: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops. There are no negative weights there — but there is a constraint of "at most k stops". Dijkstra cannot handle this directly, but Bellman-Ford's k+1 rounds exactly implement this requirement.

How to think:

1. dist array, all Infinity. Set dist[src] = 0.
2. Loop V - 1 times.
3. In each round iterate over all edges: if dist[u] + w < dist[v] then update dist[v].
4. If nothing changes in a round, everything will stay the same afterwards — stop there (early exit).
