5. Negative cycle: run a V-th round. If something still decreases → negative cycle exists.
6. K-hop version: run k+1 rounds instead of V-1, and in each round use a copy of dist — otherwise a single round could propagate information two edges ahead.

qa.q: Why does Bellman-Ford need exactly V-1 passes?
qa.a: The shortest path in a graph with V vertices uses at most V-1 edges (simple path). Each pass extends distances by one more edge, so after V-1 passes every reachable shortest path is computed.

qa.q: How do you detect a negative cycle?
qa.a: Run one extra pass. If any edge can still relax a distance, a reachable negative cycle exists and shortest paths are undefined (they decrease forever).

floyd-warshall.name: Floyd-Warshall (all pairs)
floyd-warshall.desc: Computes shortest paths between every pair of vertices using dynamic programming. For each intermediate vertex k, check if routing through k improves any (i, j) distance. Simple, dense (O(V^3)), and works with negative edges (as long as no negative cycles).
floyd-warshall.q: Why must k be the outermost loop?
floyd-warshall.qsub: What does dist[i][j] mean after processing intermediate k? · How do you reconstruct the actual path after the distances? · Can Floyd-Warshall handle negative weights? · How do you detect a negative cycle with it?
floyd-warshall.what:
Until now every algorithm ran from one source. Here the question is different: we need the shortest distance from every city to every city all at once.

Running Dijkstra from each node is one option. Floyd-Warshall is another — and its idea is so simple that the whole code is just 4 lines.

Treat each node k as a "mid-stop" one by one, and for every pair (i, j) ask: Is going through k cheaper than going directly? If yes, update the chart.

This is the DP. After the k-th round the matrix means: "the cheapest path from i to j using only nodes 0..k as intermediates”. That's why the k loop must be the outermost — it represents a DP layer.
floyd-warshall.analogy:
Airline fare chart. Consider each city as a hub one by one and look at the whole chart — "Does going via Dubai make the trip cheaper than a direct flight?" After each hub the chart improves a bit.
After looking at all hubs — the chart is now completely correct.
floyd-warshall.why:
Two things are tested. First: k must be outermost. Changing the loop order silently gives a wrong answer, and the bug is hard to catch.

Second: When is it better than Dijkstra? Answer: when V is small (up to about 400) and you need the answer for all pairs. When V grows, O(V³) becomes infeasible — at V = 1000 it already needs about a billion steps.

How to think:

1. Create a V × V matrix, initialise all entries to Infinity.
2. Set dist[i][i] = 0 — the cost to stay at the same node is zero. Don't forget this seed.
3. For each edge [u, v, w] set dist[u][v] = w. (If there are multiple edges, take the min.)
4. Three nested loops: k outermost, then i, then j.
5. Inside just one line: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]).
6. Negative cycle: after the algorithm, is any dist[i][i] < 0? That means you can leave i and return to it with a net gain — a negative cycle.

qa.q: Why must k be the outermost loop?
qa.a: Pass k assumes paths using intermediates 0..k-1 are final. If i or j were outermost, an improvement from pass k could be missed because the sub-results were not yet computed.

qa.q: When is Floyd-Warshall a better answer than Dijkstra from each node?
qa.a: For dense graphs and when V is small: running Dijkstra V times is O(V E log V), which is worse than O(V^3) when E is near V^2. Floyd-Warshall is also far simpler to write.

euler-path.name: Euler Path / Hierholzer
euler-path.desc: An Eulerian path visits every edge exactly once (Eulerian circuit if it starts and ends at the same vertex). Hierholzer's algorithm builds it by following unused edges and splicing cycles back in. Classic problem: Reconstruct Itinerary (visit every flight edge).
euler-path.q: What is the difference between an Eulerian path and a Hamiltonian path?
euler-path.qsub: State the degree condition for an Eulerian circuit. · Why does Reconstruct Itinerary require lexicographic adjacency? · How do you handle the starting vertex? · What makes Eulerian easy but Hamiltonian hard?
euler-path.what:
Until now the goal of every traversal was to visit each node once. Here the goal is the opposite: use each edge exactly once — revisiting nodes is fine.

This is called an Euler path. If it ends where it started, it is an Euler circuit. Classic example: a postman who has to walk every street once.

A nice fact: you can tell whether it is possible before running the algorithm — just count degrees. All even → circuit. Exactly 2 odd → path. Anything else → impossible.

Hierholzer constructs it, and its method is a bit unusual: keep moving forward on unused edges. Get stuck? Add that node to a list and backtrack. At the end reverse the whole list — that is the answer.
euler-path.analogy:
Imagine a courier who has to pass through every street of the city exactly once — returning to a square is fine, but repeating a street is not.
He goes as far as he can. When there is no new street ahead, he stops, notes that location and backtracks — checking that no street was missed in the middle.
euler-path.why:
First test: the difference between Euler and Hamilton. Euler = each edge once, and it can be solved in O(E). Hamilton = each node once, and that is NP-hard — there is no fast algorithm. One letter difference, a completely different world.

Second: in Reconstruct Itinerary people write naive DFS + backtracking and get TLE. Hierholzer does it in O(E) because it never re-explores an edge; it just builds the result in reverse.

How to think:

1. First count degrees. All even → start anywhere (circuit). Exactly 2 odd → start at one of the odd nodes (path). Otherwise → impossible.
2. Take a stack and push the start node onto it.
3. Does the node at the top of the stack have an unused edge? Take one, remove that edge, and push the other endpoint onto the stack.
4. No unused edge left? Add the top node to the result and pop it from the stack.
5. Repeat until the stack is empty.
6. Reverse the result. That is the Euler path.
7. Need the lexicographically smallest (Reconstruct Itinerary)? Sort each node’s adjacency list beforehand.

qa.q: What is the difference between an Eulerian path and a Hamiltonian path?
qa.a: Eulerian visits every EDGE once (easy to check via degrees, O(E)). Hamiltonian visits every VERTEX once — that is NP-hard to even decide. Interviewers test that you know which is which.

qa.q: Why does Hierholzer build the answer in reverse?
qa.a: A naive DFS dead-ends when it returns to the start too early, missing side cycles. By only popping when no edges remain, cycles are deferred to the unwind phase; reversing the pops joins them into one valid path.

trie-structure.name: Trie Structure
trie-structure.desc: A tree where each node holds children keyed by character, and a flag marking word ends. Inserting/querying a word of length m costs O(m) regardless of how many words are stored — no re-scanning shared prefixes.
trie-structure.q: Why is a Trie faster than a Set for prefix queries?
trie-structure.qsub: How do you delete a word from a Trie? · What's the worst-case memory of a Trie over a hash set? · How would you auto-complete to the top-k suggestions?
trie-structure.what:
Type ind in the Google search bar and suggestions like “india” and “indian railway” appear instantly — without scanning an entire dictionary.

If the words were in an array, you would have to scan the whole array again for each new character. A Trie turns this into a tree: from the root each edge represents a character, and reaching a node means "the portion up to here is a valid prefix".

Each node has a small flag — isEnd — that indicates "whether a complete word ends here". This flag distinguishes "apple" from "app".

The real benefit: the time to find a word depends only on its own length — O(m). Whether the dictionary has 10 words or 1,000,000, it makes no difference.
trie-structure.analogy:
Think of phone contacts. Press R and only names starting with R remain; press a and only “Ra…” names remain. Each character is a filter that narrows the path forward.
Reaching “Ra” does not mean there is a contact named “Ra” — the isEnd flag decides that.
trie-structure.why:
A hash map provides exact match. Not prefixes. "All words that start with app" — a hash map has no answer for that; you would have to scan everything.

The interviewer looks for whether you understand the space and time trade-off: by using a little extra memory you guarantee O(m) lookup, independent of the dictionary size n.

How to think:

1. The root is an empty node — it does not represent any character.
2. Each node has children — either an array of size 26 or a Map.
3. Insert: start at the root, look for a child for each character of the word. If it does not exist, create it. If it does, move to it.
4. On the node of the last character set isEnd = true. Forgetting this step is the most common bug.
5. Common prefixes are automatically shared — the c-a part of "cat" and "car" is a single path.
6. Memory: worst case each word has its own separate path — O(total characters × 26). The more prefixes are shared, the more savings.

qa.q: Why is a Trie faster than a Set for prefix queries?
qa.a: A Set can answer 'is this word present?' in O(1) but 'which words start with this prefix?' requires scanning everything. A Trie answers startsWith in O(m) by walking the prefix — the shared structure IS the index.

qa.q: Trie vs hash map for a dictionary of words?
qa.a: Trie: O(m) prefix search, memory shared across words with common prefixes, natural for wildcards-with-DFS and prefix counting. HashMap: simpler, O(m) exact lookups, but no prefix semantics and more memory per word. For pure existence checks, the map wins; for prefix work, the trie wins.

trie-ops.name: Trie Insert / Search / Prefix
trie-ops.desc: The three operations that define a trie — insert, search, and prefix search — plus the DFS extension for wildcards and word-collection. Master the walk helper and everything else is thin.
trie-ops.qsub: How do you count how many words start with a prefix? · What does the DFS base case return for wildcard matching? · How would you find the longest word where every prefix is also a word?
trie-ops.what:
The Trie is built. Now we need to perform three operations, and the path is exactly the same for all — descend one character at a time from the root. The difference is only at the end.

Insert: if a missing node is found, create it, and at the end set isEnd = true.
Search: the path must exist and isEnd must be true.
startsWith: only the path needs to exist — isEnd does not matter.

So write a walk helper that follows the path and returns the node or null. After that, search and startsWith each become a one-liner.

On top of that there is a DFS extension — a wildcard . (any character) and "extract all words below this node" — which creates autocomplete.
trie-ops.analogy: Imagine a building where each floor represents a character. Insert = as you climb, create any floor that does not exist. Search = the entire path exists and there is a house on the top floor. startsWith = just check that the path up to that floor is straight — regardless of whether there is a house on top.
trie-ops.why:
People often treat search and startsWith as the same, or place the isEnd check in the wrong place. That one-line difference is the real test.

And the wildcard DFS shows that you can combine recursion and backtracking on top of a trie — the exact skill needed for hard problems like Word Search II, where the trie cuts down the board’s backtracking.

How to think:

1. Walk helper: start at the root, look for a child at each character. If missing → null. If you reach the end → return that node.
2. search(word): get the node from walk(word). If it is not null and isEnd is true → true.
3. startsWith(p): walk(p) !== null. That's it.
4. Wildcard .: for a normal character go straight down. When . appears, DFS into every child — if any returns true, the result is true.
5. Collect all: DFS from the node downwards, concatenating characters along the path, and whenever isEnd is encountered add the word to the list — but don’t stop, longer words may follow.
6. The worst case for a wildcard is O(26^dots) — this caveat should be mentioned.
where: O(m) avg, O(26^w) worst · space: O(depth)
Collect all words from a node

qa.q: How does the wildcard '.' work?
qa.a: At the wildcard position, branch into EVERY child — if any branch completes the word, it matches. That's a DFS over the fan-out, worst case exploring all children at each '.' (O(26^k) for k wildcards), but average case is fine because each level is bounded.

qa.q: Why is a Trie ideal for Word Search II?
qa.a: Backtracking over the board would rescan shared prefixes for every word. The trie lets one DFS pass carry all word matches simultaneously — the current prefix node tells you which words are still possible, pruning the board search to only live prefixes.

xor.name: XOR Tricks
xor.desc: XOR is its own inverse: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x. That makes it the perfect tool for cancelling duplicates — every element that appears twice vanishes, leaving only the singleton. O(n) time, O(1) space.
xor.q: Why does XORing all elements find the singleton?
xor.qsub: What if TWO elements appear once (find both)? · Can XOR solve the 'appears 3 times' variant? · Why is XOR O(1) space where a hash set is O(n)?
xor.what:
In the array every number appears twice except one single element. You need to find it — O(n) time and O(1) space. Hash map not allowed.

The two XOR rules handle everything: x ^ x = 0 (XOR with itself disappears) and x ^ 0 = x (XOR with 0 leaves the same).

So: XOR the entire array together. Pairs will cancel each other, and the lone element remains. Order doesn’t matter — wherever the pair is, it cancels.

Condition: all other elements must appear an even number of times. Elements appearing three times won’t cancel — a completely different trick is needed.
xor.analogy:
In a ledger each loan entry also has its repayment written opposite it. Every entry written twice automatically cancels. In the end only the entry that has no counterpart remains.
The order in which they are cancelled doesn’t matter — a pair is a pair.
xor.why:
This directly turns a O(n)-space hash-map solution into O(1) space. Interviewers love this jump.

And a follow-up always appears: "what if two numbers are singletons?" Answer: XOR everything — the result is the XOR of the two numbers. Pick any set bit of that result — at that bit the two numbers differ. Use that bit to split the array into two groups and compute the XOR of each group separately. Explaining this earns big points.

How to think:

1. Start with result = 0.
2. XOR each element into result.
3. Anything that appears an even number of times cancels itself — x ^ x = 0.
4. Anything that appears an odd number of times remains — 0 ^ x = x.
5. Missing number: XOR all indices from 0..n together with all values. Each present number cancels with its index, leaving the missing one.
6. Two singletons: XOR everything → get a ^ b. diff = xor & -xor extracts a differing bit, use it to form two groups, XOR each group — those are a and b.

qa.q: Why does XORing all elements find the singleton?
qa.a: XOR is commutative and associative, and x ^ x = 0. Every duplicate pair cancels to 0, and 0 ^ singleton = singleton. Everything left after full cancellation is the number that appears once.

qa.q: How does XOR find a missing number?
qa.a: XOR the array with every index plus n. The value at each present index appears twice (once from the array, once from the index loop) and cancels. Only the missing number's index appears once — that's the answer.

bit-shifts.name: Bit Shifts & Masks
bit-shifts.desc: Left shift << multiplies by 2, right shift >> divides by 2. Combined with bitwise AND/OR and masks (1 << k), you can read, set, clear, and toggle individual bits — the basis of bitmask DP and packed-state problems.
bit-shifts.q: How do you check if a number is a power of two in one expression?
bit-shifts.qsub: How do you iterate every subset of a set of n elements? · What does >>> vs >> do with negative numbers? · How do you reverse the bits of a 32-bit integer?
bit-shifts.what:
Say you need to store 5 permissions for a user — read, write, execute, share, delete. Five separate booleans feel wasteful, but all five states fit into a single number using 5 bits.

Left shift x << k — moves bits k places to the left, i.e. × 2^k. Right shift x >> k — the opposite, ÷ 2^k.

Mask = (1 << k) — a number where only the k-th bit is 1 and all others are 0. With this you can read, set, clear or toggle any bit — without touching the other bits.

This is the foundation of bitmask DP and subset enumeration — where the whole state is packed into an integer.
bit-shifts.analogy: Imagine a switchboard with 8 switches, each controlling a different appliance. To toggle one switch you don’t have to move the whole board — you just touch that one. A mask is the way to indicate “only this one switch”.
bit-shifts.why:
This is the foundation of subset enumeration and bitmask DP — it will be needed repeatedly in Phases 7 and 8.

There are also two JavaScript-specific traps that interviewers watch for. First: operator precedence — x & 1 << k !== 0 parses incorrectly, so parentheses are required. Second: >> preserves the sign bit, >>> does not — this difference breaks things for negative numbers.

How to think:

1. Read: (x >> k) & 1 — shift the bit down and AND with 1. Or (x & (1 << k)) !== 0.
2. Set: x | (1 << k) — OR sets that bit to 1, leaving others unchanged.
3. Clear: x & ~(1 << k) — use the inverted mask where only that bit is 0; AND clears it.
4. Toggle: x ^ (1 << k) — XOR flips the bit.
5. Subsets: All subsets of n items correspond to numbers from 0 to 2^n - 1. Each number is a subset — bits set to 1 indicate included items.
6. In JavaScript bitwise ops work on 32-bit integers. 1 << 31 becomes negative, and 1 << 32 wraps back to 1.

qa.q: How do you check if a number is a power of two in one expression?
qa.a: n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) === 0. n - 1 flips the lowest set bit and all zeros below it; if n was a pure power of two, n & (n-1) clears its only set bit → 0. Any other n keeps at least one bit → nonzero.

qa.q: What is a bitmask and when is it worth it?
qa.a: A single integer whose bits encode a set of choices — e.g. bit k = 1 means element k is used. It turns subset/state operations into O(1) integer ops, the backbone of bitmask DP (Traveling Salesman). It's worth it when n ≤ 20 and states are combinations.

n-minus-1.name: n & (n-1) Trick
n-minus-1.desc: The expression n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit of n. Repeating it counts set bits in O(number of set bits) — faster than scanning every bit — and it powers 'is this a power of two?'
n-minus-1.q: Why is this faster than shifting every bit?
n-minus-1.qsub: How many iterations does the loop run for a number with k set bits? · How does this relate to the power-of-two check? · What happens when n = 0 in the counting loop?
n-minus-1.what:
We need to count how many 1s are in the binary representation of a number. The naive method: check each of the 32 bits one by one — even if only 2 bits are set, the loop runs the full 32 times.

n & (n - 1) is a shortcut: it always clears the lowest set bit and leaves all other bits unchanged.

How: Subtracting 1 turns the lowest 1 into 0 and flips all the 0s to its right into 1s (a borrow). Now AND the result with the original n — those flipped bits become 0 again (they were 0 in the original), and the higher bits stay the same.

So the loop runs only as many times as there are set bits — not 32 times. And a free bonus: n & (n-1) === 0 means there was only one set bit, i.e., a power of two.
n-minus-1.analogy:
Imagine all the lights in a building are on and you want to count them. There is a magical switch that, each time you press it, turns off only the lowest-still-on light, leaving the rest unchanged.
The number of times you have to press the switch equals the number of lights that were on. That's it.
n-minus-1.why:
The Hamming weight changes from O(32) to O(set bits). But the real interview question is “why does it work” — you need to explain the borrow reason, not just quote the formula.

Another confusing sibling is n & -n. It works the opposite way — it keeps only the lowest set bit and clears everything else. They are two completely different operations.

How to think:

1. Take n - 1: the lowest 1 becomes 0, and all the trailing 0s to its right become 1.
2. n & (n - 1): those flipped bits become 0 again after the AND (they were 0 in the original).
3. The higher bits are the same in both numbers — they do not change at all.
4. Result: exactly one set bit is removed, the rest stay safe.
5. Count: while (n) { n &= n - 1; count++ } — each iteration consumes one set bit.
6. Power of two: n > 0 && (n & (n-1)) === 0 — there was only one set bit, so the expression becomes zero in one step. The 0 check is required.

qa.q: Why is this faster than shifting every bit?
qa.a: Shifting checks all 32 bits regardless. n & (n-1) skips every 0 bit entirely — the loop runs once per SET bit. For sparse numbers like 8 (1000), that's 1 iteration instead of 32.

qa.q: What does n & -n compute?
qa.a: The value of the lowest set bit as a power of two. -n is two's complement (invert + 1), which keeps the lowest 1 bit and flips everything above — ANDing with n isolates exactly that bit. Useful for Fenwick trees and lowest-bit manipulation.

memo-vs-tab.name: Memoization vs Tabulation
memo-vs-tab.desc: Two ways to compute the same DP table. Memoization (top-down): recursive with a cache, compute only needed states. Tabulation (bottom-up): iterative, fill a table in dependency order. Same result, different trade-offs.
memo-vs-tab.q: When should you prefer memoization over tabulation?
memo-vs-tab.qsub: Why does naive Fibonacci blow up to O(2^n)? · What is a 'state' in DP terms? · When can you roll the table into variables?
memo-vs-tab.what:
Run fib(40) recursively — it takes minutes. That’s because subproblems like fib(35) are recomputed thousands of times.

There are two remedies, and both stop that waste — they just differ in direction.

Memoization (top-down): keep the recursion you already thought of, and add a cache. Compute the answer the first time and store it; subsequent calls return the cached value directly.

Tabulation (bottom-up): eliminate recursion. Start from the base case and fill a table forward until the final answer is obtained.

The table is the same in both approaches. In interviews, always start with memo — because it’s only a one-line change to your recursive solution.
memo-vs-tab.analogy:
Think of exam practice. Memo = whenever you solve a new problem, write the answer in a notebook — if the same problem appears again, just look it up.
Tabulation = first write down the answers to all easy problems, then use them to build the harder ones — you never need to go back.
memo-vs-tab.why:
The interviewer asks about the trade-off between the two. Memo is easy to write — it comes directly from the recursive solution — but the call stack can overflow on large inputs, and it only computes the necessary states.

Tabulation requires a bit of planning (the dependency order must be correct), but it is usually faster and safer, and it enables space optimization — “only the previous two values are needed? Then don’t keep the whole array.”

Another question that almost always appears: “Can you convert this to bottom-up?”

How to think:

1. First write a brute-force recursion. Let it be correct; we’ll optimise later.
2. Identify the state — the parameters that change between calls constitute the state.
3. Add a memo (array or Map) with key = state. At the start of the function check the cache, and at the end store the result in the cache.
4. To switch to bottom-up: the table size equals the number of states, and the loop order follows the dependency graph — fill what is needed first.
5. Seed the base cases in the table.
6. Finally, see if each dp[i] depends only on the previous 1-2 entries; if so, replace the array with a few variables — O(1) space.
where: O(#states × cost per state) · space: O(#states) + O(depth)
O(#states × cost per state) · space: O(table) or optimized O(1)-O(n)

qa.q: When should you prefer memoization over tabulation?
qa.a: Memoization is easier to write correctly (just add a cache to working recursion), only computes reachable states, and reads naturally. Prefer it unless recursion depth is a risk or the interviewer wants the iterative version — then write tabulation.

qa.q: What's the key to a space-optimized DP?
qa.a: Figure out the dependency window — if dp[i] only needs dp[i-1] and dp[i-2], keep two variables instead of the full table. 2D problems often reduce to two rolling rows (or one) when each cell only reads the row above.

identify-dp.name: Identifying DP
identify-dp.desc: The pattern-recognition step: a problem is DP when it has overlapping subproblems (same sub-solve computed many times) and optimal substructure (best answer built from best sub-answers). 'Count ways', 'min/max cost', and 'is it possible' phrasing are strong signals.
identify-dp.q: How do you recognize DP vs a greedy solution?
identify-dp.qsub: What is the difference between 'count ways' and 'min cost' recurrences? · Why does a single counterexample kill a greedy approach? · How do you define a state for a 2-string problem like Edit Distance?
identify-dp.what:
A new problem appears. First decision: greedy, plain recursion, or DP? Choosing the wrong one is the most common mistake.

Check two things. Overlapping subproblems — draw the brute-force recursion tree and see if the exact same subproblem (same parameters) appears repeatedly.

Optimal substructure — does the best answer for the whole come directly from the best answers of the parts, without rethinking any previous decision?

If both are present → DP. If only one is present → plain recursion or greedy. And a shortcut: the problem phrase often tells you — “how many ways”, “minimum/maximum cost”, “is it possible”.
identify-dp.analogy:
You are climbing a straight ladder, thinking at each step “take 1 or 2”. After a while you notice that the question “what comes after step 5” keeps appearing from different paths.
When the same question has to be asked repeatedly — that’s the overlapping subproblem, and the signal to use caching.
identify-dp.why:
This step isn’t asked directly in an interview — but the interviewer knows what’s happening. If you start coding without defining a state, the interviewer instantly sees that you don’t understand DP.

And remember the greedy trap: greedy fails with a single counterexample. In Coin Change with coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6, greedy picks 4+1+1 = 3 coins, but the correct answer is 3+3 = 2. Can’t prove it? Switch to DP.

How to think:

1. Imagine the brute-force recursion and draw its call tree (on a small input).
2. Does the same subproblem appear again? → overlapping. Caching will help.
3. Define the state: “what changes from one call to the next?” One index → dp[i]. Two indices → dp[i][j]. Index + remaining budget → dp[i][w].
4. Write the recurrence in words first, not code: “the best for this position = this choice or that choice, whichever is better”.
5. Pick the operator from the phrase: “how many ways” → +. “minimum/maximum” → min/max. “is it possible” → ||.
6. Write the base case — the smallest input whose answer is known directly.

qa.q: How do you recognize DP vs a greedy solution?
qa.a: Try greedy: does the locally best choice always lead to the global best? If you can't prove it and counterexamples exist, it's DP. Tell-tale: 'subsets/subsets with constraint' where the answer depends on ALL previous choices, not just the last one.

qa.q: What's the first question to design any DP?
qa.a: 'What is the state?' — the tuple of everything that changes between recursive calls. For Climbing Stairs it's i (steps remaining). For Knapsack it's (index, remaining capacity). Get the state right and the recurrence usually writes itself.

dp-1d.name: 1D DP
dp-1d.desc: dp[i] depends only on earlier indices (usually i-1, i-2). The Fibonacci, House Robber, and Decode Ways family. The simplest DP class — master it before anything 2D.
dp-1d.q: How do you choose the recurrence for a 1D DP?
dp-1d.qsub: When does dp[i] depend on i-2 vs all previous indices? · How do you optimize LIS from O(n²) to O(n log n)? · What's the base case trap in Decode Ways ('0' handling)?
dp-1d.what:
You are climbing a straight ladder, taking either 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many ways to reach step n? Here the answer depends only on the previous one or two steps — no older history is needed.

This pattern is called 1D DP: an array dp where dp[i] stores the answer up to position i, and it is built from dp[i-1] or dp[i-2].

Fibonacci, House Robber, Decode Ways — all belong to this family. Only the transition rule differs: sometimes you add, sometimes you take max.

And a free benefit: if you need only the previous two values, you don’t have to keep the whole array — two variables are enough. Reduce space from O(n) to O(1).
dp-1d.analogy:
A thief is planning a neighborhood raid — he cannot rob two adjacent houses in a row. At each house his decision depends only on one thing: “what was the best up to the previous one or two houses?”.
He never needs to reconsider the entire neighborhood’s history.
dp-1d.why:
This is the first DP pattern that appears in interviews, and it teaches the clearest version of state definition — one value per index.

If you are confused here (what dp[i] means, which previous states are needed), the confusion only grows with 2D and bitmask DP.

And the base-case trap is right here: handling '0' in Decode Ways, and n = 0 and n = 1 in House Robber — these are where most people stumble.

How to think:

1. Write the meaning of dp[i] in one line — “the best/count up to the first i elements”.
2. Base case: consider i = 0 and i = 1 separately. Empty input and a single element — write these two cases first.
3. State the recurrence in words: “take this element or skip it — whichever is better”.
4. House Robber: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]). Skip → dp[i-1]. Take → you must skip the previous, so use dp[i-2].
5. Fill the whole array; dp[n-1] is the answer.
6. Space: Need only the previous two values? Keep two variables — but update them in the correct order, otherwise you lose the old value.

qa.q: How do you choose the recurrence for a 1D DP?
qa.a: Answer 'what happens at index i?' for each possible choice. House Robber: either skip (take dp[i-1]) or rob (take dp[i-2] + nums[i]) — the max is the answer. Every 1D recurrence is 'the best of the choices, each expressed through earlier dp values'.

qa.q: Why is House Robber II solved by running rob twice?
qa.a: The circle breaks the linear dependency between house 0 and house n-1. Run the linear solution once excluding house 0 and once excluding house n-1, then take the max — one of those two choices must be optimal, and both are linear subproblems.

dp-unbounded.name: Unbounded Knapsack (Coin Change)
dp-unbounded.desc: Items can be reused any number of times. Coin Change (min coins) and Coin Change II (number of ways) are the templates — iterate amount first (unbounded) vs coins first (for ways, to avoid double-counting).
dp-unbounded.q: Why does the loop order differ between min-coins and ways?
dp-unbounded.qsub: When does unbounded DP degenerate into 0/1 (each item once)? · How do you recover WHICH coins were used? · What does dp[0] = 0 / dp[0] = 1 represent?
dp-unbounded.what:
Coins of 1, 5, 10 — and you can use each type as many times as you want, no limit. This is called unbounded.

Two questions are asked and they are different: "minimum number of coins" (Coin Change) and "how many ways" (Coin Change II).

And here is the thing that makes this topic tricky: the code for both is almost identical, the only difference is the order of loops — and that changes the answer completely.

Coins outer, amount inner → each coin is considered only once → combinations (order not counted). Amount outer, coins inner → for each amount all coins are tried again → permutations (order is counted).
dp-unbounded.analogy:
Coins are unlimited at the shop.
If you finish one coin completely before moving to the next — "all 1s first, then all 2s" — then {1,2} is counted only once.
But if you look at all coins again for each amount, then {1,2} and {2,1} become two different answers.
dp-unbounded.why:
The effect of loop order is very subtle but can completely change the answer — and spotting the bug from code is hard. That’s why interviewers like it.

The test is that you understand that combinations and permutations are different concepts, and the loop order determines which one you get.

Another test: difference between unbounded and 0/1. In unbounded the loop runs forward (because reuse is allowed), in 0/1 it runs backward (because reuse is not allowed). This single line changes the whole topic.

How to think:

1. Min coins: dp[a] = minimum number of coins for amount a. Fill dp with Infinity, set dp[0] = 0.
2. For each amount try every coin: dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - coin] + 1). Loop order doesn’t matter here.
3. At the end, is dp[amount] still Infinity? That means it’s impossible — return -1.
4. Ways: dp[0] = 1 (one way to make amount zero — take nothing).
5. Keep the coins loop outer, amount inner. This makes each coin considered only once and prevents duplicate combinations.
6. In unbounded the amount loop runs forward (coin to amount) — allowing the same dp[a - coin] to reuse the same coin. That is the reuse.

qa.q: Why does the loop order differ between min-coins and ways?
qa.a: For MIN coins, order doesn't matter (taking 1+2 or 2+1 costs the same), so amount-outer is fine. For WAYS, coins-outer treats combinations as sets — each coin is 'introduced' once, so [1,2] isn't counted as [2,1]. That's the difference between combinations and permutations.

qa.q: What's the recurrence for Coin Change?
qa.a: dp[a] = min over coins c of (dp[a - c] + 1). You pick one coin, reduce the amount by c, and ask for the best answer of the smaller amount — with unlimited reuse, the subproblem 'amount a-c' already allows reusing that coin.

dp-2d-grid.name: 2D Grid DP
dp-2d-grid.desc: dp[i][j] built from up (i-1, j) and left (i, j-1). Unique Paths and Minimum Path Sum are the templates — the grid's structure IS the dependency graph. Watch the boundary rows/columns.
dp-2d-grid.q: How do you derive the recurrence for grid DP?
dp-2d-grid.qsub: How do obstacle cells change the table? · What about diagonal or 8-direction movement? · Why do edge rows/cols get seeded to 1?
dp-2d-grid.what:
You stand at the top-left of the grid and need to reach the bottom-right, moving only right or down. How many unique paths are there? Or which path has the minimum cost?

Now think backwards. How do you reach any cell (i, j)? Only from two places — from the cell above by moving down, or from the cell to the left by moving right. That's it. There is no third way.

So dp[i][j] is built from those two. The shape of the grid itself is the dependency graph — you just decide whether to add (count paths) or take min/max (cost).

The first row and first column must be seeded separately, because there is nothing above or to the left of them.
dp-2d-grid.analogy:
Imagine a building layout where each apartment can be reached in only two ways — directly down from the apartment above, or across the corridor from the neighboring apartment.
Thus the total ways to reach any apartment = ways from the apartment above + ways from the neighboring apartment. You don’t need to traverse the whole building again — just the two neighbors are enough.
dp-2d-grid.why:
This is the first DP where the state is formed from two numbers, not one. This is where the dp[i][j] thinking originates and it works for LCS, Edit Distance, and knapsack — everywhere.

And this is the clearest place to learn it, because the state is visible. A grid cell itself is the state — no imagination required.

In interviews, Unique Paths and Minimum Path Sum are common warm-up questions. After that, a direct follow-up appears: “can you reduce the space?” — and the rolling-row answer comes from here.

How to think:

1. dp[i][j] means, in one line: “the answer from (0,0) to (i,j)”.
2. Ask: how could you have arrived at this cell? With right/down moves, only from up and left.
3. Choose the operator — if you’re counting use +, if it’s cost use min, if it’s profit use max.
4. Boundary seed: The first row and first column each have only one neighbour. In Unique Paths everything is 1, in Min Path Sum it’s a running sum.
5. Loop top-to-bottom, left-to-right — so both neighbours are already computed.
6. The answer is at dp[m-1][n-1].
7. Space: Need only the previous row? Keep a single row and overwrite it left-to-right as you go.

qa.q: How do you derive the recurrence for grid DP?
qa.a: Ask: how can you ARRIVE at cell (i,j)? For right/down moves, only from above (i-1,j) or left (i,j-1). Count problems SUM those ways; min/max problems take MIN of the two incoming costs, plus the cell's own value.

qa.q: How do you reduce 2D DP to O(cols) space?
qa.a: Each cell only reads its left neighbor (current row) and up-neighbor (previous row). So keep just the previous row — compute the new row left-to-right. You never touch rows older than the last one.

dp-2d-seq.name: 2D Sequence DP (LCS / Edit Distance)
dp-2d-seq.desc: Two strings/arrays compared cell by cell. dp[i][j] = answer for first i chars of A and first j chars of B. When chars match you diagonal-step; when they don't you take a min/max of the insert/delete/skip options.
dp-2d-seq.q: Why the +1 sentinel row and column?
dp-2d-seq.qsub: How do you recover the actual LCS, not just its length? · Why is Longest Palindromic Subsequence just LCS(s, reverse(s))? · When is space O(min(m,n)) achievable?
dp-2d-seq.what:
We have two strings and need to compare them — how much they have in common (LCS), or how many operations are needed to turn one into the other (Edit Distance).

dp[i][j] means: “the answer for the first i characters of A and the first j characters of B”. Not the whole strings — only the initial parts.

Now each cell asks a single question — do the current two characters match?

Match: advance one step in both strings and add a score of +1. This is the diagonal cell.
Mismatch: you have to skip a character on one side — either from A or from B. These are the up and left cells, and you take the best of them.

This gives a table of size (m+1) × (n+1). The extra row and column are for the empty string — they provide the base case and avoid if complications.
dp-2d-seq.analogy:
Two friends are listening to their own playlists together.
If the song is the same — both are happy, both move forward, count +1.
If the song is different — one of them has to skip their song. There are two choices, and the choice that yields more matches later is the correct one.
The table simply remembers all these decisions so you don’t have to think about them again.
dp-2d-seq.why:
LCS and Edit Distance are two faces of the same table, and once you learn them an entire family opens up — Longest Palindromic Subsequence, Distinct Subsequences, Interleaving String, Regex Matching. All follow the same pattern.

Edit Distance is real-world: spell-check, git diff, DNA alignment, the “did you mean” feature in a search bar — all run this algorithm.

In interviews it checks whether you can define the state. If you can explain in words what dp[i][j] represents, the recurrence comes out naturally.

How to think:

1. Build a table (m+1) × (n+1) — extra row/col for the empty string.
2. Fill base cases: In LCS everything is 0. In Edit Distance the first row is = j and the first column is = i (turning an empty string into j characters needs j insertions).
3. For each cell compare a[i-1] and b[j-1] — minus one, because the table starts at 1 while strings start at 0.
4. Match: LCS → 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]. Edit Distance → simply dp[i-1][j-1] (no cost).
5. Mismatch: LCS → max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Edit Distance → 1 + min(the three neighbours).
6. The answer is at dp[m][n] — not at m-1, because the table is 1-indexed.
7. Space: you only need the previous row → keep two rows, O(min(m, n)).
where: O(m × n) · space: O(m × n) or O(min(m,n))
O(m × n) · space: O(m × n) or O(n)

qa.q: Why the +1 sentinel row and column?
qa.a: dp[i][j] is 'first i of a vs first j of b'. With i=0 or j=0, the answer is the length of the other string (empty vs non-empty). Padding the table with an empty-string row/col gives clean base cases: LCS empty = 0; Edit Distance empty = j or i.

qa.q: What's the Edit Distance recurrence in words?
qa.a: If the current chars match, carry the diagonal answer. If not, it's 1 plus the cheapest of: delete a char (dp[i-1][j]), insert a char (dp[i][j-1]), or replace (dp[i-1][j-1]). The three operations ARE the three neighbor cells.

knapsack.name: 0-1 Knapsack
knapsack.desc: Each item is taken at most once — choose or skip. The capacity dimension makes it 2D: dp[i][w] = best value using first i items within weight w. Partition Equal Subset Sum and Target Sum are its classic LeetCode masks.
knapsack.q: Why must the capacity loop run backward in 0/1 knapsack?
knapsack.qsub: How does Target Sum map to knapsack (transform the equation)? · What's the difference between subset-sum and partition? · How do you recover WHICH items were chosen?
knapsack.what:
There is a bag with a fixed weight limit and several items — each item has its own weight and value. Each item can be taken only once. What is the maximum total value you can fit?

For each item you have exactly two choices — take or skip. That’s why it’s called 0/1.

dp[i][w] = “best value using the first i items within weight w”. Two dimensions are needed because two things change: which item you are considering and how much capacity remains.

The most important point, the heart of the topic, is this: when you squeeze dp into a single 1D array, the capacity loop must run backward (from high to low). If you iterate forward, dp[w - wt] will already contain the current item — causing the item to be used twice. This single line distinguishes 0/1 from unbounded knapsack.
knapsack.analogy:
Think of a buffet where each dish is served only once.
If you update your plate starting from the smallest portion upward, you may count the dish you just added all over again.
So go backward — start from the largest portion first. That way, whatever you look at is always the plate as it was before this dish.
knapsack.why:
This pattern never appears on LeetCode under its original name. It shows up as Partition Equal Subset Sum, Target Sum, Last Stone Weight II, Ones and Zeroes — and if you recognize knapsack, they all turn into the same problem.

The backward-loop trick is the most important “why” in DP. Once you get it, you won’t need to memorize the recurrence — you’ll derive on your own which direction the loop should go.

Interviewers often ask exactly this: “why is the loop backward?” — it’s just one line, but it reveals whether you truly understand DP or are just reciting a template.

How to think:

1. Identify: you need to choose a subset + there is a capacity/target + items cannot be reused → 0/1 knapsack.
2. State: dp[w] = “best value achievable with weight ≤ w” (or a boolean — “can we achieve weight w”).
3. Seed: dp[0] = 0 (or true). An empty bag is always valid — forgetting this seed is the most common bug.
4. The outer loop iterates over items.
5. The inner loop iterates over capacity, backward: for (w = cap; w ≥ wt; w--).
6. dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - wt] + val) — skip or take.
7. In Subset Sum: replace value with a boolean, dp[w] = dp[w] || dp[w - num].
8. In Partition: if total is odd, return false immediately. Otherwise set target = total / 2 and run subset-sum.

qa.q: Why must the capacity loop run backward in 0/1 knapsack?
qa.a: dp[w] should consider each item once. Going forward, dp[w - x] might already include the current item (updated earlier in the same loop) — that's unlimited reuse. Backward means dp[w - x] is still the previous item's value, so the item is used at most once.

qa.q: How do you recognize a knapsack problem?
qa.a: A subset-selection constraint with a capacity-like bound: 'subset sums to target', 'can we fit items under weight W with max value'. If items are limited to one use each → 0/1; reusable → unbounded; ordered arrangements → different dimension.

dp-state-machine.name: State Machine DP
dp-state-machine.desc: Track multiple STATES of ownership/position per day — for Buy/Sell Stock, whether you currently hold a share. dp[i][state] where state ∈ {not holding, holding}. Transitions model buy/sell/hold decisions.
dp-state-machine.q: What does 'state' mean in state-machine DP?
dp-state-machine.qsub: What does the cooldown state add? · Why start hold at -Infinity? · When is the single-pass min-so-far solution enough?
dp-state-machine.what:
You're given a stock's price each day. Buy, sell, or do nothing — what's the maximum profit?

If you write only dp[i] = “max profit up to day i” here, you'll get stuck. Because the next decision depends on one more thing that isn't in this number: do you hold a stock right now or not?

If you hold a stock you can sell today. If you don't, you can buy. The options themselves are different.

So put that fact into the state. dp[i][0] = the best when you don't hold a stock, dp[i][1] = the best when you do. Now on each day each state has just two roads — stay where you are, or switch to the other state (by buying or selling).

That's the pattern. And it scales too — add a third state for a cooldown, add one more dimension for k transactions.
dp-state-machine.analogy:
Imagine a vegetable vendor. Every morning he is in one of two situations — the produce is in stock, or only money is in his pocket.
In each situation his future options are completely different: if he has produce he can sell, if he has money he can buy.
So his accounting isn't a single number but two numbers — “best up to today if the produce is in stock” and “best up to today if it isn't”.
dp-state-machine.why:
The entire Buy and Sell Stock family (I, II, III, IV, cooldown, fee) — six different LeetCode problems — can be built from the same template. Only the number of states changes, the thinking stays the same.

And even more important: it teaches how to expand the state. When your DP doesn’t work, the usual reason is that a necessary piece wasn't added to the state. This topic becomes that reflex.

In interviews this is a very common follow-up chain: first the simple version, then “add cooldown”, then “add at most k transactions”. For the state-machine approach all three are the same idea.

How to think:

1. Write the states — what factor changes the future options? Whether you have the stock or not. If there is a cooldown, add a third: sold today.
2. Write the transitions for each state — where you can go from this state and what the cost is.
3. Initialize: cash = 0 (nothing done), hold = -Infinity (holding without buying is impossible). Setting it to 0 here is the most common bug.
4. Each day update both states. Both lines need the old values — therefore update cash first, or copy first.
5. At the end the answer is cash — not hold. You don’t count profit while holding stock.
6. Fee? Subtract it when selling. Cooldown? Add a third state. k transactions? Add a dimension for k.

qa.q: What does 'state' mean in state-machine DP?
qa.a: The condition that changes your options — holding vs not holding a share. dp[holding] and dp[cash] evolve day by day: each can 'stay' or 'transition'. Any flag that gates decisions (cooldown, transaction limit) is another state dimension.

qa.q: How does the k-transaction version change?
qa.a: Add k as a dimension: dp[k][holding] vs dp[k][cash]. Buying moves you to the next transaction count. The same transition logic applies, just indexed by how many trades you've used.

dp-interval.name: Interval DP
dp-interval.desc: dp[i][j] describes a segment from i to j. The answer for a segment combines answers of smaller segments split at some k. The canonical shapes: longest palindromic substring/subsequence and burst-balloon-style 'choose the last to act'.
dp-interval.q: How do you know interval DP applies?
dp-interval.qsub: How does palindromic subsequence use LCS? · What makes burst-balloon O(n³)? · When is expand-around-center better than table DP?
dp-interval.what:
Until now dp[i] meant “answer up to a point”. In interval DP, dp[i][j] means “the answer for the entire segment [i..j]” — a range, not a single point.

And here’s the twist. A larger segment can't be built directly from smaller ones. You have to choose a split point k inside the range, and add dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] — plus whatever cost or value is created at that split.

Which k is correct? You don’t know. So try all of them and keep the best. That’s why the complexity is O(n³).

Another important point: dp[i][j] needs the smaller segments inside it. So the table must be filled in order of increasing length — first len 1, then len 2, then len 3. If you loop directly over i and j, you’ll read half-filled cells.
dp-interval.analogy:
Imagine you have to break a long chocolate bar and each cut has its own cost.
The question is where to make the first cut — because after that the two smaller bars will be handled separately.
You can’t know the best cut in advance, so try cutting at every position and keep the one with the lowest total cost.
dp-interval.why:
This is the final classic DP shape. In 1D, 2D grid, 2D sequence, knapsack — the state was built from one or two points. Here the state is a range, and the transition is a split. This way of thinking is different and needs to be learned.

Burst Balloons is the most famous interview question in this category, and it is hard because people think about which balloon to pop first. The correct thinking is the opposite — which balloon to pop last. Then the segments on both sides become independent.

Matrix Chain Multiplication, Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick, Palindrome Partitioning — all are manifestations of this same idea.

How to think:

1. Write what dp[i][j] means — “the best answer for segment [i..j]”.
2. Base case: Fill len = 1 (and also len = 2 for palindrome) by hand.
3. Outer loop over LENGTH: for (len = 2; len ≤ n; len++). This is the most important line.
4. Inside, iterate i and compute j = i + len - 1.
5. The innermost k runs from i to j-1 — try every split.
6. dp[i][j] = best(dp[i][j], dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + cost).
7. Burst Balloons twist: treat k not as the “first” but as the “last to pop”. Then both sides become independent and the neighbor stays fixed.
8. The answer is at dp[0][n-1] — the whole segment.

qa.q: How do you know interval DP applies?
qa.a: The answer is defined over a contiguous range [i, j] and decomposes by splitting into smaller ranges — a palindrome [i,j] is a palindrome iff s[i]===s[j] AND [i+1,j-1] is a palindrome. The 'segment built from sub-segments' structure is the signature.

qa.q: Why expand around center for palindromic substring?
qa.a: There are 2n-1 centers (each char + each gap). Expanding each takes O(n), total O(n²) time and O(1) space — beating the O(n²) space DP for SUBSTRING (contiguous). The DP table only wins when you need the palindromic SUBSEQUENCE, which isn't contiguous.

dp-bitmask.name: DP with Bitmasks
dp-bitmask.desc: When the state includes which elements are used, encode it as an integer bitmask: bit i set means item i is taken. Combined with memo, this handles subset-partition, TSP, and assignment problems in O(2^n * n) — exponential but often the intended answer for n <= 20.
dp-bitmask.q: When do you recognize bitmask DP is the tool?
dp-bitmask.qsub: How do you check if bit i is set in mask? · How do you add item i to the mask? · Why does n have to be small? · How do you prune a partition DP for speed?
dp-bitmask.what:
Sometimes the state needs to keep track of which items have been used so far — not just how many, but which ones.

Storing a set in an array or Set to use as a memo key is awkward. But if the number of items is small (n ≤ 20), the whole set fits into a single integer.

Each bit is an item. Bit i being 1 → item i has been used. 1011 means: items 0, 1 and 3 have been taken, item 2 remains. This number is 11 — and that becomes your array index.

The real benefit is: the same set that comes from different orders becomes one state. So n! permutations shrink to 2ⁿ subsets. It is still exponential, but 2²⁰ = 1,000,000 — that works. 20! is about 2.4 quintillion — that does not.
dp-bitmask.analogy:
Imagine a bus booking chart — each seat has a box, filled or empty.
To describe the whole bus you don’t need a list of seat numbers, just one line is enough: 1011.
If two people book the same seats in different orders, their charts will look exactly the same. That is the thing that does half the work.
dp-bitmask.why:
This topic gives you a new weapon: when the state is a set, turn it into an integer. This trick works not only in DP — but also in graph, backtracking, and state-space search.

And a very practical signal: if the problem constraints say n ≤ 20 or n ≤ 15, then this almost always hints at a bitmask solution. Such a small limit is not required for a polynomial-time solution — it is given because the intended solution is exponential.

Travelling Salesman, Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets, Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes — all appear in interviews and all follow this pattern.

How to think:

1. Look at n. Proceed only if n ≤ 20.
2. Give each item a bit — item i → bit i.
3. Write the state: dp[mask], or dp[mask][last] if it also matters which item was taken last (as in TSP).
4. Base case: mask = 0 (nothing taken) or mask = (1 << n) - 1 (everything taken).
5. Transition: try each unused item — if (!(mask & (1 << i))) → new mask mask | (1 << i).
6. Apply memo — array of size 1 << n. Faster than a map because the key is already an integer.
7. Prune: in partition problems sort items in descending order (big first), skip duplicates, and return as soon as the target is exceeded. This boosts practical speed manyfold.

qa.q: When do you recognize bitmask DP is the tool?
qa.a: The state is "which items are used" and n <= ~20. If the same used-set can recur through different orders, memoizing on the mask collapses all those orders into one state.

qa.q: Why is it O(2^n * n) rather than O(n!)?
qa.a: Bitmask DP merges all permutations with the same used-set into a single state. n! orderings collapse to 2^n subsets, each considering n next choices — that is the whole win.

dp-digit.name: Digit DP
dp-digit.desc: Counts integers in a range [0, N] satisfying digit constraints (e.g. no consecutive 1s, only digits from a set, not exceeding N). The state is (position, tight, extra flags): tight means the prefix already equals N's prefix, so the current digit is capped.
dp-digit.q: What does the "tight" flag actually do?
dp-digit.qsub: How do you compute f(L, R) from f(N)? · Why is tight only a boolean, not a range? · What changes for properties like digit sums? · When would you need a "started" flag?
dp-digit.what:
The question is: “How many numbers from 0 to N have no repeated digit?” And N is 10¹⁸. Checking each number individually is impossible.

The whole idea of Digit DP is: don’t view the number as a single value, view it as a line of digits that you are constructing from left to right. There may be billions of numbers, but only up to 19 digits.

Now at each position there is only one question — which digit can I place here? The answer comes from a flag: tight.

tight ON means that the digits placed so far are exactly equal to N’s digits. In that case the current digit cannot exceed N’s digit — otherwise the number would become larger than N. But as soon as you place a smaller digit, the number is definitely less than N — and from then on every position can freely use any digit from 0 to 9. tight never turns ON again.
dp-digit.analogy:
Imagine setting a number on an odometer, turning each dial one by one, with a limit of N.
As long as every dial is exactly on N’s digit, you are on the edge — you cannot turn the next dial beyond N.
But once any dial is set a little behind, you have moved off the edge — now you can turn the remaining dials however you like and the number will stay smaller than N.
dp-digit.why:
This is the most specialized topic in Phase 7, and it’s important to state clearly: it appears very rarely in typical product-company interviews. It does show up in competitive programming and some hard LeetCode problems.

But it teaches a big idea that works everywhere: by adding a flag to the state you can handle a whole range constraint. tight is a boolean that encodes “am I still on the upper limit?”.

And a reusable trick: reduce a range to a prefix — answer(L..R) = f(R) - f(L-1). This works from prefix sums to digit DP.

How to think:

1. Convert N to a string — you will work on positions.
2. Write the state: (pos, tight, started, problem-specific flag).
3. At each position compute the limit: if tight then N[pos] else 9.
4. Recurse on each allowed digit d. New tight = tight && (d === limit).
5. Base case: pos === N.length → decide whether this number counts.
6. Memo: cache only when tight is off (and include started in the key). Paths with tight on are visited only once, so caching them gains nothing.
7. Range: f(R) - f(L-1).
8. Leading zeros: keep a started flag — zeros before the first non-zero digit are not counted as digits.

qa.q: What does the "tight" flag actually do?
qa.a: It encodes whether the digits chosen so far exactly match N's prefix. If yes, the current digit must not exceed N's digit (and if it equals it, tight stays on). Once any digit is smaller, everything later is free.

qa.q: How do you handle leading zeros?
qa.a: Add a "started" flag: zeros before the first nonzero digit do not count as digits. Enable it once a nonzero digit is placed, then allow zeros normally.

heap.name: Heap / Priority Queue
heap.desc: A binary tree stored in an array that keeps the min (or max) at the root. Insert and extract-min are O(log n), peek is O(1). The tool for 'top k' and 'smallest/largest/closest' problems. JS has no built-in heap — write one or polyfill via a priority queue.
heap.q: Why is a heap better than sorting for top-k?
heap.qsub: What's the difference between min-heap and priority queue? · How do you implement a max-heap in JS? · Why is heapify O(n) instead of O(n log n)?
heap.what:
Suppose you have a large list and repeatedly need only the smallest (or largest) element — and new items keep arriving in between. Sorting the whole list is wasteful because you don’t need the full order.

Heap is a structure that gives just one guarantee: the root always holds the smallest (or largest) item. That’s it. There is no order among the other elements. This limited guarantee makes it very cheap.

It looks like a binary tree, but it is stored in an array — the children of index i are at 2i+1 and 2i+2. No pointers, no node objects.

peek is O(1), push and pop are O(log n) — because the tree height is log n and an element moves only along that path up or down.
heap.analogy:
Think of the line in an emergency ward. The entire line isn’t ordered by seriousness — the only guarantee is that the most critical patient is at the front.
If a new critical case arrives, it moves to the front, and the others shift back a bit — the whole line isn’t rebuilt.
heap.why:
“Top k” questions are very common in interviews — Kth Largest, Top K Frequent, K Closest Points, Merge k Sorted Lists. The naive answer is to sort (O(n log n)), the heap answer is O(n log k).

And an important point: a heap works on a stream. Data keeps arriving and you can answer at any time. Sorting would have to start over each time.

JS does not have a built-in heap — so interviewers often want to see whether you can write a small heap yourself. You need to be able to implement it, not just know the name.

How to think:

1. Store in an array. parent(i) = (i-1) >> 1, children(i) = 2i+1, 2i+2.
2. push: insert at the end, then while the parent is larger — swap upward (siftUp).
3. pop: remove the root, place the last element at the root, then swap with the smaller child to move down (siftDown).
4. Need a max-heap? Two ways — reverse the comparator, or store the negative of the values.
5. Counter-intuitive rule for top k: if you want the k largest, keep a min-heap of size k. Insert a new element only if it is larger than the root, and then remove the root.
6. Prevent the size from exceeding k — this gives O(n log k).
7. Ties: if priorities are equal, add a counter or a secondary key; otherwise the order will be random.

qa.q: Why is a heap better than sorting for top-k?
qa.a: A size-k heap is O(n log k) — for k much smaller than n that beats O(n log n) sorting. And a heap handles a live stream of items; sorting must restart from scratch each time. When k ≈ n, sorting wins on constant factors.

qa.q: How do you find the median of a data stream with heaps?
qa.a: Keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, balanced in size. Median is the max of the lower heap (odd count) or the average of both roots (even). Each insert rebalances in O(log n) — see the Two Heaps lesson.

heap-variations.name: Heap Variations
heap-variations.desc: The two heaps pattern (median of a stream), k-way merge, and lazy deletion (mark-and-sweep stale entries). These variations turn the basic heap into a solution for 'Find Median from Data Stream', 'Merge k Sorted Lists', and scheduling problems.
heap-variations.q: How does the two-heap median pattern work?
heap-variations.qsub: When does the two-heap trick fail? · What's the running time of k-way merge vs merging one by one? · Why does Task Scheduler need the cooldown-aware reinsert?
heap-variations.what:
A basic heap only knows one operation — “give me the smallest”. Real problems often require a bit more. Three variations cover everything.

1. K-way merge. You need to merge k sorted lists into one. Keep only the current first element of each list in the heap. Extract the smallest, add it to the output, and push the next element from that same list into the heap. The heap never grows beyond k — so the total cost is O(n log k).

2. Lazy deletion. Removing an arbitrary element from a heap is O(n). So instead of deleting immediately, mark it “stale”, and silently discard it when it reaches the root.

3. Count then heapify. In problems like Task Scheduler, first count frequencies, then build a max-heap, run one task, and push it back after its cooldown.
heap-variations.analogy:
Think of a station with 10 platforms where trains arrive and you need to create a single arrival board.
You don’t look at the full list of trains — you only look at the next train on each platform, write the earliest arriving one on the board, and then check the following train on that platform.
The board never holds more than 10 entries, even if there are thousands of trains in total.
heap-variations.why:
These three patterns appear directly in major LeetCode problems — Merge k Sorted Lists (hard), Task Scheduler, Sliding Window Median, Smallest Range Covering K Lists.

They also teach a mindset useful later: when a data structure doesn’t provide the operation you need, instead of changing the structure, reshape the problem to fit the structure. Lazy deletion is the clearest example — can’t delete? Then don’t delete; just ignore.

External sorting (when data doesn’t fit in RAM) is essentially a k-way merge — it shows up in system design as well.

How to think:

K-way merge:
1. Insert the first element of each list into the heap, together with [value, listIndex, pos].
2. Extract the smallest → output.
3. Push the next element from that list (if any). Repeat until all lists are exhausted.

Lazy deletion:
4. Keep a Set or counter of “which items have been removed”.
5. Before pop, run a while loop — discard the root while it is stale.
6. Real size = heap size − stale count.

Task Scheduler:
7. Count frequencies, build a max-heap.
8. In one round extract up to n+1 distinct tasks, then push back those with remaining count.
where: O(log n) per insert · space: O(n)

qa.q: How does the two-heap median pattern work?
qa.a: The lower half lives in a max-heap, the upper in a min-heap, sizes differ by at most 1. Insert: add to lower, then shift the max into upper to keep the invariant. Median = lower's max when sizes are unequal, else average of both roots.

qa.q: What is lazy deletion and when do you need it?
qa.a: Heaps only expose the root for removal. To 'remove' an arbitrary element, mark it stale (a tombstone) and filter it out when it surfaces as the root. Standard for Task Scheduler and 'max heap with update' patterns where real deletion would cost O(n).

heapify.name: Heapify / Build Heap in O(n)
heapify.desc: Turning an arbitrary array into a valid heap. Sift down each node starting from the last internal node down to the root — this is O(n), not O(n log n). The intuition: most nodes are near the leaves, and their sift-down depth is small.
heapify.q: Why is heapify O(n) instead of O(n log n)?
heapify.qsub: What index is the last internal node of a heap? · Why is sift-down building faster than inserting n times? · How do you do heapsort with this? · Where does the O(n) come from mathematically?
heapify.what:
Say you have a random array that you need to turn into a heap. The straightforward way: keep push() each element. Each push is O(log n), total O(n log n).

But there is a better method that takes only O(n) — and it surprises many people.

Heapify works in reverse. Start from the array’s last internal node (i = n/2 - 1) and move backward toward the root, performing siftDown on each node.

Why is this cheaper? Because most nodes sit near the bottom, where the work is smallest. Leaves (about half of all nodes!) are already valid heaps — their work is zero. The next n/4 nodes above them move down only one level. The only node that can fall the full height is the root.

Adding it all up, the series sums to less than 2n — hence O(n).

The push method is expensive because it works the opposite way: half the nodes are leaves, and in siftUp those same nodes may have to climb the full height.
heapify.analogy:
Imagine reorganizing a whole company by seniority.
If you start from the CEO, every change propagates all the way down.
But if you start from the smallest teams — fix a couple of people among themselves — and then move upward, by the time you reach the top very little work remains, because at the higher levels only a few people are involved.
heapify.why:
“How long does it take to build a heap?” — this is a very common interview question, and O(n log n) is a very common wrong answer.

Giving the correct answer and stating the reason in one line ("half the nodes are leaves, their work is zero") immediately shows that you understand the complexity, not just memorized it.

It also matters in practice: for Top-K style problems where the whole array is already present, heapify plus k pops gives O(n + k log n). Heapsort also relies on this — O(n log n) time, O(1) space, guaranteed (unlike quicksort it doesn’t degrade in the worst case).

How to think:

1. Find the last internal node: i = (n >> 1) - 1. Everything after it are leaves.
2. Run the loop backwards — from i down to 0.
3. Perform siftDown on each node — not siftUp. This makes all the difference.
4. Reason for the reverse order: when you reach a node, both of its children are already valid heaps. So each siftDown only has to fix one node against its children.
5. Everything happens in place — no extra memory — O(1) extra space.
6. Heapsort: build a max-heap, then repeat n times: swap the root with the last element, shrink the heap by one, and run siftDown.
7. In an interview say one line: "heapify is O(n) because half the nodes are leaves and their sift-down work is zero."

qa.q: Why is heapify O(n) instead of O(n log n)?
qa.a: Because most nodes are near the leaves and sift down only a few levels. Summing each node's height over the whole tree gives a geometric series that converges to < 2n. Insert-based building is O(n log n) since n/2 nodes sift up the full height.

qa.q: Why start at the last internal node and sift down?
qa.a: A leaf is already a valid heap of size 1. Working bottom-up guarantees every child is heapified before its parent, so one sift down per node fixes the whole array. Sifting up instead would be O(n log n).

timed-mocks.name: Timed Mock Sessions
timed-mocks.desc: 45-minute, no-hints, talk-out-loud problem solving under a timer — the closest rehearsal for the real thing. You have been doing one per week since Phase 3 — here the cadence goes up to one every other day for 30 days (10+ more mocks). The goal is performance, not learning new algorithms.
timed-mocks.q: How do you choose mock problems?
timed-mocks.qsub: How do you handle a problem you've never seen? · When should you stop coding and talk? · How do you simulate the phone-screen format?
timed-mocks.what:
You’ve solved 200 problems — in your own room, without a timer, in your own editor. Then in an interview you get 45 minutes, a person watching you think, and your mind goes blank.

This is not a knowledge gap. It’s a performance gap — and it requires separate practice.

A timed mock creates exactly that situation: a 45-minute timer, no hints, no Google, and you must speak your thought process out loud the whole time — even if no one is in the room.

The real benefit isn’t in the mock itself, but in the review afterward. Watch the recording — where were you silent for 40 seconds? At which point did you need a hint? Did you state the complexity correctly? After each mock, fix one habit.

Stop learning new patterns today. Now learn to produce what you know under pressure.
timed-mocks.analogy:
Full-length timed papers before board exams aren’t given to make you revise the syllabus.
They are given so you learn how to allocate time in three hours, and if you get stuck on a hard question you don’t let panic cause you to miss the rest of the paper.
This skill never comes from just reading chapters — it only comes from sitting with a clock ticking.
timed-mocks.why:
The interviewer isn’t just looking for the correct answer. They score four separate things: problem solving (what you do when you get stuck), coding (clean code), communication (is your thought process audible?), and testing (do you catch mistakes yourself?).

Three of these have nothing to do with the LeetCode grind. They come only from mock practice.

And a practical point: onsite interviews have 4-5 rounds back-to-back. This also builds stamina. If you’ve never done two 45-minute sessions in a single day, your mind will tire by the third round — and that round decides the outcome.

How to think:

1. Choose a new problem — one you haven’t seen, from your weak patterns.
2. Set the timer to 45 minutes. Start a screen recording (with audio).
3. Keep talking the whole time. Staying silent is the biggest mistake — the interviewer needs to see your thinking.
4. State the brute-force approach first, no matter how naive it looks. Optimization follows from that.
5. Before you start coding, get the approach confirmed. Jumping straight into code can waste 20 minutes on the wrong path.
6. At the end, test yourself — one normal case and one edge case. Don’t wait for the interviewer to ask.
7. Review (15-20 min): watch the recording, write down three things — where you were silent, where you needed a hint, whether the complexity analysis was correct.
8. Log every mock. After a week, redo the same problem — this shows retention, not just first-try success.
where: 15-20 min after · space: write down gaps

qa.q: How do you choose mock problems?
qa.a: Draw from your weakest patterns — the ones you mark 😰 in confidence scores. Rotate: one mock from a weak area, one from a strong area. Repeat the same problem a week later to measure retention, not just first-try success.

qa.q: What should the review focus on?
qa.a: Three things: (1) silence — where did you stop talking? (2) the moment you reached for hints — could you have pushed through? (3) correctness of your complexity analysis. Each mock should fix ONE concrete habit, not just 'do better'.

system-design.name: System Design Basics
system-design.desc: Design a large system in 45 minutes: requirements → estimations → data model → API → components → deep dive. For DSA interviews, a basic framework beats memorized systems — know URL shortener, rate limiter, and chat app cold.
system-design.q: What's the difference between a senior and mid design interview?
system-design.qsub: When do you choose a queue over synchronous calls? · What does 'eventually consistent' mean for a feed? · How do you estimate storage for 100M users?
system-design.what:
Imagine the interviewer says “design a URL shortener” and you immediately start writing the database schema. Five minutes later they ask “what's the scale?” — and you have no answer.

The biggest risk in a system design round is improvising. Something important gets missed every time, and it’s different each time.

The cure is a framework that you apply to every question, whatever the topic:

Requirements → Estimations → Data model → API → Components → Deep dive.

It doesn’t make you smarter — it stops you from forgetting things. And the interviewer sees that you are breaking a vague problem down methodically.

And one more thing: there is no single correct answer here. You don’t get points for the answer — you get points for discussing trade-offs. “I chose this, its downside is X, and in this case that downside is acceptable.”
system-design.analogy:
A wedding planner doesn’t jump straight to decoration.
First how many people and what budget (requirements), then how large the venue is (estimation), then who sits where (data model), then move on to stage and catering details (deep dive).
Following the order lets any large event run without chaos — and skipping it makes even a small one go wrong.
system-design.why:
In senior and staff rounds, system design makes up 40-60% of the onsite. Mid-level candidates now also have one round.

And this is a completely different skill from DSA. In DSA there is a single correct answer; here there isn’t. In DSA you solve a problem; here you drive the conversation.

The difference between mid and senior also shows up here: a mid-level candidate needs prompts (“and caching?”, “what if it fails?”), while a senior candidate raises those points on their own and discusses trade-offs.

And a practical tip: memorize three reference systems cold — URL shortener, rate limiter, chat app. Most questions are built from these building blocks (hashing, sharding, queue, fan-out, websocket, cache).

How to think:

1. Requirements (5 min). Both functional and non-functional. Also trim the scope — “I’ll leave analytics out for now; I’ll add it later if time permits.”
2. Estimations (5 min). DAU × requests ÷ 86,400 = QPS. Peak = 2-3×. Storage = size × count. State numbers out loud — this is where most people stumble.
3. Data model (5 min). Which entities, which indexes, SQL or NoSQL — and why.
4. API (5 min). Two-three endpoints are enough. What goes in, what comes out.
5. Components (10 min). Boxes and arrows. Client → LB → service → cache → DB. Use a queue when work can be asynchronous.
6. Deep dive (15 min). Pick one difficult part — hot key, ID generation, consistency, fan-out. Choosing a trivial part is the biggest mistake.
7. For every major choice also mention its downside. This habit can change the whole round.
where: Req → Est → Data → API → Comp → Dive · space: ~10 min each

qa.q: What's the difference between a senior and mid design interview?
qa.a: Seniors are expected to drive the conversation and handle trade-offs — consistency vs availability, caching strategy, failure modes — without being fed prompts. A clear framework + explicit trade-off reasoning is what separates the two.

qa.q: How deep should estimations go?
qa.a: One or two levels: daily active users × requests per user → QPS; storage per item × items → total. Exact numbers matter less than the reasoning chain and order-of-magnitude sanity (thousands vs billions).

spaced-repetition.name: Spaced Repetition & Review
spaced-repetition.desc: Revisit every problem you got wrong across phases 0-8 at increasing intervals: next day, 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks. Re-solve WITHOUT looking at old notes. This converts 'I've seen this' into 'I can solve this cold'.
spaced-repetition.q: Why spaced repetition and not mass review?
spaced-repetition.qsub: How do you decide a problem 'graduated'? · What do you do with a problem that keeps failing? · How many problems should be in the active review queue?
spaced-repetition.what:
You solved a hard DP problem. You understood the solution and felt good about it. Three weeks later the same problem appears — and you get stuck again.

This is normal. The brain discards anything it doesn’t use, and the forgetting pattern is predictable.

Spaced repetition exploits that predictability: re-solve each wrong problem at increasing intervals — next day, then after 3 days, then after 1 week, then after 2 weeks. Each time you review just when you were about to forget, the memory becomes stronger.

And the most important rule: don’t open your old note and read it. Solve from zero first. Open the note afterward — to compare, not to prompt you.

Because reading is only recognition (“yes, I’ve seen this”), while solving is recall. Interviews measure the latter.
spaced-repetition.analogy:
Think of a gym log. Lift a weight once and stop — after two weeks your strength is back where it started.
But lift the same weight at increasing intervals repeatedly (tomorrow, then three days later, then a week later) — and that strength stays permanently.
Miss a day? Then shorten the interval again. That’s it.
spaced-repetition.why:
The interviewer doesn’t ask this directly — but the result is obvious. When you read a problem and instantly think “this is a sliding-window” without analysis, that’s the outcome of spaced repetition.

The first and most important step in an interview is recognizing the pattern. If you spend five minutes on that, writing the full solution in 45 minutes becomes hard.

It also saves time. Solving 300 problems is less effective than mastering 150 problems you can actually solve. People who do 300 still go blank in interviews — because they never practiced recall.

How to think:

1. Every day log any problem you got wrong, needed a hint, or found very hard, with today’s date.
2. Next day: re-solve it. Without looking at the note. Try from zero first.
3. If you solve it cleanly (within the time, without hints), increase the interval — 3 days.
4. If you get stuck, bring the interval back to 1 day. No shame — the system is built for exactly this.
5. Ladder: 1 day → 3 days → 1 week → 2 weeks → graduate.
6. After solving, open your old note and compare — was the approach the same? Was there a better method?
7. Keep the queue under 10. If it grows, stop adding new problems and finish the backlog first.
8. Failing the same problem three times isn’t a problem with that problem — it’s a problem with the pattern. Review the topic again, then put it back in the queue.

qa.q: Why spaced repetition and not mass review?
