qa.a: Forgetting curves are predictable — revisiting right before you'd forget strengthens the memory most efficiently. Spaced intervals beat re-solving everything in one weekend both for retention and for time budget.

qa.q: Why re-solve before reading your own notes?
qa.a: Reading your solution first tests recognition, not recall — you'll nod along without being able to reproduce it. Re-solving cold forces retrieval, which is what an interview measures. The note becomes the comparison, not the prompt.

behavioral.name: Behavioral Prep (STAR)
behavioral.desc: 5 polished STAR stories (Situation, Task, Action, Result): toughest challenge, team conflict, failure + lesson, mentoring/leading, and a data-driven decision. Numbers and ownership language turn a story into a signal.
behavioral.q: What makes a STAR story strong vs generic?
behavioral.qsub: How do you answer 'tell me about a failure' without sounding bad? · What's a good question to ask the interviewer? · How do you handle behavioral questions in a system-design round?
behavioral.what:
Imagine the interviewer asks: “Tell me about a time you had a disagreement with a teammate.” You ramble for five minutes — no clear situation, no clear result. All the interviewer sees is that you can’t explain your work clearly.

STAR is a framework that turns your real experience into a tight 2-3 minute story:

Situation — where, when, what the context was (20%)
Task — what your responsibility was (10%)
Action — what you did, and why (60%)
Result — what happened, with numbers (10%)

The idea isn’t to create something new. The idea is to frame what you actually did so the interviewer clearly sees what you thought and what you did.

Two things make a big difference: use “I” instead of “we”, and include a number in the result.
behavioral.analogy:
Think of a good wedding speech: first the context (how you met), then the challenge, then what happened, and end with a clear toast.
The speech that jumps straight to the result feels empty; the one that wanders in details without a point feels boring.
STAR simply keeps the story in that tight shape.
behavioral.why:
The behavioral round is the first 30 minutes of every onsite — and that round creates the first impression that lasts the rest of the day.

Interviewers use it because coding skill and teamwork are two different things. They want to see how you actually handle conflict, failure, and ambiguity — not hypothetically.

And this is the round that candidates prepare the least for. So a small amount of effort here yields the biggest return. Even good engineers appear vague or defensive without prepared stories when a pressure question comes up.

In large companies, leveling also shifts based on this round — the language of scope, ownership, and impact is heard here.

How to think:

1. Choose five stories from your career — the toughest project, a team conflict, a mistake and the lesson, a time you taught or led someone, and a data-driven decision.
2. Write each in STAR format. Action should be the longest — that’s where your decisions show.
3. Include a number. Not “it got faster” — “p95 latency dropped from 800 ms to 120 ms”. If no number, describe the before-and-after difference.
4. Say “I”. Give team credit in a separate line, but keep your contribution clear.
5. Rehearse out loud and record. Reading in your head isn’t enough — speaking reveals where you wander.
6. Keep it 2-3 minutes. If it’s long, trim it. The interviewer will ask for more if needed.
7. “Why this company” prepared in three lines — what they do (specific), why you like it, and what you’ll bring.
8. Prepare two questions for them. “No questions” is a bad signal.
where: S → T → A → R · space: 60/20/10 ratio on A
out loud, 3+ times · space: record yourself

qa.q: What makes a STAR story strong vs generic?
qa.a: Specificity and ownership. Use real numbers, name the tools, and make the interviewer feel YOUR contribution — not 'we'. The Action step should be the longest and show your decision-making, and the Result should be measurable.

qa.q: How do you prepare for 'why this company'?
qa.a: Three sentences: what they do (specific, not a tagline), why that excites you (tie to your experience), and what you'd bring (one concrete skill). Memorable, rehearsed, and adaptable to the interviewer's team.

platforms.name: Practice Platforms
platforms.desc: Where to grind: neetcode.io for pattern-based roadmaps, LeetCode weekly contests for speed under pressure, and Pramp/interviewing.io for free peer mocks. Use each for its strength.
platforms.q: NeetCode vs LeetCode Top 150 vs Grind 75 — how to choose?
platforms.qsub: How many problems a day is sustainable? · When do you use company-tagged problem sets? · What role do editorial videos play (and when do they hurt)?
platforms.what:
Say you started doing random LeetCode problems — sometimes easy arrays, sometimes hard graphs. After two months your problem count has gone up, but nothing feels solid.

The issue isn’t the platform. The issue is that an interview demands three different things, and no single place provides all three:

1. Pattern recognition — the moment you read a problem you should think “this is a sliding-window”. That comes from neetcode.io, because the problems are organized by pattern, not by topic.

2. Speed — solving while the clock is running. That comes from LeetCode contests. One per week, 90 minutes, and the real benefit is in the post-contest review.

3. Coding in front of a person — that only comes from peer mocks like Pramp or interviewing.io. Test cases don’t judge you; a human does.

And one tip that saves a lot of time: which list you pick matters the least. NeetCode 150, Grind 75, Top Interview 150 — about 80 % of the problems overlap. The real decision is to pick one list and finish it.
platforms.analogy:
In the gym, different machines build different things — treadmill for stamina, weights for strength, and a sparring partner for the feel of a real fight.
Running on the treadmill for three months won’t teach you a punch.
And switching to a new gym every week prevents progress on any machine.
platforms.why:
Most people waste time here — they keep changing the roadmap, increase the count with easy problems, and think they’ve learned by watching solution videos.

None of that resembles an actual interview.

People especially skip contests because they’re uncomfortable — and that is their real value. In a contest you see a new problem with the clock ticking, exactly like an interview. Rank is meaningless; the review of the problems you failed is everything.

And peer mocks: coding aloud in front of a stranger feels very odd the first time. After the fourth or fifth mock it becomes normal — and that’s the difference you’ll see in a real interview.

How to think:

1. Pick one list — NeetCode 150 is good because it’s organized by pattern. Work through it in order, not jumping around.
2. Solve 2-3 problems daily. Anything more isn’t sustainable, and you need time for review.
3. Spend 20-30 minutes on each problem yourself first. Only after that look at the solution.
4. One contest per week. Full 90 minutes. Forget the rank — review which problems you missed and why.
5. One peer mock per week (Pramp is free). Being the interviewer teaches you as much as being the candidate.
6. When to start contests? When you can solve medium problems comfortably without a timer. Before that, contests only demotivate.
7. Company-tagged problems should be done 2 weeks before the onsite. Doing them earlier has no benefit.
8. Don’t watch an editorial video before you’ve attempted the problem; watch it after you’ve written your own solution.

qa.q: NeetCode vs LeetCode Top 150 vs Grind 75 — how to choose?
qa.a: They overlap heavily. Pick ONE structured list (NeetCode 150 is well-organized by pattern) and work it in order. The list matters less than consistent pattern-to-problem mapping and spaced review. Contests add the pressure dimension.

qa.q: When should you start contests?
qa.a: When you can solve mediums untimed consistently — contests measure speed, and speed without correctness is noise. One contest a week is enough; the real value is the post-contest review of problems you failed.

backtracking.name: Backtracking
backtracking.desc: Systematic exhaustive search over choices: make a choice, recurse, then UNDO it. One template covers subsets, permutations, combinations, and board search. Prune early to avoid exploring dead branches.
backtracking.q: What's the ONE template behind all backtracking?
backtracking.qsub: When is backtracking the right tool vs DP? · How do you prune board search (Word Search) early? · Why must you copy the path before pushing it?
backtracking.what:
Some questions don’t ask “what’s the best” — they ask “list all possibilities”. All subsets, all permutations, all valid boards. There’s no shortcut here — you have to examine everything. The only requirement is to look methodically and abandon wrong paths early.

Backtracking has three steps, and only three:

1. Choose — pick an option and put it into path.
2. Explore — recurse on the remaining decisions.
3. Unchoose — remove that option (path.pop()).

The third step is the real one. If you don’t remove it, the next branch will start with leftover garbage from the one you just explored — and the answers will be wrong. That’s the most common backtracking bug.

And one thing that turns a mediocre solution into a good one: pruning. As soon as a branch is guaranteed to fail, return there — the entire sub-tree is saved.
backtracking.analogy:
While walking through a maze, leave a chalk mark at every turn.
Hit a dead-end? Come back and erase your mark — otherwise the next time you walk that path you’ll think you’ve already been there.
Erasing the mark is exactly path.pop().
backtracking.why:
This is the single key for an entire family. Subsets, Subsets II, Permutations, Permutations II, Combination Sum I/II/III, Palindrome Partitioning, Letter Combinations, N-Queens, Sudoku Solver, Word Search — all share the same three lines. Only pruning and the base case differ.

That’s why mastering it gives a huge return. Nail one template and a dozen interview questions open up.

And the interviewer also checks whether you can state the complexity honestly. Saying O(n × 2ⁿ) — and understanding that the n factor comes from copying the answer — this small detail makes a big difference.

How to think:

1. Ask: what are the choices at each step? And when should you stop?
2. Keep a path array that stores the choices made so far.
3. Base case: Is the path complete? Then res.push([...path]) — copy it, otherwise all entries become references to the same (empty) array.
4. For each choice three lines: push → recurse → pop.
5. Prevent repeats: In combinations increment the start index; in permutations use a used[] array.
6. Duplicates: First sort, then if (i > start && a[i] === a[i-1]) continue.
7. Prune: Sum exceeds target? Board invalid? return there — the entire remaining sub-tree is saved.

qa.q: What's the ONE template behind all backtracking?
qa.a: Choose → explore → unchoose. Build the answer incrementally, recurse on the remaining decisions, then undo the last choice so sibling branches start from the same state. Subsets, permutations, combinations, and board search all fit it — only the pruning differs.

qa.q: How do you avoid duplicates (Subsets II, Permutations II)?
qa.a: Sort the input first, then skip a value when it equals the previous one AND the previous occurrence wasn't used at this level: if (i > start && nums[i] === nums[i-1]) continue. This prunes sibling branches that would produce identical results.

greedy.name: Greedy
greedy.desc: Make the locally optimal choice at each step, hoping it yields the global optimum. Greedy only works when a proof (or strong intuition) shows local choices can't block a better global outcome. Interval scheduling and jump-game are the classics.
greedy.q: How do you know a greedy is correct?
greedy.qsub: Why does sorting by end maximize non-overlapping intervals? · When does the two-pointer greedy fail? · How would you disprove a greedy with a counterexample?
greedy.what:
Greedy means: at each step take the choice that looks best right now, and never look back. No table, no recursion — the job is done in one pass.

When it works it's the cleanest and fastest solution. There's only one problem: it often doesn't work, and when it doesn't, no error appears — the answer is simply wrong.

So the real work of greedy isn't writing code, it's deciding whether greedy will work.

There are two ways. Exchange argument: suppose the optimal answer did something else at the first step — now swap it for the greedy choice. If the answer never gets worse, greedy is right. Or a counterexample: find one small input where greedy fails. Found it? Then greedy won't work — reach for DP.
greedy.analogy:
You have a single hall and need to fit in as many meetings as possible during the day.
Instinct says take the one that starts first. Wrong — a meeting that starts at 9 am and ends at 6 pm would consume the whole day.
The correct rule is: take the one that finishes earliest. The sooner the hall becomes free, the more meetings can fit.
greedy.why:
Interviewers ask greedy problems because misusing greedy is such a common mistake. People apply a greedy approach to a DP problem, get 5 test cases passed, and then fail the hidden ones. They want to see whether you think first or just code straight away.

And when greedy is correct, it gives O(n log n) or O(n) where DP takes O(n²) — that’s a big difference.

Interval problems (Merge Intervals, Non-overlapping Intervals, Meeting Rooms) and reachability problems (Jump Game, Gas Station) are very common, and their intended solution is greedy.

A line that sounds great in an interview: “I first check whether greedy is safe — if an exchange argument works then greedy, otherwise DP.”

How to think:

1. Write the greedy rule — "at each step I will choose this".
2. Test it: run it by hand on 3-4 small inputs. Failed? Then you need DP — but you saved 20 minutes.
3. Prove it: exchange argument — replace the optimal solution’s first choice with yours and see if the answer gets worse.
4. The sort key is the most important. Non-overlapping intervals → sort by end. Merge intervals → sort by start. Doing the opposite breaks everything.
5. Keep a "best-so-far" variable — farthest reach (Jump Game), current end (scheduling), running sum (Gas Station).
6. Run it in a single pass. If you need to go back, greedy wasn’t applicable.
7. Complexity often becomes O(n log n) because of sorting.
where: O(n log n) or O(n) · space: O(n)

qa.q: How do you know a greedy is correct?
qa.a: Write the exchange argument: if the optimal solution does something different from the greedy at this step, swapping in the greedy choice never worsens the result. Interval scheduling's proof — replacing the first picked interval with the earliest-ending one always works — is the model to imitate.

qa.q: Greedy vs DP — how do you decide fast?
qa.a: If the 'locally best' choice always stays optimal regardless of future input → greedy. If later decisions can undo earlier ones, or the future depends on accumulated choices (subsets, paths) → DP. When unsure, a single counterexample settles it; DP is the safe fallback.

monotonic-stack-2.name: Monotonic Stack
monotonic-stack-2.desc: A stack that stays strictly increasing or decreasing. Pop elements that break the invariant, then push. Because each element pushes and pops once, it's O(n) — the answer to 'next greater/smaller' and 'largest rectangle' family problems.
monotonic-stack-2.q: When is the answer computed — push or pop?
monotonic-stack-2.qsub: How do you handle circular arrays (Next Greater II)? · What's the invariant that makes it O(n)? · Why store indices and not values?
monotonic-stack-2.what:
In Phase 1 we used a monotonic stack to extract the next greater. Here the same idea moves one step further — now we need both edges of each element, and from them we get an area or contribution.

Think of the Largest Rectangle in a Histogram. For each bar the question is: how far can this bar extend at its full height? The answer comes from two things — where the first smaller bar is on the left, and where the first smaller bar is on the right.

The monotonic stack provides both in a single pass. When an element pops, two facts become known at once: the current element is its right boundary, and after the pop the new top is its left boundary.

So the most important rule here is: the answer is formed on pop, not on push. Push is only bookkeeping.
monotonic-stack-2.analogy:
Stand in front of a building and ask how far its view extends.
The answer isn’t known until there is a taller building on each side.
The left side is already known. Once the right side appears, the whole calculation for that building is completed at once — and it is removed from the list.
monotonic-stack-2.why:
This whole family comes with a “hard” tag and follows a single trick — Largest Rectangle in Histogram, Maximal Rectangle, Sum of Subarray Minimums, Trapping Rain Water, Next Greater Element II.

The naive solution is O(n²) and will get TLE on large inputs. A monotonic stack gives O(n) — and being able to explain this difference is a big point in interviews.

It also teaches a mindset that is useful later: count each element’s contribution separately. In Sum of Subarray Minimums you don’t iterate over all subarrays — you ask each element, "for how many subarrays are you the minimum?" and that count comes from the boundaries.

How to think:

1. Decide whether the stack should be increasing or decreasing. For Largest Rectangle it is increasing (heights rise).
2. Push indices onto the stack, not values — you need positions to compute width.
3. For each new element: while the top of the stack violates the order, pop — and on each pop write the answer for that element.
4. Width formula: i - stack[top] - 1. Here stack[top] is the top after the pop — that is the left boundary.
5. Insert a -1 sentinel into the stack at the start — the if for the index-0 case resolves automatically.
6. At the end, pop any remaining elements — their right boundary is the end of the array. (Or append a 0 to the heights.)
7. Circular? Loop up to 2n and use index i % n, but only push during the first pass.

qa.q: When is the answer computed — push or pop?
qa.a: Compute on POP. When the current element pops a stack top, the current element IS the 'next greater' (or the right boundary for histograms) of the popped element. Pushing is just bookkeeping; the pop is where the information is revealed.

qa.q: Why does the histogram use a sentinel -1?
qa.a: The rectangle's width is i - leftBound - 1, where leftBound is the new stack top after popping. A -1 sentinel makes that formula work even when the popped bar's left bound is the array's very start — no special-casing index 0.

two-heaps.name: Two Heaps
two-heaps.desc: A max-heap for the smaller half and a min-heap for the larger half, balanced to a size difference of at most one. Gives O(log n) insert and O(1) median peek — the canonical answer for 'Find Median from Data Stream'.
two-heaps.qsub: How does sliding-window median use lazy deletion? · What breaks if the heaps use different comparators? · Why is low allowed to be one element bigger but not high?
two-heaps.what:
Numbers arrive one by one and after each new number we must immediately report the median. Sorting each time costs O(n log n) per query — wasteful. Keeping a sorted array and inserting also costs O(n) per insert because elements have to be shifted.

The trick is: don’t search for the median — keep it always at hand.

Split the data into two parts. The smaller half goes into a max-heap (so its largest element is on top), and the larger half goes into a min-heap (so its smallest element is on top). Keep the sizes of both heaps equal, or let low have one extra.

Now the median sits at the top of the two heaps — no search, O(1).

When inserting, perform a round-trip: always insert the new number into low, then move low’s max to high, then if high becomes larger move its min back to low. These three lines maintain both invariants (correct halves + balanced size) together.
two-heaps.analogy:
At a school assembly, split the children into two lines based on height — a short line where the tallest child stands at the front, and a tall line where the shortest child stands at the front.
To find the class’s “middle height”, you don’t need to look at the whole assembly — just look at the first child of each line.
When a new child arrives, put them into one line and rebalance the lines — that’s it.
two-heaps.why:
Find Median from Data Stream is a classic hard question that appears in Amazon, Google, and Microsoft. And Sliding Window Median is its even harder sibling.

But the bigger insight is: don’t keep searching for something you need repeatedly — keep it as an invariant of your data structure. This same idea appears in LRU cache, sliding window maximum, and many design questions.

It also shows that you can think with streaming data — in real systems data keeps arriving (stock prices, latency metrics, sensor readings) and re-sorting everything is impossible.

How to think:

1. Create two heaps — low = max-heap (smaller half), high = min-heap (larger half).
2. Insert (three lines, always this order):
  low.push(num)
  high.push(low.pop())
  if (high.size > low.size) low.push(high.pop())
3. This round-trip guarantees both things at once — the halves are correct and the size is balanced. No need for separate if statements.
4. Median: sizes equal? → (low.top + high.top) / 2. Otherwise → low.top.
5. Decide once that low will hold the extra element, not high. Then follow that rule throughout the code.
6. Sliding window median: Removing the element that leaves the window immediately is expensive — apply lazy deletion and keep separate size counters.

qa.q: Why does this stay balanced?
qa.a: After every insert: add to low, move low's maximum to high, then if high is bigger move high's minimum back. That round-trip guarantees low always holds the smaller half and the halves differ by at most one — so the median is always at the two roots.

qa.q: What's the alternative to two heaps?
qa.a: A balanced BST (like a sorted array + binary search) also gives median, but array inserts are O(n). Two heaps make insert O(log n) and median O(1), which is why it's the accepted solution for streaming medians.

frequency-counting.name: Frequency Counting
frequency-counting.desc: Count how many times each value appears with a Map (or a 26-slot array for letters). Questions about "how many", "same letters" or "most common" become one O(n) pass.
frequency-counting.q: How do you check whether two words are anagrams in O(n)?
frequency-counting.qsub: Why a Map and not a nested loop? · When is a 26-slot array better than a Map? · Why does a Set not work here?
frequency-counting.what:
A tea-stall owner puts a tally mark in a notebook for every cup sold: one line for masala chai, one for ginger, one for plain. At closing time he does not recount the cups. He just reads the notebook.

Frequency counting is that notebook. Walk through the data once. For each value, read its count (or 0 if it is new), add 1, and store it back. A Map (or a plain object) is the notebook, and the values are the keys.

After one pass of O(n), a question like "how many times does a appear?", "which value is the most common?" or "do these two words use the same letters?" is answered in O(1) per lookup, with no new loop.
frequency-counting.analogy: The tally notebook at a tea stall. You do not recount the cups at night; you read the totals you kept while serving.
frequency-counting.why:
Counting is the first move in a large group of problems: anagrams, first unique character, top frequent elements, majority element, ransom note. They all start with "count everything once".

How to think: ask "do I need to know how many, or only whether I saw it?" If you need how many, use a Map. If you only need seen or not seen, a Set is enough.

When the keys come from a small fixed alphabet (like a to z), an array of 26 numbers is faster and uses O(1) space.
where: O(n) · space: O(k) for k distinct values

qa.q: How do you check that two words are anagrams in O(n)?
qa.a: Count the letters of the first word, then subtract one for each letter of the second. If the lengths match and no count goes below zero, they are anagrams. For lowercase letters, a 26-slot array gives O(1) extra space.

qa.q: When do you pick a Set over a Map?
qa.a: When you only need to know whether a value was seen. If the number of occurrences matters (anagram, most frequent, majority), you need a Map, because a Set forgets the counts.

fast-slow-pointers.name: Fast & Slow Pointers
fast-slow-pointers.desc: Two pointers move through a linked list at different speeds. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle, and if there is a cycle, fast catches slow. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
fast-slow-pointers.q: How do you find the middle of a linked list in one pass?
fast-slow-pointers.qsub: Why does fast move by 2 and not 3? · How do you detect a cycle without extra memory? · Which middle do you return for an even length?
fast-slow-pointers.what:
Two friends run on a track. One runs at normal speed, the other at double speed. On a straight road, the fast friend reaches the end exactly when the slow one is half way. On a circular track, the fast friend comes from behind and catches the slow one, so they must meet.

That is the whole idea. Start slow and fast at the head. In every step, slow moves one node and fast moves two. Keep looping while fast && fast.next both exist.

One loop gives two answers. When it ends, slow is the middle. And if the list has a cycle, slow and fast meet. There is no length counting, no second pass, and no extra memory.
fast-slow-pointers.analogy: A slow runner and a fast runner on the same track. On a straight road the fast one finishes when the slow one is at the halfway mark. On a circular track the fast one comes up from behind and catches the slow one.
fast-slow-pointers.why:
A linked list has no index, so you cannot jump to the middle. The slow way is to count the length first and walk again, which is two passes. For cycles, remembering every visited node in a Set costs O(n) memory. Fast and slow pointers fix both.

How to think: 1. Start both at head. 2. The loop condition is fast && fast.next, so you never read next of null. 3. For an even length, decide which of the two middles you want.
where: Nth node from the end (keep a gap of n)

qa.q: Why do fast and slow always meet inside a cycle?
qa.a: Once both are inside the loop, fast gains exactly one node on slow every step. The gap shrinks by 1 each step, so it must reach 0, and then they stand on the same node.

qa.q: Which middle do you get for an even-length list?
qa.a: With the condition fast && fast.next, slow stops on the second middle. To get the first middle, stop earlier with fast.next && fast.next.next.

top-k.name: Top-K Pattern
top-k.desc: To get the k largest (or k most frequent) items, keep a min-heap of size k. Push each item, and pop the smallest when the heap is bigger than k. O(n log k) time, O(k) space.
top-k.q: How do you find the k-th largest number without sorting everything?
top-k.qsub: Why a min-heap for the largest? · When is sorting still fine? · What changes for the k smallest?
top-k.what:
A cricket selector keeps the 11 best players. When a new player impresses, the selector compares him with the weakest of the 11. If the new one is better, the weakest leaves and the new one joins. The selector never sorts the whole country.

Top-k works the same way. Keep a min-heap of size k. Push each number. If the heap now has more than k numbers, pop the smallest. The heap always holds the k biggest numbers seen so far, and its top is the smallest of them, which is the k-th largest.

Each push or pop costs O(log k), so the whole scan costs O(n log k). Sorting costs O(n log n) and needs every number in memory.
top-k.analogy: A selector who keeps only the best 11 players and always compares a newcomer with the weakest of them. The weakest one is the one at the top of the min-heap.
top-k.why:
Top-k shows up all the time: top k frequent elements, k closest points, k-th largest element, a leaderboard that updates live. Once you see "the best k of many", think of a heap of size k.

How to think: 1. Say what you are keeping (the k best). 2. Ask who should leave first when the group is full (the worst of the k). 3. That "worst of the k" is the top of the heap, so pick the heap type that puts it on top: a min-heap for the largest, a max-heap for the smallest.
where: O(n log n) · space: O(1) to O(n)

qa.q: Why a min-heap to find the k largest?
qa.a: The top of a min-heap is the smallest of the kept numbers, so it is exactly the one to throw away when a bigger number arrives. What stays in the heap are the k largest. A max-heap of size k would keep the k smallest instead.

qa.q: When is simply sorting good enough?
qa.a: When the list is small, or you need the answer only once. A heap wins when k is much smaller than n, or when numbers keep arriving in a stream and you must always know the current top k.

cycle-detection.name: Cycle Detection
cycle-detection.desc: Find out whether a graph loops back on itself. Directed graph: DFS with three states (not visited, visiting, done). Undirected graph: a visited neighbour that is not your parent. O(V + E).
cycle-detection.q: How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph?
cycle-detection.qsub: Why is a visited set not enough? · How does an undirected graph differ? · How does this lead to Course Schedule?
cycle-detection.what:
On a road trip you drop a pebble at every junction on your current route. If you reach a junction that already has a pebble from this same route, you have driven in a circle. If the pebble is from an old route you already finished, that is fine.

This is cycle detection in a directed graph. Give every node one of three states: not visited, visiting (on the path you are walking now), or done (all its neighbours are fully explored). Meeting a visiting node means the path loops back: a cycle. Meeting a done node is safe.

In an undirected graph, every edge can be walked both ways, so the neighbour you came from is always visited. The rule changes to: a visited neighbour that is not your parent means a cycle. Both versions take O(V + E).
cycle-detection.analogy: A pebble at every junction on your current route. Meeting your own pebble means you drove in a circle. Meeting a pebble from a finished route means nothing.
cycle-detection.why:
Cycle detection answers a very practical question: "can this ever finish?" Course prerequisites, build order, deadlock between tasks. If the dependencies loop, nothing can start.

How to think: 1. Is the graph directed or undirected? 2. Directed: use three states, because "visited" alone gives a false cycle on a diamond. 3. Undirected: pass the parent along. 4. Start a DFS from every node, because the graph may have separate parts.

qa.q: Why is a plain visited set not enough in a directed graph?
qa.a: A node can be reached by two different paths without any loop (a diamond: 0 to 1 and 2, both to 3). The second arrival finds the node already visited, which looks like a cycle but is not. You must know whether the node is on the current path.

qa.q: How does cycle detection in an undirected graph differ?
qa.a: The edge you just used shows up again from the other side, so meeting your parent is normal. A real cycle is a visited neighbour that is not your parent. Union-Find also works: an edge between two nodes already in the same set closes a cycle.
